title: Nebraska Supreme Court judge rejects Democratic objection to new party’s Senate candidate
description: LINCOLN — A Nebraska Supreme Court judge rejected a last-minute objection from the state’s Democratic Party to the Senate candidacy of the chairwoman of the new Nebraska Working People Party. Supreme Court Justice Stephanie Stacy reaffirmed state Secretary of State Bob Evnen’s decision to allow Robin Richards to run as the Senate nominee for the […]
text:
The seal of the Nebraska Supreme Court. May 4, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A Nebraska Supreme Court judge rejected a last-minute objection from the state’s Democratic Party to the Senate candidacy of the chairwoman of the new Nebraska Working People Party.
Supreme Court Justice Stephanie Stacy reaffirmed state Secretary of State Bob Evnen’s decision to allow Robin Richards to run as the Senate nominee for the Nebraska Working People Party. The Democratic Party objected because she had been a Democratic write-in candidate for Legislative District 12 this spring. 
Stacy, in her order, said the Democratic Party’s interpretation of state law that determines who can be on the general ballot is wrong. 

“In other words, the statute is permissive; it explains ways other than the primary-election process that a voter “may” appear on the ballot. What it does not do is exclude other routes to the general election ballot.” Stacy wrote. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This short legal fight is the latest in a laundry list of lawsuits that ended up in Nebraska’s high court this midterm cycle. The Nebraska Working People Party and America First Party had to fight in court to exist after facing lawsuits from the state’s Democratic and Republican parties. 
The Democratic Senate candidate, Cindy Burbank, had to appeal to the Supreme Court to stay on the ballot in the May primary. She then faced another lawsuit after she dropped out for Osborn, as the loser of the Democratic Senate primary wanted to force the party to replace her. 
The deadline to certify the ballot is Sept 11. 
So far, the Senate field has five candidates. The main two are nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn and incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts. The others are Legal Marijuana NOW’s Mike Marvin, who suspended his campaign but will still appear on the ballot; Richards; and America First Party candidate Chuck Conboy. 
Nebraska Democrats worked to clear the field for Osborn throughout the cycle. 
The general election is Nov 3.

title: Most Nebraska GOP officeholders, candidates skip midterm convention
description: LINCOLN —  Among Nebraska politicians, only U.S. Rep. text:
Cutouts of President Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance at the Nebraska Republican Party booth at the Nebraska State Fair on Aug 29, 2025. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN —  Among Nebraska politicians, only U.S. Rep. Adrian Smith and GOP nominee for Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District Brinker Harding are going to Texas for the first-ever GOP midterm convention. 
National Republicans and President Donald Trump aim to use the event to highlight achievements from the first two years of Trump’s second administration, as well as draw a contrast with what they call Democrats’ “extreme” positions — a strategy that Nebraska 2nd District voters have gotten a taste of. 
Smith, who represents Nebraska’s 3rd Congressional District, plans to go, according to Chris Peterson, his campaign manager. Smith’s district includes central and western Nebraska and much of the state’s northeastern and southeastern edges. It’s considered one of the nation’s most conservative districts. He is facing four candidates trying to beat him in November. 
A campaign person told the Examiner that Omaha City Councilman Brinker Harding plans to attend. 
Harding is looking to defend the swing district, which includes all of Douglas and Saunders Counties and a significant slice of western suburban and rural Sarpy County, against Democratic candidate Denise Powell for House Republican as Rep. Don Bacon is retiring. 
Bacon told the Examiner he will be in Ukraine. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Trump and Vice President JD Vance are set to give keynote addresses at the two-day affair in Dallas, with several Republican candidates and leaders also scheduled to speak. No Nebraska candidates or elected officials are scheduled to speak.
More than 100 Republican House members and candidates are expected to be in Dallas, according to the AP. Politico reported that 70 GOP candidates and members planned not to go or were still deciding whether to attend the event, informally dubbed “Trumpapalooza.” 
The same Politico story said members were being asked to donate at least $25,000 to go. The event comes as Election Day is less than 60 days away. Midterm elections are typically an uphill battle for the party that controls the White House. Trump’s latest approval rating is at 32%, a new low. 
Nebraska Rep. Mike Flood won’t attend because of meetings and events, including his son’s high school football game, in the 1st Congressional District, according to a spokesperson. 
The 1st District comprises 12 counties and includes heavily Democratic Lincoln, as well as more conservative smaller cities and rural areas. Flood is running against Democratic challenger Chris Backemeyer and two other candidates.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen isn’t going to the convention, according to his spokesperson. Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers also will not go, citing government business, according to a campaign spokesperson. 
U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer won’t go as she had previously scheduled a trip related to her work on the Senate’s Armed Services Committee, according to her office. 
The campaign for Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts hasn’t responded to a request for comment on whether he plans to go to the convention. Ricketts is in a heated race against registered nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn. 
Democrats plan to have their own counterprogramming for the event. 
The general election is Nov. 3.

title: New Mexico sues feds over refusing to reimburse state for $61M in wildfire costs
description: New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Tuesday announced that her office had sued the Federal Emergency Management Agency for failing to reimburse the New Mexico National Guard for at least $61 million in costs it incurred fighting a 2022 wildfire that the federal government inadvertently ignited.
text:
New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Sept. 8, 2026, announced that her office had sued the Federal Emergency Management Agency for refusing to reimburse the New Mexico National Guard for costs related to the 2022 Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Tuesday announced that her office had sued the Federal Emergency Management Agency for failing to reimburse the New Mexico National Guard for at least $61 million in costs it incurred fighting a 2022 wildfire that the federal government inadvertently ignited.
The 2022 Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire burned a roughly 534-square-mile area in northern New Mexico after two federal prescribed burns escaped containment lines and merged into the state’s biggest-ever wildfire. 
Congress later that year approved a multi-billion-dollar compensation program for families, businesses and government agencies that suffered losses or incurred costs while responding to the blaze. They also tasked FEMA with overseeing the compensation fund. 
New Mexico governor preparing FEMA lawsuit over outstanding $445M wildfire claim 

But New Mexico, which has filed a claim for damages from the fire, has not received reimbursement for costs related to the National Guard, which deployed to the area in 2022 to help people safely flee the fire, remove debris and prevent flood damage. The FEMA Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire Claims Office, which is tasked with distributing the $5.5 billion compensation fund, has instead twice denied the state’s claims for the National Guard, the governor’s office said Tuesday. 
“It’s unconscionable that FEMA refuses to pay for a National Guard response that must continue for many years due to federal negligence,” Lujan Grisham said in a statement Tuesday. 
Spokespersons for FEMA or the claims office did not immediately respond to SourceNM’s request for comment late Tuesday. The lawsuit itself was also not immediately available in a federal court record system. 
In addition to the $61 million in National Guard costs, the state has 22 other claims pending before the FEMA office. In total, the state is seeking $128 million in compensation from the claims office, according to the governor’s office.
As of Aug. 31, the office had distributed roughly $3.8 billion from the fund, according to the latest figures from FEMA.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Scanlon: CT fiscal guardrail reform could help address special education crisis
description: Comptroller Sean Scanlon said Tuesday that CT can help address a special education funding crisis and still shrink its pension debt.
text:
Special education programs face a funding crisis this year that cannot be solved unless Connecticut reforms controversial state budget caps that have diverted billions of dollars to pay down pension debt, Comptroller Sean Scanlon said Tuesday.
The state’s chief fiscal watchdog, who is involved with two analyses of how Connecticut funds local schools and other municipal services, estimated special education services will cost $96 million more than their available resources.
“The way that we fund education generally, and specifically special education, is very broken,” Scanlon, a Guilford Democrat, said during his monthly media briefing on state fiscal and economic issues. “I think you’ve seen report after report showing that year after year — and yet nothing changes.”
The special education funding crisis is happening even after Gov. Ned Lamont and the Democratic-controlled General Assembly used emergency procedures last spring to exceed the state’s chief budget cap to send an extra $183 million to local schools and another $100 million in general aid to cities and towns.
But Lamont, a fiscally moderate Democrat, wouldn’t consent to legislators’ requests to make that an ongoing exception.
In other words, lawmakers were allowed to exceed the cap once. But if they want to maintain those payments 12 months from now, they will have to cut spending elsewhere or seek gubernatorial permission for another exception.
But Scanlon and other education advocates say the special education crisis facing local schools won’t be solved in one year.
Nearly one in five Connecticut students, 19.1%, was identified as having a learning disability in the 2025-26 academic year, Scanlon reported, citing data from the state Department of Education. It was less than 15% just eight years ago.
Those numbers are rising, partly because some local educators have gotten better at identifying students in need, said Fran Rabinowitz, executive director of the Connecticut Association of Public School Superintendents.
But the biggest driver of those numbers, she added, is a dearth of intervention services that could identify and address students’ learning challenges early — averting the need for special instruction entirely.
“We don’t have a robust system of intervention in many of our districts,” Rabinowitz said.
Lisa Hammersley, executive director of the School and State Finance Project, said “districts are at a breaking point” trying to cover special education costs.
Federal law mandates districts provide special services that some children need. State government will send $221 million to districts through its chief special education grant this fiscal year, leaving cities and towns to grapple with billions of dollars in additional expenses.
Scanlon has spent the past year working with a bipartisan panel of 14 mayors and first selectmen to examine Connecticut’s heavy reliance on municipal property taxes to fund many public services, not just education. He also has been assisting a 100-member citizens’ assembly tasked this summer by the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities with undergoing a similar review.
The comptroller said Tuesday the state can do little to help communities solve a special education crisis until it reviews state budget caps, labeled “fiscal guardrails” by supporters, that have forced unprecedented surpluses since 2017.
Lawmakers created one “guardrail” that has removed huge chunks of income and business tax receipts from the budget — without first studying how much would likely be removed or the ramifications for programs.
In the two decades prior, the average state budget closed with a surplus equal to one-tenth of 1% of the General Fund. In the nine years under the “guardrails,” the average surplus is nearly 9%.
The bulk of those captured funds have been used to pay down Connecticut’s considerable pension debt, which still exceeds $30 billion, and to build a record-setting $4.5 billion rainy day fund.
After initially resisting most efforts to modify these caps, Lamont has compromised with Democratic legislators over the past two years to divert more dollars for education, healthcare, social services and municipal aid, though many lawmakers argue the system still is heavily skewed in favor of saving and paying down pension debt.
Lamont’s budget spokesman, Chris Collibee, noted the governor formed his own working group this year to study education issues, including special education costs. That panel, which includes many education advocates, is expected to issue recommendations when the 2027 General Assembly convenes in early January.
“As students’ needs evolve, the state’s approach to funding education must keep pace,” Collibee said.  “This review is an opportunity to ensure that state investments reach students where they are needed most and that every child, in every community, has access to a high-quality public education.”
Lamont’s GOP opponent, Sen. Ryan Fazio of Greenwich, says the governor has compromised far too much and needs to adhere strictly to the existing caps.
But Scanlon says Connecticut’s perspective has changed greatly, and the state can invest more in special education and other vital programs and still shrink pension debt.
The 2010s were marked by two of the largest state tax hikes in Connecticut history, a string of budget deficits and a sluggish economy.
Connecticut has chopped more than $11 billion off its pension debt since then and cut state income taxes in 2023.
Meanwhile, the coronavirus pandemic in the early 2020s dramatically increased demands for social services while placing strains on hospitals and other healthcare providers, problems that still exist today. And unprecedented cutbacks in human service programs are threatening thousands of Connecticut residents.
Connecticut has run up significant deficits in its Medicaid program in each of the past three fiscal years as demand has grown, and the Lamont administration reported $25 million in Medicaid cost overruns in July alone — the first month of the new fiscal year.
“We are in a significantly different situation, and yet the ‘guardrails’ are the same, Scanlon said. “I believe that [budget caps] need to be adapted to meet moment that we’re in.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: House panel takes no action on Oklahoma lawmaker’s alleged misconduct, sets another meeting
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — House lawmakers met behind closed doors for about eight hours Tuesday to review the findings of investigations into allegations of misconduct by an Oklahoma lawmaker but took no formal action.  Following allegations from House staff of “improper behavior” from Republican Rep. Danny Williams, chamber leadership ordered investigations and charg[...]
text:
House Sergeant Mark Ford, left, sits on a stool to prevent people from entering the hallway of the state Capitol near where the House Rules Committee met Sept. 8 to investigate Rep. Danny Williams. Tori Garrett, director of communications for the House Republican Caucus, stands to the right of the doorway. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — House lawmakers met behind closed doors for about eight hours Tuesday to review the findings of investigations into allegations of misconduct by an Oklahoma lawmaker but took no formal action. 
State Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, attends a special session of the state House at the Oklahoma Capitol on Oct. 3, 2023. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)
Following allegations from House staff of “improper behavior” from Republican Rep. Danny Williams, chamber leadership ordered investigations and charged the chamber’s Rules Committee with reviewing investigations into the claims and taking action, if necessary. The specifics of the allegations or investigations have still not been made public. 
Rep. Mike Osburn, R-Edmond, who leads the committee, said they have requested further information from House legal staff and plan to reconvene Thursday morning. 
“Today was an opportunity for members to examine the investigation, ask questions, hear directly from Rep. Williams and his counsel, and consider all the information available to us,” Osburn said following the meeting. 
Williams, R-Seminole, did not immediately return a phone call requesting comment Tuesday. He previously told a KFOR reporter that he was told not to publicly discuss the allegations. He said he didn’t remember what all the claims were but said they weren’t sexual in nature and denied any wrongdoing.
“I think after he read the summaries of the reports, and listened to the questions, and answered the questions, I think everybody’s pretty close on the same page,” Osburn said Tuesday. 
Williams and his counsel were before the Rules Committee for over an hour and he was given the opportunity to answer questions, Osburn said.
Rep. Mike Osburn, R-Edmond, applauds during the State of the State Address on Feb. 2, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)
Thursday’s meeting will begin behind closed doors, but if any formal action is taken it will happen during an open meeting, he said. 
“This is a personnel matter, and there’s a lot of confidential information that is being discussed,” Osburn said. “And so we feel at this point we need to keep it closed.”
If action is taken, it will require a vote of the full House, he said, but it could range from expulsion, to censure, to no action. 
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, informed lawmakers in a July 23 email that Williams was being investigated by a private, third party law firm following allegations of “improper behavior” toward chamber staff and that an internal HR investigation found “potential misuse of state resources.” 
Hilbert wrote that referring the matter to the Rules Committee follows House precedent from 2017, a year with multiple separate investigations into lawmakers that led to resignations, recommended sanctions and potential votes for expulsion. 
He also suspended Williams from his committees and moved his office at the Capitol.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Chesapeake Bay grasses notch best numbers since 2018
description: Aerial surveys show that underwater grasses in the Chesapeake Bay had a strong year in 2025, covering 89,385 acres, the most since 2018 and a 7% improvement over 2024. Despite the gains, some advocates said the results are a mixed bag.
text:
Brooke Landry, left, an SAV expert with Maryland's Department of Natural Resources who chairs the Chesapeake Bay program work group on underwater grasses, speaks with an attendee during a kayaking trip to the Susuqehanna Flats on July 24, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Aerial surveys show that underwater grasses in the Chesapeake Bay had a strong year in 2025, taking up the most acreage since 2018.
The numbers are a 7% improvement over 2024, covering 89,385 acres — just below a previous 2025 goal calling for 90,000 acres.
But since then, the goalposts have moved.
In December, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) and other bay governors signed a new pledge for the Chesapeake Bay. It calls for the bay states to achieve 196,600 acres of grasses across the entire bay — and maintain that number once they get there. But it stretches the agreement out, calling for 90,000 acres of submerged aquatic vegetation, or SAV, by 203o, 95,000 acres by 2035 and 100,000 acres by 2040.
Brooke Landry, the Maryland’s Department of Natural Resources bay grass expert, holds a flowering piece of stargrass during a Susquehanna Flats kayaking trip on July 24, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
In a news release Tuesday, Maryland officials touted a 13% increase in bay grasses in the Maryland portion of the Chesapeake Bay.
“More underwater grass means more habitat for blue crabs and fish, cleaner water, and a more resilient Chesapeake Bay,” Maryland Department of Natural Resources Secretary Josh Kurtz said in the release.
“This year’s increase is welcome progress, but it also reinforces the work ahead. We need to keep reducing pollution, protecting existing underwater grass beds, and restoring the shallow-water habitats that allow these plants and the Bay life that depends on them to thrive,” Kurtz said.
Brooke Landry, SAV program chief for Maryland DNR and chair of the Chesapeake Bay Program SAV Workgroup, called the 2025 numbers “especially encouraging” because “the gains were not confined to one place.”
Seven different Maryland river or bay segments met or exceeded their individual SAV restoration goals for 2025, including the Back River, the Upper Gunpowder and the Upper Chester. And on the Eastern Shore, eight rivers or river segments increased their SAV acreage by 50% or more, even though they did not meet their goals.
For freshwater grasses, it was a rebound after losses in 2023. And for moderately salt-tolerant grasses in the mid-bay, it was a rebound from 2024, according to the DNR news release. But this progress is fragile.
In Maryland’s mid-bay, for example, much of the grasses are made up of two species: sago pondweed and widgeon grass. The latter species can thrive in a variety of salinity types, but it is particularly vulnerable when other environmental conditions deteriorate, including water clarity, Landry said in the news release.
Submerged aquatic vegetation, or SAV, is visible from the surface on July 24, 2026 in the Susquehanna Flats, an underwater grass bed in the Chesapeake Bay near Havre de Grace. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
“These communities are dynamic: when light, salinity and other growing conditions align, species such as widgeon grass can spread quickly,” Landry said. “The flip side is that the same beds can decline just as quickly when conditions deteriorate.”
There were also areas of the bay that performed poorly in 2025’s study. Overall, the tidal fresh zone, which includes geographically isolated rivers and embayments, actually experienced a small decline in 2025, from 20,221 acres to 18,653 acres. Researchers at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science, which produces the annual study, noted particularly significant losses in Virginia’s Rappahannock River.
The survey’s overall gains also “mask troubling declines” in rivers such as the Patapsco, Gunpowder and James, read a news release from the nonprofit Chesapeake Bay Foundation, a leading bay advocacy group.
“Underwater grass gains across the Bay are welcome news, but Maryland’s rivers tell a more complicated story,” said Julie Luecke, the foundation’s Maryland coastal research scientist, in the release. “Declines in places like the Patapsco, Gunpowder, and Potomac show the pressure from polluted runoff and increasingly intense rainstorms.”
But the salty waters near the bay’s mouth had a second straight record-setting year, improving more than 11%. Researchers at VIMS believe this occurred because of improved water clarity in the lower bay.
“It’s been remarkable to watch how fast the lower Bay meadows are expanding right now,” said Christopher J. Patrick, associate professor and director of the SAV Program at VIMS. “It’s another example of how rapidly seagrass can recover when conditions are right and gives us hope that the ultimate seagrass restoration goals for the Chesapeake Bay remain achievable.”
Submerged aquatic vegetation, or SAV, is visible o rom above the water on July 24, 2026 in the Susquehanna Flats, an underwater grass bed in the Chesapeake Bay near Havre de Grace. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Former NC Gov. Pat McCrory works to overcome public suspicion of election results
description: Voters should be assured of the safeguards that produce accurate election results and of the professionalism of those responsible for correct counts, said former Republican Gov. Pat McCrory. To that end, McCrory, who is the North Carolina leader of a group called RightCount, invited reporters on his tour of the inner workings of the Wake […]
text:
Former Republican NC Gov. Pat McCrory(left), former Republican Wake Co. Sheriff Donnie Harrison (center), and James Hardaway, who works with veterans' nonprofits, on a Sept. 8, 2026 tour of the Wake County Board of Elections headquarters.  McCrory is working to build public confidence in election results. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)Voters should be assured of the safeguards that produce accurate election results and of the professionalism of those responsible for correct counts, said former Republican Gov. Pat McCrory.
To that end, McCrory, who is the North Carolina leader of a group called RightCount, invited reporters on his tour of the inner workings of the Wake County Board of Elections on Tuesday as staff prepares for the general election.
McCrory said transparency and education will help counter misinformation and build trust in results for both the public and candidates. 
“They’re only hearing what they want to hear to justify their position,” McCrory said. “All politicians who run for office, both Republicans and Democrats, are paranoid about this process. A lot of it is due to them even having a lack of understanding about the professionalism that you saw today and about the process you saw today.”
McCrory is speaking from experience. The former long-time mayor of Charlotte and North Carolina’s latest Republican governor was on the losing end of a close election when Democrat Roy Cooper defeated him by about 10,000 votes in his bid for a second term in 2016. McCrory led the vote count until ballots from Durham were added late on election night. 
At the time, McCrory claimed voter fraud, saying that election errors and illegal voters had changed the outcome of his election. But ten years later, he says suspicion about how the process works hurts democracy. 
“We need to bring back confidence in our democracy. And that comes from someone who was declared the winner one night and then…” McCrory said, before trailing off. 
“We need to overcome that suspicion for our democracy to be sustainable,” he said. “And that’s very important to me because I want to encourage people to vote and have confidence in their vote, and I want to encourage people to run.”
The visit fit in with the Wake election board’s outreach efforts.
In the shadow of the federal fight over absentee ballots, NC is ready to start mailing them out

“There’s a lot of information out there and people don’t know how it works,” said Olivia McCall, Wake’s election director. “They don’t understand that there’s checks and balances in place starting well before you ever vote.”
Several thousand precinct officials will be trained to work in Wake County this election season. The training room will become the “war room” on Election Day, with staff sitting by the phones starting at 5:30 am to troubleshoot any last-minute problems at polling sites. 
Bipartisan teams are now putting all voting machines through tests of their coding. 
After each election, every county also double-checks their machines’ accuracy by performing hand counts of two sample groups of ballots chosen by the state Board of Elections.  
James Hardaway, an Apex resident and U.S. Army veteran who is involved in veteran nonprofits, accompanied McCrory on the tour of Wake election headquarters. Hardaway completed his first poll worker training five years ago. 
“When I left my initial training five years ago, I was a little nervous, but as Election Day rolled around I was very prepared,” Hardaway said. “Now I’ve done that training every year since and they do a great job of ensuring that the poll workers, old and new, are all spun up on the new policies and new rules that come into effect.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Meta settlement money should be used to build something better for kids
description: South Dakota is set to receive at least $52.6 million from Meta, with the total potentially reaching $73.5 million. The money will be paid over the next decade because of the harm social media platforms have caused young people. Now comes the question that will determine whether this settlement changes their lives: What will South […]
text:
Facebook owner Meta agreed to pay nearly $18 billion to an array of U.S. states over claims its platforms intentionally addicted teens. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)South Dakota is set to receive at least $52.6 million from Meta, with the total potentially reaching $73.5 million. The money will be paid over the next decade because of the harm social media platforms have caused young people. Now comes the question that will determine whether this settlement changes their lives: What will South Dakota do with the money?
For years, the conversation about young people and social media has focused on what we should take away: phones during class, push notifications, harmful content, endless scrolling and screen time that turns 15 minutes into two hours before anyone notices. But if we are serious about helping young people, we cannot stop at telling them to put their phones down. We also have to give them something meaningful to step into when they do.
That means afterschool and summer programs, sports, arts, recreation, outdoor experiences, libraries, community centers, mentors, trusted adults, youth jobs, leadership opportunities and mental health support that young people can reach. These are sometimes treated as extras. They are instead part of the infrastructure of a healthy childhood and, in South Dakota, part of what allows families to work and communities to thrive.
South Dakota attorney general urges beefed-up consumer protection after $53 million Meta settlement

The problem is not a lack of interest. Young people want these opportunities, and families are looking for them. Too often, however, the opportunity is too expensive, too far away, already full or simply does not exist. A recent South Dakota report estimated that roughly 60,000 school-age children need afterschool or summer care, while only about 20,000 are currently being served. That leaves 40,000 young people without access to a program their families want or need.
Cost, location and transportation are among the biggest barriers, especially in rural and tribal communities, where the nearest option may be 30, 40 or even 60 miles away. A good program does not help a family if there is no open seat or no practical way for a child to get there.
The Meta settlement gives South Dakota an opportunity to close some of those gaps. It also gives us an opportunity to repeat old mistakes. Large tobacco and opioid settlements have shown how money intended to address a specific harm can be diluted, diverted or absorbed into unrelated spending when clear priorities and public accountability are missing. South Dakota should decide that this money will be different.
Before settlement dollars are spent, state leaders should establish a clear, public and youth-informed plan. The money should directly prevent, reduce and repair harms associated with social media while supporting healthy development. It should add to current investments, not replace funding for education, mental health, recreation, libraries or youth development elsewhere in the budget. The public should be able to see where the money goes, who benefits and what results are measured.
Young people and families should have a voice in those decisions alongside educators, mental health professionals, and organizations that serve youth. Leaders should pay close attention to communities with the fewest options, neighborhoods without safe gathering spaces and areas facing shortages of transportation, programming or mental health professionals.
South Dakota should resist spreading the money across a collection of short-term projects and calling the job finished. One-time grants can help, but lasting change requires capacity: trained and stable staff, more program slots, dependable transportation, safe facilities and stronger networks connecting families with care and opportunity. Fund IRL is a coalition working to ensure any payouts from current social media lawsuits help fund programs and services that promote youth wellbeing and healthy development. Its guidance offers a practical framework, calling for investment across a continuum that includes positive youth development, real-life alternatives, safer digital engagement and mental health services delivered through community organizations, schools and clinical settings.
No single program will meet every young person’s needs. A teenager might find belonging on a basketball court, confidence on a stage, purpose through a summer job or support from a counselor. What matters is that the opportunity exists and that they can reach it.
The goal cannot simply be fewer hours on a phone. It should be more hours spent building friendships, discovering talents, moving, creating, learning, working and being surrounded by adults who know a young person’s name and notice when they do not show up.
South Dakota has the chance to turn corporate accountability into real-life opportunity. Before the first dollars are spent, our leaders should commit to a transparent, youth-informed plan that invests in the programs, places, relationships and support young South Dakotans need to thrive. Money intended to repair harm to young people should reach young people. That is what real repair can look like.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Governor proposes 4.7% flat income tax rate
description: Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte announced Tuesday his administration will propose a 4.7% income tax rate, which drew immediate criticisms from Democrats. The state currently has a two-tiered, graduated income tax system that tops out at 5.4%. Many Montanans already have a 4.7% tax rate, which is the case for households filing jointly for taxable income […]
text:
Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte speaks during a Mountain States Policy Center event. CEO and President of the organization, Chris Cargill, stands to the side on Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026 in the Montana Capitol in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte announced Tuesday his administration will propose a 4.7% income tax rate, which drew immediate criticisms from Democrats.
The state currently has a two-tiered, graduated income tax system that tops out at 5.4%.
Many Montanans already have a 4.7% tax rate, which is the case for households filing jointly for taxable income of as much as $95,000. Montana has gone from seven tax brackets to two since Gianforte took office in 2021.
Earlier this year, a Montana Legislative Fiscal Division report said that a flat 4.7% income tax would reduce state tax collection by up to $130 million per year by 2029.
The governor announced the policy proposal at an event co-hosted with Mountain States Policy Center, a nonprofit research organization that’s part of the larger State Policy Network, a coalition of conservative think tanks. 
Gianforte said the move was driven by the state’s strong economy and a desire to bring more people and jobs to the state. Other states around Montana, including South Dakota and Wyoming, don’t have income taxes, with the governor saying that puts the state at a disadvantage. Idaho also has a flat-tax rate.
“It would provide certainty to Montanans as well as business owners looking to invest in our state and create jobs,” Gianforte said on Tuesday. “But what’s the real advantage of a flat tax? Once you get there, it’s really hard for future legislatures to raise it because they’ve got to raise it on everybody.”
Americans for Prosperity, a conservative political advocacy group partly backed by the Koch brothers’ fortune, has previously praised the state’s efforts to move to a flat tax.
In a message to those who oppose the flat-tax idea, Gianforte said that the hit to the budget will be mitigated by a disciplined budgeting practices.
“I know some opponents of this proposal, what they’re going to say, they say a flat, fair tax will harm the state budget,” Gianforte said. “To them I say, ‘Look at what we’ve done with our strong conservative budgeting.’”
The governor pointed to Montana’s fiscal health, which he said had moved from No. 22 in the nation to No. 8 according to Truth in Accounting, a tax-focused nonprofit connected to the Searle Freedom Trust, a former conservative grant-making foundation. He added “there’s just no way to tax your way to prosperity” and added prosperity happens with “lower taxes and common sense budgeting.”
State Democrats and the Montana Budget and Policy Center, which is a nonprofit focused on budget issues, opposed the idea and spoke out Tuesday. 
“This proposal is a $120 million tax break for the wealthiest income earners. If there’s one thing we have learned, it’s that trickle-down economics is a myth,” Rep. Mark Thane, a Missoula Democrat and the vice chair of the House Taxation Committee during the 2025 session, said in a new release. “The state is currently failing to honor the agreed upon 3% provider rate increase for Medicaid, jeopardizing our rural hospitals and healthcare providers. What have other states done when faced with revenue shortfalls? They instituted a statewide sales tax.”
Thane added that Democrats also would “never” support a statewide sales tax, which has been discussed among state Republicans heading into the 2027 legislative session.
Rose Bender, the director of research at the Montana Budget and Policy Center, said it was a giveaway to rich Montanans and would have little impact on most people. Analysis by the nonprofit says the top 20% wealthiest households will receive 95% of the income tax reductions. 
“When you look at the top 1% of those earning over $900,000 each year, they’re going to see over almost $9,000 in annual average tax cuts. So it’s a choice essentially to give $120 million more away each year in tax cuts for the wealthy,” she said.
Gianforte and Mountain States Policy Center CEO Chris Cargill promised more jobs. Cargill pointed to Janicki Industries moving to the state as one example.
“I think the fact that Montana has low electricity prices, lots of land value, and also makes it easy for businesses to open and operate here is very, very attractive for a lot of businesses who are out of state,” Cargill said, adding that in Jancki’s case, it was “because it thought the business environment in Washington was terrible” and that some tax changes in the Evergreen State are scaring away business.
Montana’s economy is also heavily tied to the real estate market and by gross domestic product, real estate has been Montana’s largest industry for about two decades and added $12.2 billion to the state GDP in 2025.
Bender said it left her wondering what the “end goal” of the tax cuts were.
“If this is a bid to be more competitive as a place for folks to move, I think we should look at what that is doing to housing costs in Montana, and what it means for affordability for folks already living here,” Bender said. “And what do Montanans actually want?”

title: Former Arkansas secretary of state hopeful removed from local Republican committee
description: A former candidate for Arkansas secretary of state is objecting after he was removed from his local Republican Party committee and accused of violating party rules. Bryan Norris, who lost the March runoff to state Sen. Kim Hammer, said the State Executive Committee of the Republican Party of Arkansas expelled him from the Independence County […]
text:
A van depicting language in support of a paper ballot initiative in Independence County is parked in Batesville on Oct. 30, 2024. (Mary Hennigan/Arkansas Advocate)A former candidate for Arkansas secretary of state is objecting after he was removed from his local Republican Party committee and accused of violating party rules.
Bryan Norris, who lost the March runoff to state Sen. Kim Hammer, said the State Executive Committee of the Republican Party of Arkansas expelled him from the Independence County GOP committee. Pulaski County Chairman Michael White said in a Facebook video he had also been expelled from the Pulaski County Republican Committee.  
Norris said in a news release Friday the complaint against him was filed in July and cited a lawsuit he filed over Independence County officials rescinding a voter-approved measure requiring elections to be conducted using hand-marked, hand-counted paper ballots.
The party also took issue with Norris for paying the filing fee of an individual who tried to join the Independence County GOP but withdrew his application after learning he lived outside the county, according to the news release.
UPDATED: Hammer wins Republican nomination for Arkansas secretary of state

Norris narrowly lost the GOP primary runoff to Hammer, who had the backing of top GOP officials and an outside group linked to Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ senior political adviser. His expulsion comes as Libertarian candidates are hoping to capitalize on rifts within the GOP in the midterm election.
Norris endorsed three Libertarian candidates for executive branch offices Thursday after his expulsion from the Independence County GOP. Another charge leading to his expulsion “was that he stated publicly that [Colt] Shelby, the Libertarian nominee for governor, will appear on the November ballot,” Norris’ news release states.
The party’s executive committee did not allow Norris to review the complaint against him and the evidence supporting the charges, he said. He also did not receive a hearing in his home county, and he said this was against the party’s rules.
The Arkansas Republican Party did not comment specifically about Norris or White, but said that “several” members were removed from local committees. The state  GOP said in an emailed statement Tuesday that it made “complete rules reviews” before the removals.
“Members of the party are expected to follow party rules and not work against the interests of the Republican Party,” according to the statement. “If party rules are broken, there will be accountability.”
In the past few days, Norris has expressed frustration via Facebook with the state party’s decision to punish him and White for their social media activity.
White said in his Facebook video that the Arkansas GOP claimed he “publicly showed favoritism” to Norris in a complimentary social media comment during the GOP secretary of state primary race.
Norris’ request for a recount in multiple counties did not change the results. A state judge in June dismissed Norris’ lawsuit challenging the election results.
The state GOP also took issue with White’s apparent support for Shelby’s candidacy against Sanders. White said in his video that posting a photo with Shelby online was not an endorsement.

text:
Soybeans and corn in central Iowa Sept. 8, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) With a statewide average weekly temperature of 79.8 degrees Fahrenheit, Iowa had one of its hottest starts to September on record, according to State Climatologist Justin Glisan.
The weekly average temperature was more than 11 degrees above the normal for the week, according to Glisan’s weekly weather report, which accompanies the state’s crop report. The National Weather Service reports that the hottest September on record in Iowa was in 1939, with triple-digit high temperatures on Sept. 3, 6, and 7.
According to U.S. Department of Agriculture figures in the report, there were no reports of harvested corn during the Aug. 31 through Sept. 6 reporting period, though corn maturity reached 17%. The percent of corn acres in this stage is behind last year’s crop by 7 percentage points and 2 percentage points behind the five-year average.
Corn in the dough stage reached 96% and corn in the dented stage, at 79%, is slightly ahead of the rates from last year and of the five-year average. Iowa’s corn crop continues to rate well, with 77% of the crop rated good or excellent, according to USDA. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Soybeans also rated well for the period – 75% good to excellent – and the crop was behind last year’s pace, with a reported 6% of soybeans dropping leaves as of the reporting period. 
The statewide average precipitation for the week was 0.37 inch, about half an inch below the normal. Northern Iowa received the majority of the showers for the week, which Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig said will “help chip away” at soil moisture deficits in the region. 
According to the latest maps from the U.S. Drought Monitor, all northwest Iowa is in abnormally dry or moderate drought conditions. 
“Farmers are busy chopping silage and preparing for harvest as we wait for corn and soybeans to dry down and fully mature,” Naig said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah should put a competency clock on AI adoption
description: Utah employers adopting artificial intelligence can measure almost everything about the technology: usage, speed, cost and output. They should also measure how quickly their people become independently capable. Utah’s apprenticeship system provides the model. Apprenticeship Utah describes an earn-and-learn structure that combines on-the-job learning with rel[...]
text:
Competency is a better measure of whether artificial intelligence is strengthening Utah’s workforce rather than merely speeding up today’s tasks. (Illustration by Alex Cochran for Utah News Dispatch)Utah employers adopting artificial intelligence can measure almost everything about the technology: usage, speed, cost and output. They should also measure how quickly their people become independently capable.
Utah’s apprenticeship system provides the model. Apprenticeship Utah describes an earn-and-learn structure that combines on-the-job learning with related classroom instruction. The state’s youth pathway, the Talent Ready Apprenticeship Connection, allows participants to combine high school, work with a partner employer and an Associate of Applied Science degree.
The common thread is progression. People do not become skilled merely by having access to a tool. They become skilled by practicing, receiving feedback and taking on more demanding work.
AI can speed that progression or quietly interrupt it.
The Stanford Digital Economy Lab’s August 2026 update found that the employment shortfall for workers ages 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations widened from 15% in the July 2025 data vintage to 19% by June 2026. That is not a 19% overall job-loss rate. The shortfall is relative to a counterfactual and appears mainly through weaker hiring in work where AI can automate tasks.
Many of those tasks were entry-level preparation. A junior employee summarized records, built a first spreadsheet, drafted a standard communication or assembled research. AI can now perform much of that quickly.
If the only metric is time saved, the organization may miss whether a beginner is learning less.
A competency clock makes the development visible.
Start it on the employee’s first day. Define a small set of milestones: verify an AI output against source material; identify a routine exception; explain why an apparently plausible answer is wrong; make a recommendation using incomplete information; handle a recurring decision without help; recognize when to escalate.
Then measure how long it takes the employee to achieve each milestone reliably.
AI should make the clock run faster. The tool can remove busywork, generate practice cases and free experienced employees from some documentation so they can coach. A new worker can spend more time near the edge of judgment rather than on mechanical preparation.
But if tool usage rises while the milestones take longer, management has a warning sign. The employee may be producing more without understanding more.
Utah’s apprenticeship model also shows why supervision matters. Young apprentices do not jump straight from instruction to independent responsibility. Their learning is connected to real work and an employer relationship. AI-era office roles need the same bridge.
A competency clock would change the question managers ask about AI. Instead of “How much did the tool save?” the question becomes “How much faster did this person become capable?”
That is a better measure of whether artificial intelligence is strengthening Utah’s workforce rather than merely speeding up today’s tasks.

name: WyoFile
title: Wilderness advocates delay removal of tree ‘Yellowstone Forest Reserve’ surveyors inscribed in 1893
description:
The Shoshone National Forest may still authorize a helicopter to extricate a section of the tree, but other options — like a 3D replica — are being considered after advocates objected to altering designated wilderness. 
The post Wilderness advocates delay removal of tree ‘Yellowstone Forest Reserve’ surveyors inscribed in 1893 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Public opposition will slow plans to remove and display a section of a dead Shoshone National Forest tree that surveyors mapping Yellowstone Forest Reserve boundaries inscribed 133 years ago.
The dead Engelmann spruce still stands about 28 miles from the nearest trailhead in the Washakie Wilderness. Plans to recover the artifact via helicopter have been underway for years, and there’s even a place in the Wyoming State Museum to display it.  
But as plans advanced, federal land managers did not loop in the general public nor advocacy groups whose mission it is to uphold the Wilderness Act. When they ultimately learned about the project, advocates publicly objected — and let Shoshone National Forest Supervisor Ken Coffin know it. 





Click to enlarge: The Yellowstone Timber Land Reserve, pictured here, was passed by Congress in March 1891. (General Land Office map, 1892)

“I got probably somewhere around 200 emails from people from across the country who had legitimate concerns about the project because it’s in the wilderness,” Coffin told WyoFile. “Admittedly, we worked with the folks who believe that the removal is an appropriate thing to do —  I happen to be in that camp — but we didn’t really work with the other side. I thought they had a point.” 
Concerns about the tree removal emanated from Wilderness Watch, a Missoula, Montana-based advocacy group that seeks to preserve and steward lands and rivers in the National Wilderness Preservation System. In mid-August, Katie Bilodeau, the group’s legislative director and policy analyst, wrote a blog post encouraging folks to send the Shoshone National Forest their thoughts about the tree removal plan. 
Readers wrote in droves contesting the plan, which required a “minimum requirements analysis” because the tree removal would require use of a helicopter and other mechanical equipment in designated wilderness, where it’s not normally allowed.
“It would have also included at least four helicopter landings in the wilderness,” Bilodeau told WyoFile. “Wilderness is a place where nature should govern. We shouldn’t be so eager to jump in with our tools, because we can radically alter things pretty quickly.”
After hearing from Bilodeau and others, Coffin paused the project. As a result, the beetle-killed tree will not leave the remote reaches of the southern Absaroka Mountains in 2026. 
And it might stay in the 9,100-foot-high basin permanently. The Shoshone National Forest is in talks with Wyoming State Parks about using a 3D scan to create a replica of the inscribed tree instead of displaying the real thing in Cheyenne. 
“If we walk away from that meeting feeling like that [3D scan] serves our purpose,” Coffin said, “then it’s possible that we would not remove the tree.” 
If project proponents, led by Wyoming State Parks, aren’t appeased by that plan, then the Shoshone National Forest would resume its approval process for removing the tree. 

Phillp Gallaher, surveyor. (Lawrence Todd/Courtesy)

The tree in question has been researched by historian Lawrence Todd, a Colorado State University emeritus professor who lives in Meeteetsee. Surveyors inscribed the spruce on Oct. 3, 1893 while mapping the Yellowstone Forest Reserve, which is the forebear to the Shoshone National Forest. The mapping party, led by Phillip M. Gallaher, took shelter near the tree during a snowstorm that slowed their surveying and carved their names into its trunk “probably out of boredom, more than anything else,” Todd told WyoFile in early 2024.
Its historic value is clear. The tree was inscribed just 21 years after Yellowstone National Park’s establishment and three years after Wyoming gained statehood, and it’s a reminder of Americans’ early efforts to “reserve” some forests rather than harvest them all. The 1.2 million-acre forest reserve designated in 1891, was the first piece of land set aside for inclusion in what would eventually become the National Forest System. 
A century and three decades later, the tree was standing dead. In 2024, Wyoming lawmakers debated setting aside some funding to recover the inscribed section and temporarily put it on display at the Wyoming State Museum in Cheyenne. Long-term, the plan is to put the tree section at the Buffalo Bill Center of the West Museum in Cody.
The first attempt at funding died, but Wyoming State Parks secured a $25,000 allocation during the Legislature’s 2025 session, plus another chunk of money through a state grant program to celebrate the American sesquicentennial anniversary.
State Parks Director Dave Glenn told WyoFile on Tuesday he agrees with Coffin’s decision to “slow roll” the project to “make sure everybody’s supportive” of it. And Glenn’s open to 3D printing a hologram of the tree — he’s seen the scans and said they turned out really well.
Still, Glenn prefers that the tree be removed from the wilderness so it doesn’t topple over and rot.
“From our perspective, we’d still like to get the tree [out of] there, just because it’s so historic,” Glenn said. “That history is going to go away. It’s going to fall down and be gone.” 
Bilodeau at Wilderness Watch, meanwhile, has shared gratitude for Coffin pausing the project. On Tuesday, she wrote another blog piece commending that decision and thanking her members for writing to the national forest.
“Y’all saved the survey tree,” she wrote. “While trees don’t have as many lives as cats do, they do have a meaningful second life when they die and become snags, spending years giving back to the ecosystem that had given them life… Removing this ‘deceased’ tree would have devalued this tree’s second life as a snag.”
While it remains to be seen if wilderness advocates will succeed at permanently preventing the survey tree’s removal, it would not be the first time their advocacy has shaped or slowed projects planned in designated wilderness in Wyoming. In 2017, the Bridger-Teton National Forest caught an earful about its plans to helicopter in a new Yellowstone River bridge at Hawks Rest, though the bridge was ultimately replaced four years later.
Plans to stock naturally fishless Mystery Lake in the Teton Wilderness also were scrapped in 2016 as a result of concerns shared by wilderness proponents.

name: VTDigger
title: Former EPA official Melissa Hoffer to lead Vermont Law and Graduate School
description:
Hoffer, who currently serves as Massachusetts’ climate chief, succeeds Rodney Smolla, who served as president from 2022 to 2025.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Former EPA official Melissa Hoffer to lead Vermont Law and Graduate School.
text:
Melissa Hoffer is the new president of Vermont Law and Graduate School in South Royalton. She will begin her tenure on Dec. 1. (Courtesy Vermont Law and Graduate School)

This story by Liz Sauchelli was first published in the Valley News on Sept. 7, 2026.After more than a year of interim leadership, Vermont Law and Graduate School has hired a new president.
Melissa Hoffer, who currently serves as Massachusetts’ climate chief, will begin her tenure Dec. 1, according to a news release from the South Royalton-based school, which is also known as VLGS.
She succeeds Rodney Smolla, who served as president from 2022 to 2025. Smolla — who specializes in constitutional and civil liberties law, as well as defamation and libel law — returned to teaching at the school after stepping down as president. Law school dean Beth McCormack and graduate school dean Dan Bromberg have served as interim co-leaders since Smolla left his role as president, according to the release.
Hoffer was selected, in part, because of her background in litigation, regulatory policy and public service, according to the release.
“Melissa Hoffer’s vision and expertise complement the goals and mission of VLGS,” said board chair Glenn Berger in the release. “Together, we will support up-and-coming law and policy leaders, build broad support for the school’s efforts and ensure its continued success.”
Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey appointed Hoffer as the inaugural climate chief for the Office of Climate Innovation and Resilience, which the governor created when she took office in 2023. Prior to that role, Hoffer served as principal deputy general counsel for the Environmental Protection Agency during the Biden administration.
“From advancing clean energy and resilience to making sure our investments reach the neighborhoods that need them most, Melissa has helped our state lead the nation on climate innovation while keeping affordability and opportunity front and center,” Healey said in the release.
Hoffer earned her bachelor’s degree from Hampshire College in Amherst, Massachusetts, her master’s degree in education from the University of Massachusetts and her law degree from Northeastern University School of Law.
“I am honored and thrilled to join Vermont Law and Graduate School as its next president. VLGS has long been a national leader in environmental law and policy and public interest law, and the institution is uniquely positioned to lead in this time of momentous and intersecting challenges,” Hoffer said in the release. “I cannot wait to get to work with the VLGS community and help build on its remarkable legacy of educating leaders who are ready to make a difference.”

name: VTDigger
title: Residents voice concerns over cannabis proposal in Royalton
description:
The town’s public safety committee held a meeting last week to discuss the upcoming decision on whether to allow cannabis sales in Royalton.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Residents voice concerns over cannabis proposal in Royalton.
text:
Shannon Morrill, of South Royalton, departs her cannabis dispensary, Something Wicked, in Bethel, Vt., to go to a meeting on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. At her request the Royalton Selectboard approved putting the decision on whether to allow retail cannabis sales before voters in November, without requiring a petition signed by 5% of registered voters. Photo by James M. Patterson/Valley News

This story by Sofia Langlois was first published in the Valley News on Sept. 4, 2026.ROYALTON —​​ The Selectboard approved putting cannabis retail on the November ballot per request by a nearby dispensary owner, but some community members aren’t thrilled about the idea.
The town’s public safety committee held a meeting Wednesday to discuss the upcoming decision on whether to allow cannabis sales in Royalton, with Shannon Morrill, the owner of Something Wicked dispensary in Bethel, present to answer questions.
Despite providing more context about her store and its precautions, Morrill still faced some opposition.
“I don’t think we should normalize drug use in our community,” said Beth Wilhite, chair of the public safety committee.
Back in 2020, Vermont passed an act allowing towns to “opt-in” to cannabis retail. With it, dispensaries may open if a majority of residents vote in favor. In the Upper Valley, Hartford, Bethel, Bradford, Fairlee, Randolph, Strafford, Windsor and Woodstock have opted in, but Royalton has not.
At least, not yet.
Morrill, a Royalton resident, has operated her dispensary in Bethel since 2023. Due to the location being down a flight of stairs off Main Street — which is not as accessible or visible as she’d like — Morrill is looking into other options for when her lease ends in November.
Having grown up in Royalton and with a customer base from Vermont Law and Graduate School in town, it’s her first choice for relocation. Before Morrill can start looking into empty storefronts, she needs permission from the townspeople.
“It’s a big project, so we wouldn’t even be looking until February or March to be getting started. And I didn’t want to get my hopes up on any one property,” Morrill said at the Wednesday meeting.
Earlier this summer, Morrill approached the Royalton Selectboard, asking that cannabis retail be placed on the August ballot. Due to limited time to warn voters, the November election was a natural next step.
While member Christopher “Kip” Bergstrom felt that Morrill should submit a petition signed by 5% of the voters before adding a retail cannabis question, other members said voters should just decide on election day. They approved it for the Nov. 3 ballot, 3-2.
At the Selectboard’s Aug. 11 meeting, the public safety committee urged the board to reconsider. The committee then held its own meeting Wednesday, where members and residents raised concerns.
One possibility raised is that any dispensary owner can come in once the item is approved, and that person may not be as willing to listen to public input. Committee members also said that if Royalton later opts out, a dispensary already licensed and operating has the right to stay.
Morrill responded that the process is long and complicated, so it’s unlikely someone will beat her to it, and that there’s not enough business to support two retailers.
Considering worry over intoxication in public or on the roads, Morrill noted that it’s illegal to use cannabis in a retail establishment or in public, and that she’s seen minimal loitering outside her Bethel store.
“We know that most of our customers take this stuff home. They use it in the evening instead of a glass of wine,” said Morrill, who added that her concern is intoxicated driving from the bars.
Some of the edible products sold at Morrill’s store resemble candy in the form of chocolates and gummies, and a single package can contain up to 100 milligrams of THC. Under state law, those packages have to be divided into servings of no more than 5 milligrams each.
Wilhite said a child who ate an entire package could be seriously harmed, depending on the child’s age and size. Symptoms of marijuana toxicity in small children could include “respiratory depression, respiratory failure, altered mental status, ataxia, hypotonia, seizure, and unresponsiveness,” according to the National Institutes of Health.
Morrill responded that they provide locked cases and can educate parents on how to keep it out of reach. She added that there is plenty of marijuana making its way through the high school system, which is unregulated and unsafe.
“I’m not sure that having a dispensary or not is going to change how our teenagers see pot,” said Morrill. “It’s everywhere right now, and we probably should be having much more honest conversations with them.”
Due to state regulations, product at the dispensary may not be visible from street level and would be hidden by frosted windows up to 7 feet high, said Morrill.
At the Bethel location, there was one break-in where someone allegedly popped out an air conditioner and slipped through the 6-inch window opening, according to Morrill.
“He grabbed three jars of gummies from the display area, and all of a sudden, on the videotape, you see him grab his ears as the alarm starts to go off, and he dove back out the window,” said Morrill.
When the alarm goes off, state police are dispatched to the store, said Morrill. If the dispensary were in Royalton, local police may respond instead depending on the time.
With the dispensary would come additional security cameras outside the store. Robin Maynard Seaver, who owns Green Mountain Linen on Chelsea Street, said in a comment that increased monitoring could help mitigate more severe drug-use problems in town.
“And it’s not pot; it’s much worse,” she said.
Morrill said they require photo ID from customers immediately upon entry if they appear to be under 35 years old, but everyone is ID’d at checkout no matter what. No one under 21 may enter the store, even infants accompanying a parent shopper.
One resident, Toni Ventrella, said she had a different experience when she visited with her daughter, who was a customer.
“I was in your shop. Nobody asked for ID,” Ventrella said to Morrill.
“That employee doesn’t work for us anymore,” Morrill responded.
After the meeting, Morrill said she checked her records and found that Ventrella’s ID was scanned when she visited the store. Although she did not have Ventrella’s daughter’s name, she said she was either scanned in, asked to leave or did not buy anything.
The state conducts an annual full check to ensure compliance with all regulations before license renewal and may visit unexpectedly, said Morrill. Those who wish to work at Something Wicked undergo a full FBI background check and may not be intoxicated on the job under any circumstances.



“It’s not a few stoners who are running a shop. There’s so much regulation and so many moving parts and details that you have to be on your toes back there,” said Morrill.
Committee member Sam Wood asked Morrill how she’d prevent the smell of the cannabis from going into nearby restaurants. She responded that the products are closed and she uses fans and open windows for ventilation.
Resident Peggy Ainsworth said that while she supports medical marijuana for those who need it, she worries about people self-medicating and perhaps exacerbating mental illness.
Asked by Wilhite what benefits Something Wicked would bring to Royalton, Morrill said she constantly refers customers to other local businesses, especially those who drive into town specifically for her dispensary.
Royalton itself would not collect anything on cannabis sales. Retail cannabis carries a 14% state excise tax on top of Vermont’s 6% sales tax, but that money goes to the state.
Only towns that have adopted a 1% local option sales tax take a share. Royalton has never adopted a local option tax of any kind; a proposal to tax meals, lodging and alcohol failed on a 51-51 tie in 2025.
A second forum on the ballot measure is scheduled for 7 p.m. Oct. 1 in the Academy Building, 4182 VT-14. It will be moderated by the selectboard, and the public is encouraged to attend.
“I will live with whatever the vote is,” said Morrill. “I’m not out there campaigning for it. I’m just trying to make sure everyone has the facts.”

title: University of Iowa begins national search for chief financial officer
description: The University of Iowa has launched a national search for a new financial leader, with plans to shift other leadership responsibilities. The Iowa City public university announced in a news release it has formed a search committee to find a new chief financial officer after Terry Johnson, who currently holds the role, announced his April […]
text:
The University of Iowa has contracted with a search firm and created a committee to select a new chief financial officer. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The University of Iowa has launched a national search for a new financial leader, with plans to shift other leadership responsibilities.
The Iowa City public university announced in a news release it has formed a search committee to find a new chief financial officer after Terry Johnson, who currently holds the role, announced his April 5 retirement.
Search firm Spencer Stuart has been contracted by the university to help with the search, according to the release, and UI Vice President for External Operations and senior advisor to the president Peter Matthes and College of Public Health Dean Edith Parker will head the search committee.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Whoever is selected for the job will report directly to UI President Barbara Wilson, the release stated. The position will also have some new duties previously undertaken by Senior Vice President for Finance and Operations Rod Lehnertz, who will have “finance” dropped from his title to focus more on “the physical, administrative and operational infrastructure that supports the university’s missions.”
“Our financial strength gives us the opportunity to think strategically about how we invest in the university’s future,” Wilson said in the release. “Having the CFO report directly to the president will bring that financial perspective into our highest-level decisions and ensure that our resources continue to be aligned with our priorities. At the same time, having dedicated leadership for campus operations will allow our infrastructure functions to have the focus they need to serve the university well.”
Iowa Board of Regents member Nancy Dunkel has a role on the search committee following rule changes to the board’s policy manual requiring a board member to sit on search committees for all university positions that report directly to the president. Dunkel spoke out against the rule changes during the meeting, and voted against the measure with Regents Greta Rouse and Lucy Gipple.
Other search committee members include Director of Athletics Beth Goetz, Division of Student Life Business Officer Scott Seagren, Faculty Senate past president Craig Just, UI Health Care Associate Vice President Brad Haws, College of Liberal Arts and Sciences Senior Director for Business and Financial Administration Ryan Kirkey and Staff Council President-elect Ashley Peters.
“Working closely with university and health care leaders, the Iowa Board of Regents, and stakeholders across the institution, the chief financial officer will align financial resources with strategic priorities and support institutional decision-making through analysis and forecasting,” the release stated. “The CFO also will promote transparency, accountability, and stewardship of university resources.”

title: Rockville diner group files lawsuit against airport concessionaire
description: A Rockville-owned and operated diner chain is suing a Germany-based corporation for what it says are attempts to end its decades-long operations at Baltimore-Washington Thurgood Marshall International Airport.
text:
A concourse at Baltimore-Washington Thurgood Marshall International Airport. (Photo courtesy Maryland Department of Transportation)A Rockville-owned and operated diner chain is suing a Germany-based corporation for what it says are attempts to end its decades-long operations at Baltimore-Washington Thurgood Marshall International Airport.
Silver Diner filed the lawsuit in Anne Arundel County Circuit Court against Fraport, the airport concessions operator. The diner, which has operated inside the airport for two decades, is alleging breach of contract and fraudulent misrepresentation on the part of Fraport.
In a 48-page lawsuit, Silver Diner alleges it entered into an agreement with Fraport in 2022 as the concessionaire was seeking a new contract with the state. That contract was meant to ensure that the restaurant, which employs 120, would remain at the airport if Fraport was successful in its bid for the new contract.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The tortured search for a new operator started in the final year of the second term of then-Gov. Larry Hogan (R). Fraport, the incumbent operator, was awarded a lucrative 23-year contract to oversee concessions at the airport in February 2025.
“Within days of the award, Fraport unilaterally and without contractual authority imposed a new ‘Gutting Requirement’ that included a complete rebuild of the kitchen and other requirements not included in the Collaboration Agreement, which was focused exclusively on the customer dining space,” Silver Diner said in a press release accompanying the suit.
The “gutting requirement” called for the diner to shut down for a year and spend $8 million to $10 million on renovations, the suit said. The company said it had expected to spend $1.5 million on renovations as part of its 2022 agreement with Fraport.
A spokesperson for Fraport did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: NASA leaders urge Iowa State University students to join lunar base program
description: State and federal officials connected to U.S. space exploration detailed plans of eventual moon habitation Tuesday to a room packed to the brim with Iowa State University students, hoping to entice their interest in using their education to aid in the newest space race. National Aeronautics and Space Administration Administrator Jared Isaacman and Moon Base[...]
text:
NASA Moon Base Project Manager Carlos García-Galán speaks at Iowa State University Sept. 8, 2026, about the mission to establish a permanent base on the moon. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)State and federal officials connected to U.S. space exploration detailed plans of eventual moon habitation Tuesday to a room packed to the brim with Iowa State University students, hoping to entice their interest in using their education to aid in the newest space race.
National Aeronautics and Space Administration Administrator Jared Isaacman and Moon Base Project Manager Carlos García-Galán toured the Ames National Laboratory and then held a presentation for ISU students to show the three phases of moon base development. They were joined by U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, U.S. Assistant Secretary for Postsecondary Education David Barker, Nuclear Regulatory Commission Ho Nieh, ISU President David Cook and others.
NASA announced in March a plan to return to the moon in 2028 and build a permanent base there by 2032. The NASA officials told students Tuesday the education and training they are pursuing are just what NASA is looking for — if they’re willing to “pick up the fire of exploration and join us on this extraordinary adventure,” Isaacman said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“You could help us build the moon base. You could operate it in mission control. You could walk on the lunar surface or be the nuclear engineer building the spacecraft to take us to the next destination on this endless mission of discovery,” Isaacman said. “And decades from now, when the history books look back on this moment — the moment humanity became a true spacefaring civilization — the people responsible, the generation that will have made it happen, are represented right here in this room.”
ISU already has a strong relationship with NASA and many of its projects, Cook said, with the university leading close to 30 active NASA-funded projects and collaborating on nine more. The Ames National Laboratory and the Iowa Space Grant Consortium are also housed at the university, he said, bringing more connection and collaboration on important projects.
Isaacman said current and future ISU students “are part of the most exciting era of exploration since Apollo.”
NASA and its partners will build the moon base in three different phases, García-Galán said, taking the mission from establishing consistent contact with the lunar surface to setting up infrastructure for astronaut residence to having astronauts live on the moon’s surface for at least one month.
The first phase of the mission is already underway, García-Galán said, and should wrap up in 2029. NASA selected the moon’s south pole as the place to explore and develop, and will send rovers and equipment to the area to both better map it out and establish “reliable access to the lunar surface.” The south pole provides a mix of sunlight and shadow and houses spots that are permanently shadowed, offering potential findings that could reveal information billions of years old.
Iowa State University students listen to a NASA presentation on Sept. 8, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Four landers holding different rovers and equipment are currently being developed for the mission, García-Galán said, alongside lunar vehicles for astronauts, drones and other technology.
“In phase one, we’re not going to be afraid to fail. We really want to test the things that work or don’t,” García-Galán said. “We’re doing everything we know how to, to make those things successful, even the tech demonstrations, but we want to see the operations and the area; the things that are not going to work, we actually want to find them out in phase one.”
Phase two will involve deploying necessary infrastructure for moon base missions, including power, habitation, communications, moving cargo and more. García-Galán said up to four astronauts will live in a central region and explore areas around it, with the U.S. working with partners in Japan and other countries to develop rovers and hubs where people could survive.
Phase three would bring with it the development of permanent living environments on the moon for astronauts.
ISU students packed into Howe Hall’s atrium — sitting in chairs, leaning on walls and craning to see over staircase and balcony railings — were the first to see early concept designs for the “habitation cluster” for lunar surface residents, García-Galán said. They were also shown imaging of the moon’s south pole and renderings of how the base and research areas would be set up.
Students can bring their hard work and passion to the moon base mission in many different ways, Isaacman said, as NASA will need technicians, entrepreneurs, researchers, operators, explorers, astronauts and more to be the first to have humans living on the moon.
García-Galán asked students to not treat the information provided to them Tuesday as a presentation but a “briefing,” as they will need to know these things for their future should they wish to join the ranks of scientists, researchers, engineers and others contributing to the space race.
“What’s exciting for me here at Iowa State is seeing the vision, and then seeing the role our students are going to have looking forward,” Cook said. “Really exciting to be on the cusp of something that truly is a moonshot.”
