title: Top New Mexico Senate Republican accuses lawmaker of inappropriately helping fund DA’s office
description: New Mexico Senate Minority Leader Bill Sharer (R-Farmington) on Tuesday accused a state lawmaker who recently resigned from her controversial job with a local prosecutor of engaging in a “pay to play” scheme by appropriating taxpayer dollars to the DA’s office before taking a job there.
text:
New Mexico Senate Minority Leader Bill Sharer (R-Farmington) accused Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe), pictured on Jan. 20, 2026, during the opening day of the legislative session, of improperly sponsoring state funding for a district attorney’s office before accepting a job with the office months later. (Photo by Kate Russell for Source NM)New Mexico Senate Minority Leader Bill Sharer (R-Farmington) on Tuesday accused a state lawmaker who recently resigned from her controversial job with a local prosecutor of engaging in a “pay to play” scheme by appropriating taxpayer dollars to the DA’s office before taking a job there.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sharer in a statement accused Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe), who currently leads the state’s commission dedicated to investigating the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, of “self-dealing” by sponsoring $100,000 in spending in the 2026 legislative session’s capital outlay package for the First Judicial District Attorney’s Office, which hired her later in the year.
“New Mexicans need to ask a simple question: did Representative Romero send $100,000 in taxpayer money to an office that turned around and put her on the payroll a few months later?” Sharer said in a statement. “That is the definition of pay to play. Whether or not it violated the letter of the law, it is exactly the kind of self-dealing our ethics laws exist to prevent, and it’s exactly why voters have lost trust in this Legislature policing itself.”
Catherine Lynch, a spokesperson for First Judicial District Attorney Mary Carmack-Altwies’ office, in an email to Source NM said allegations that Romero and the district attorney traded state funding for a part-time job were “patently false, outrageous and defamatory.”
“The FJDA rejects any suggestion that Andrea Romero’s employment was connected to capital outlay funding for this office,” Lynch said. “When Andrea was considered for the part-time position, the office’s focus was on whether her employment was permissible and her qualifications to perform the work. As we have previously stated, Andrea had proactively sought guidance from the Attorney General’s Office before accepting the position, and our office also conducted its own ethics and conflict review.”
Romero did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Sharer previously called on Romero to resign from both the Epstein commission and the state House of Representatives. He and House Minority Whip Alan Martinez (R-Rio Rancho) have filed complaints against her with the State Ethics Commission.
Romero resigned from her job with the DA last week after New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez sent a letter to district attorneys statewide, instructing them not to hire any sitting lawmakers and to part ways with any lawmakers they employed.
At the time, Romero issued a statement via the Epstein commission’s contracted public relations firm saying she was “deeply disappointed” by Torrez’s letter but would resign from her job at the DA’s office. She added that she would continue to serve as chair of the Epstein “truth commission” and as a state representative for Santa Fe.
The two Republican members of the Epstein “truth commission” subsequently criticized Romero for allegedly tapping the commission’s contracted PR firm. Romero then issued a second statement backtracking her criticism of Torrez and announcing that the commission and the PR firm were “parting” ways.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Lancaster County judge dismisses challenge to Nebraska K-12, collegiate sports ballot measure
description: LINCOLN — A district court judge dismissed all objections Tuesday to a last-minute legal effort seeking to disqualify a ballot measure that would cement sex-separate school sports requirements in the Nebraska Constitution. Lancaster County District Court Judge Lori Maret ruled against Cara Ullman of Lincoln, who asserted that because the Fairness for Girls c[...]
text:
Lancaster County District Judge Lori Maret listens to attorneys during a hearing where the Nebraska Attorney General's Office is challenging a Lincoln city ordinance enacted in response to a new state minimum wage law at the Lancaster County Courthouse on Thursday, July 2, 2026, in Lincoln. (Pool photo by Kenneth Ferriera/Lincoln Journal Star)LINCOLN — A district court judge dismissed all objections Tuesday to a last-minute legal effort seeking to disqualify a ballot measure that would cement sex-separate school sports requirements in the Nebraska Constitution.
Lancaster County District Court Judge Lori Maret ruled against Cara Ullman of Lincoln, who asserted that because the Fairness for Girls campaign lacked detail in some specific petition language, known as an “object statement,” she signed a petition to place the measure on the general election ballot without fully knowing what it would do.
Maret disagreed and said in a five-page decision Tuesday that while the Fairness for Girls object statement was “certainly brief,” state law only requires that the statement be “concise.”
The statement, which went through the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office, reads: “The object of this petition is to amend the Nebraska Constitution to establish constitutional protections for sex-separate athletics to ensure equal access to athletic opportunities for females.”
“In sum, the petition’s object statement is a concise statement of the legal effect of the filing of the petition and the object sought to be secured,” Maret wrote. “It is therefore ordered, adjudged and decreed that the action is dismissed.”
Lancaster County judge hears challenge to Nebraska K-12, collegiate sports ballot measure

Ullman is appealing Maret’s ruling to the Nebraska Court of Appeals. The matter could be expedited to the Nebraska Supreme Court, which might again refuse to hear the case. The Supreme Court declined Sept. 1 to hear the challenge, so Ullman filed it before Maret. 
Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen must certify the ballot by Friday.
The Fairness for Girls proposal would make permanent part of a 2025 state law requiring public K-12 schools, colleges and universities, and any private schools or colleges in the state playing against those schools, to designate sports and teams as male, female or coed. Male students couldn’t play on female-only teams.
The ballot measure would not define “sex” in the constitution. State law defines sex as whether someone “naturally has, had, will or would have, but for a congenital anomaly or intentional or unintentional disruption, the reproductive system that at some point produces, transports and utilizes” either eggs (female) or sperm (male) for fertilization.
Attorney Sydney Hayes, on behalf of Ullman, had argued last week that if object statements could be so broad, it could be “open season for vague, incomplete and misleading” statements.
Former state Sen. Andrew La Grone, an attorney, representing the Nebraska Republican Party, presents his case during a hearing at the Lancaster County Courthouse on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Kenneth Ferriera-Pool/Lincoln Journal Star)
Former state Sen. Andrew La Grone of Dunbar, on behalf of the three sponsors behind Fairness for Girls, disagreed and said the campaign followed the law as written. He said the sponsors — including former state Sen. Julie Slama of Dunbar and University of Nebraska Regent Rob Schafer — had a broad First Amendment right to the object statement they provided.
Maret said that while Ullman’s attorneys argue that an object statement needs to state the “major provisions” or “major features” of a proposal, those standards are “nowhere” in the law. 
“Our Legislature has chosen not to add such requirements,” Maret wrote. “The court must defer to the Legislature.”
Such a “strict interpretation,” Maret added, would “unduly restrict the power of the initiative.”
Hayes had also pointed to the measure’s “ballot title,” a separate 100-word statement that will go on ballots this fall. But Maret said the comparison is not “helpful” because an object statement, written by sponsors, and a ballot title, written by the Nebraska Attorney General’s Office, are used in different circumstances and under different legislatively set requirements.
Maret also echoed an argument from the Nebraska AG’s Office: If a voter wants more information before signing, they can flip the page over and read the full proposal.
Absent appellate intervention, voters will see the following language on the Nov. 3 ballot:
“Shall the Nebraska Constitution be amended to provide: (1) Schools must expressly designate each athletic team or sport as one of the following based on biological sex: (a) males, men or boys; (b) females, women or girls; or (c) coed or mixed; and (2) Athletic teams or sports designated for females, women or girls shall not be open to students of the male sex? The amendment would apply to all athletic teams or sports sponsored by public schools or postsecondary educational institutions and private schools or educational institutions whose athletic teams or sports compete against public schools or institutions.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont regulators finalize 5.5% rate increase for Green Mountain Power customers
description:
The decision from the state’s Public Utility Commission sought to balance affordability concerns with a desire to shore up electrical infrastructure against weather damage.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont regulators finalize 5.5% rate increase for Green Mountain Power customers.
text:
Green Mountain Power in Colchester in December 2019. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
Regulators will allow Green Mountain Power to raise electricity rates by 5.5% for its more than 275,000 Vermont customers — a smaller hike than the 7.5% increase the company initially sought. 
The billing change, ordered late last month by Vermont’s Public Utility Commission, will take effect Oct. 1.
The first proposal from the state’s largest electric utility drew criticism from dozens of consumers during the public comment process. The Vermont Department of Public Service, which represents the public interest in regulatory decisions, opposed parts of the spending plan, and the Public Utility Commission, a quasi-judicial body that issues decisions in such cases, opened an investigation into Green Mountain Power’s financial circumstances in March. 
In an order published Aug. 28, the three-member commission said that the majority of the rate increase request was “largely outside GMP’s control,” and noted that “nearly all” electric companies in the state had requested relatively large hikes over the past several years. Electricity supply and transmission costs have risen across the region on top of general inflation, the filing noted. Public Service Commissioner Kerrick Johnson estimated last fall that Vermonters’ electric bills would climb 25% by 2030, with some cost pressures still difficult to quantify.
One central point of disagreement between Green Mountain Power and state officials at the Department of Public Service was “resilience spending.” The company asked to earmark up to about $341 million over the course of a four-year period for extra work shoring up its infrastructure against weather damage in the long term.
“Storms are increasing in frequency and severity — Vermonters are feeling it,” said Kristin Carlson, a spokesperson for Green Mountain Power, in an interview Tuesday. “The goal is to deliver projects that keep customers with their lights on, keep them safer and then over time lower storm restoration costs.”
So far, such improvement projects in Vermont have resulted in sharp decreases in power outages and growing financial savings, Carlson said. Green Mountain Power received permission in 2024 to spend about $150 million over the following two years to “harden” its electric networks through projects such as burying power lines. To incentivize infrastructure improvements, Vermont allows utility companies to keep a portion of the returns on such investments without making a direct profit from the sale of electricity.
The Public Utility Commission elected this year to approve about $113 million in resilience spending — roughly a third of the $341 million the company requested. The decision needed to balance what the panel called a legitimate desire for a more robust power grid with officials’ concerns about costs passed on to customers, as well as the completeness of the company’s planning for those improvements.
“There is no dispute that Vermont’s climate is changing,” last month’s decision read. But affordability concerns for residents, the document stressed several times, was “central to our analysis.” 
The agreed-upon amount should cover upgrades to Green Mountain Power’s 10 worst-performing circuits over the next four years, the regulators added, while reducing the immediate impact on customers as much as is practical.
More than 50 public comments on the matter were overwhelmingly critical of Green Mountain Power’s initial proposal.
“I cannot afford taxes, utilities, insurance and food anymore,” said Janice McCann in a written statement to the panel. “Something has to give. Please consider the less fortunate people in Vermont.”
John Tatro agreed, adding: “We do not have a choice in power companies to our location so there is no competition.”
Green Mountain Power’s request is far from isolated. Electric departments in Swanton, Hyde Park and Jacksonville have submitted rate hike requests of roughly 30%, 15% and 18% respectively for the coming months.
The price surges come as Vermonters face energy cost increases on all fronts. The state remains among the nation’s most reliant on heating oil, prices for which remain high and volatile. Gasoline prices are also a worry for residents.

title: O’Donnell to speak at Trump-led Republican midterm convention in Texas
description: Marty O’Donnell, the video game composer challenging Democratic U.S. Rep. Susie Lee in Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District, is 1 of 12 Republican candidates scheduled to speak at an atypical party convention later this week. Conventions are typically held every four years in conjunction with the selection of presidential nominees. Republicans have never held[...]
text:
Nevada Republican congressional candidate Marty O'Donnell posted this photo of himself and Donald Trump on O'Donnell's campaign website following Trump's visit to Las Vegas in April, 2026. (Official White House Photo by Daniel Torok)Marty O’Donnell, the video game composer challenging Democratic U.S. Rep. Susie Lee in Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District, is 1 of 12 Republican candidates scheduled to speak at an atypical party convention later this week.
Conventions are typically held every four years in conjunction with the selection of presidential nominees. Republicans have never held a midterm convention before but President Donald Trump and his allies believe a midterm convention will rally supporters and donors ahead of November.
The convention — dubbed ”Trumpapalooza” — is scheduled to take place in Dallas on Wednesday and Thursday.  The president will speak both days, according to a GOP release. 
Vice President J.D. Vance, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, and Donald Trump Jr. are among other MAGA allies scheduled to speak. O’Donnell was announced as one of at least a dozen congressional candidates who will appear and give comments.
O’Donnell has been endorsed by Trump and spoke at a rally the president held in Las Vegas last month.
Inflation and high gas prices, trade wars, the war in Iran, and Trump’s steady preoccupation with his Washington D.C. remodeling priorities have combined to earn him some of the lowest approval ratings of either of his terms as president. 
Politico reported last week that dozens of Republican congressional contenders were either taking a pass on the Trumpapalooza, or declined to say whether they would be attending.
“As the lone Nevadan on the program, Marty is honored to speak at the RNC Convention on Thursday,” O’Donnell campaign spokesman Keith Schipper. “He will be talking about how Susie Lee created our affordability crisis, refused to apologize for it, and how he will work to finish more of the Trump agenda so every family can get ahead on one good job.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: BLM oil and gas leases threaten critical Colorado wildlife corridors, lawsuit says
description: Two environmental groups sued the Trump administration Tuesday, alleging the Bureau of Land Management violated federal law when it leased more than 134,000 acres of public lands in Colorado for oil and gas drilling earlier this year. In their lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court of Colorado, Wilderness Workshop and The Wilderness Society say […]
text:
Gas wells operate near Interstate 70 in Garfield County near Parachute, June 9, 2023. (William Woody for Colorado Newsline)Two environmental groups sued the Trump administration Tuesday, alleging the Bureau of Land Management violated federal law when it leased more than 134,000 acres of public lands in Colorado for oil and gas drilling earlier this year.
In their lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court of Colorado, Wilderness Workshop and The Wilderness Society say the BLM’s June 2026 lease sale would “allow the development of oil and gas wells in habitat critical to some of the United States’ largest, and last remaining, migrations of pronghorn antelope, mule deer and elk.”
The agency’s failure to withhold sensitive wildlife areas from development violates its own rules and the Federal Land Policy and Management Act, the lawsuit argues. Plaintiffs want the court to vacate the lease sales and a Trump administration memorandum the agency has used to ramp up oil and gas leasing in Colorado and other western states.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Our public lands are not commodities for the oil and gas industry,” Adina Nadler, associate attorney with The Wilderness Society, said in a press release. “They are spectacular landscapes that give us the freedom to explore and enjoy the outdoors, while providing essential habitat for wildlife. The administration has flagrantly cast aside these values to appease the oil and gas industry, and we will not stand for it.”
A BLM spokesperson said the agency “does not comment on pending or current litigation.” The agency previously described the June lease sale as consistent with the Trump administration’s goal to “meet the energy needs of U.S. citizens and solidify the nation as a global energy leader long into the future.”
The sale was the largest the BLM has held in Colorado in 15 years, with a total of 170 parcels spanning nearly 156,000 acres of land put up for auction — more than the available acreage in the previous six lease sales combined, according to the group Taxpayers for Common Sense. A majority of the 134,000 acres sold were located in northwestern Colorado, and a “large majority” of the parcels lie in areas designated as big game habit and migration corridors.
Another 29 parcels totaling 14,095 acres of Colorado public lands are up for auction by the BLM later this week, including a parcel near the Aurora Reservoir in Arapahoe County.
Under existing BLM rules and federal law, the wilderness advocates allege, the agency should have applied “preference criteria” to the parcels leased in June and withheld sensitive areas from the auction. Despite protests from conservation groups at the time, the agency said a 2025 Trump administration memo on lease sale procedures overrides those criteria.
“Although BLM’s own analysis showed numerous conflicts with crucial big game habitats and migration corridors and with the preservation of pristine wilderness-quality lands,” the lawsuit says, “BLM’s June 2026 lease sales offered hundreds of thousands of acres of public lands for lease without withholding any parcels based on the preference criteria, in violation of BLM’s own regulation and FLPMA.”
“The lands leased by BLM in Northwest Colorado are public lands that I have enjoyed and hunted on for years,” said Luke Schafer, Wilderness Workshop member and lifelong sportsman. “It is disheartening that productive public lands that are enjoyed by so many — lands that are critical to sustaining wildlife populations — could soon be carved up by well pads, pipelines, and access roads.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas attorney general says stabbing death shows need for greater police cooperation with ICE
description: Attorney General Kris Kobach is urging city and county law enforcement agencies across Kansas  to join with ICE in a national immigration crackdown.
text:
Attorney General Kris Kobach encourages local law enforcement agencies to work with ICE to detain people scheduled for deportation. During a Topeka news conference, KBI interim director Robert Jacobs, center, and Shawnee County Sheriff Brian Hill, left, share Kobach's belief that collaboration with ICE is beneficial to Kansas. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector) TOPEKA — Attorney General Kris Kobach asserted a stabbing death in southwest Kansas could have been averted through compliance with a federal court order for deportation of the man later charged in the slaying.
Kobach, a Republican who is seeking reelection against Democrat Chris Mann, said the tragedy made clear why it was important for city and county law enforcement agencies in Kansas to sign cooperative agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to track down fugitives without the right to be in the United States. Currently, the Kansas Bureau of Investigation, 35 counties and 10 cities have implemented collaborative pacts with ICE.
Honduran citizen Erlin Lagos-Gonzales, a 43-year-old resident of Garden City, was accused of voluntary manslaughter in the Aug. 31 killing of Adonis Edgardo Aguilar-Juarez of Lakin. The men were involved in an apparent quarrel at Kansas Dairy Development, a large calf and heifer facility in Deerfield. During the encounter, Aguilar-Juarez sustained life-threatening injuries. He was driven by private vehicle to Kearny County Hospital, where he died.
Lagos-Gonzales was charged Sept. 3 and has been held in Finney County Jail on $500,000 bond. On Tuesday, Lagos-Gonzales made his first appearance in Kearny County District Court. The attorney general said his office would work with the county attorney to prosecute the case.
On July 24, 2025, a U.S. immigration judge issued a deportation order for Lagos-Gonzales, but the directive wasn’t carried out. State prosecutors said they believe Lagos-Gonzales had been living in the United States since 2019 without legal permission.
“This killing never should have happened,” Kobach said. “Erlin Lagos-Gonzales is an illegal alien who received a final order of removal more than a year ago. He should have left the United States then. Instead, he remained in Kansas, continued working, and now stands charged with taking the life of another man.”
Kobach said the case illustrated a nationwide problem in which more than 1.5 million “fugitive aliens” remained at large. The comparable number in Kansas would be in the thousands, Kobach said.
“The problem is too big for ICE alone,” Kobach said. “There is simply no way that the federal officers in ICE can ever remove the 1.5 million fugitive aliens without state and local help.”
Mann, the Democratic nominee for attorney general, said there was no question the perpetrator of the killing had to be held accountable.
He said resources available to sheriffs and police chiefs in Kansas were stretched thin without inserting officers into an immigration enforcement crackdown under the so-called “287g” program.
“Kris Kobach has not taken the time to speak with sheriffs across the state about their decision to sign or not sign a 287g agreement,” Mann said. “I have spoken to dozens of sheriffs, chiefs of police and law enforcement, and what I’ve heard is that they don’t have the resources to take on additional responsibilities, and they need more support — support they are currently not getting from the attorney general.”
Mann said decisions of local law enforcement agencies shouldn’t be dictated by politicians working in Topeka.
“I trust our local sheriffs to make the decision that is best for their community and, as attorney general, I will work with each of them to ensure they have the resources needed to hold violent criminals accountable and keep their communities safe,” Mann said.
Kobach ordered the KBI in early 2025 to acquire 287g authority so the agency could work alongside ICE throughout the state.
Kobach said he expected half the 70 county law enforcement agencies yet to sign 287g deals with ICE to eventually get on board.
As an incentive, the Kansas Legislature enacted a bill guaranteeing the Attorney General’s Office would represent local law enforcement agencies if litigation arose from involvement in the program affiliated with ICE. There had been apprehension in some counties that insurance policies wouldn’t adequately cover that contingency.
“Anyone who thinks that local law enforcement should not collaborate with ICE immigration removals is 100% wrong. Such collaboration saves lives and keeps our streets safe. It will remain a high priority of mine as long as I’m attorney general,” Kobach said.
So far, KBI interim director Robert Jacobs said the KBI’s routine criminal casework had identified 11 people with deportation orders and 14 others ripe for deportation who were on the state’s offender registries.
Brian Hill, the Shawnee County sheriff, said the county’s participation in the 287g program was beneficial. He recalled seven instances in which a person subject to a deportation order was identified through the process of running names through a database.
“I think if local law enforcement is part of this program it does allow them the access to know these people are here illegally and you’re not letting people go back to the community that shouldn’t be there,” the sheriff said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Tribal consortium achieves long-desired ownership of Alaska Native Medical Center
description: The Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium, along with Southcentral Foundation, has operated the facility for decades, but it was owned until now by the Indian Health Service
text:
The main entrance to the Alaska Native Medical Center is on Sept. 6, 2026. The building's design incorporates  elements of Alaska's Indigenous cultures, and has been recognized by professional architecture and design organizations. The hospital was previously owned by the Indian Health Service. A transfer made effective in late August gave ownership to the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The nation’s biggest tribal health organization now owns the Anchorage hospital it has long operated.
The Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium gained title to the Alaska Native Medical Center, the hospital at the center of the organization’s 140-acre campus in Midtown Anchorage. Ownership was officially transferred from the Indian Health Service last month.
The long-sought acquisition was an important milestone, said ANTHC President Natasha Singh.
“Alaska Native people have done a great job operating the Alaska Native Medical Center. The hospital is truly the heart of our system and now we officially own it. This gives us more control over our own future,” she said in an interview.
The hospital, the second largest in Alaska after Providence Alaska Medical Center, opened in 1997, the same year that ANTHC was founded. Until now, the Indian Health Service was the facility owner. Through a compact with the Indian Health Service, ANTHC operated most of the services at the hospital, while Southcentral Foundation, the Tribal health provider for the local region, operated some of the primary care services.
Federal ownership had some downsides, Singh said. Because of it, the consortium did not qualify for certain federal funds that it would have otherwise been able to use, she said. And investment in the facilities was too slow to meet patient needs, she said.
The hospital acquisition was preceded by several preliminary steps over the past several years.
 

The Alaska Native Health Campus is seen on Sept. 6, 2026, with a sign pointing the direction to the Alaska Native Medical Center. The hospital is at the heart of the campus. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	There were some Congressional acts transferring federal land to ANTHC, including a bill sponsored by the late Rep. Don Yong that was signed by President Barack Obama in 2013. There was a formal decision by the ANTHC board, which has members from all of the state’s regional tribal health organizations, on how and when to take ownership. And there was an official request submitted to the federal government a little over a year ago, Singh said.
“It’s been our longtime vision, but I think our federal partners acted quickly when we put in the request,” she said.
Even before the ownership changed, the board approved over $462 million in improvements, including an expansion of the emergency department, Singh said. It was the largest investment in the hospital’s history, intended to counter “decades of underinvestment,” she said.
“So half a billion dollars (was) essentially planned to go into a building the Tribes did not even own, but the ANTHC board knew how much it really matters,” she said.
The transfer also followed a $400 million settlement with the federal government for shortfalls in funding of administrative services, facilities maintenance and other functions.
The modern hospital evolved from historic services provided by the Indian Health Service, which began serving Alaska Natives in the 1940s, according to a summary compiled by Southcentral Foundation. In 1953, the federal government opened a hospital in Anchorage, primarily to serve patients suffering from a tuberculosis epidemic, according to the summary. Despite impacts from the 1964 Great Alaska Earthquake, it continued to operate through the disaster, and even cared for patients evacuated from Providence Hospital. The modern hospital replaced that facility.
The modern hospital was designed with elements of Alaska Native cultures, and it and its adjacent facilities have won awards for their innovative architecture, including one in 2018 for patient housing and one from last year for the emergency department expansion.
With the transfer of ownership, ANTHC now owns most of the buildings on the campus. There is still a federally owned building that houses the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Arctic Investigations Program, and Southcentral Foundation owns some other buildings.
The Alaska Native Medical Center and other buildings on the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium campus in Midtown Anchorage are reflected in lake water on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

text:
The Montana Commissioner of Securities and Insurance building is pictured on Monday, March 9, 2026, in Helena, MT. James Brown is currently the state auditor.  (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)State Auditor James Brown permanently revoked the license of Laine Kendall Callahan, a bail bondsman of Kalispell accused of trading services for sexual favors, the auditor announced in a news release.
The news release said Callahan initially denied receiving sexual acts in exchange for services, but he did not dispute the suspension order.
Brown suspended Callahan’s license early last month after an investigation found he abused his authority as a bail bond producer “in multiple ways.”
The news release said a federal court recently sentenced a Billings bail bondsman following a multiagency investigation initially led by Brown that found the bondsman leveraged his position for sexual favors from at least one female inmate.
The auditor said early last month he intended to seek permanent revocation of Callahan’s license, and it said Callahan could challenge the proposed revocation.
But Callahan did not dispute the factual allegations outlined in the temporary suspension order, nor did he challenge the proposed revocation, said the news release announcing the permanent order.
Callahan did not respond to the Daily Montanan’s questions Tuesday or last month about the allegations.
Brown said his office began investigating Callahan after a referral from the Department of Justice, and the investigation found the following problems:

Callahan allegedly compelled a witness to perform oral sex to “work off” what she purportedly owed him;
A different witness alleged that he had him do unlicensed work as “a de facto bail agent” to work off his debt on a bond; and
Callahan routinely took possession of vehicle titles as collateral for bail bonds without proper documentation.

Brown said because of the volume of business Callahan conducted, he determined his operations posed a threat to the public. The news release said Callahan had issued 133 bonds totaling more than $1 million in just four months.
“Callahan’s behavior not only violated Montana law, but it also eroded public trust in our justice system,” Brown said in a statement. “My agency will investigate and prosecute any bad actor in the insurance industry, especially bail bondsman, who hold particular power over the Montanans in need of their help. That power comes with a heightened level of professional and moral responsibility.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC senator who resigned with Alzheimer’s diagnosis receives state’s highest honor
description: Lawmakers praised Sen. Roger Nutt's leadership on a law guaranteeing certain rights to nursing home residents
text:
State Sen. Roger Nutt, a Spartanburg County Republican, pictured at the Statehouse in Columbia, S.C., resigned his seat following an Alzheimer's diagnosis in 2025. (Photo by Mary Ann Chastain/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)thCOLUMBIA — A state senator who resigned following an Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis received the state’s highest civilian honor Tuesday.
In giving Sen. Roger Nutt the Order of the Palmetto, lawmakers celebrated his work during his five years in the Statehouse, especially his leadership in passing a law that guaranteed residents of nursing homes certain rights.
SC senator resigns seat following Alzheimer’s diagnosis

After 10 years on Spartanburg County Council, Nutt first won election to the House in 2020. Voters elected him to the Senate in 2024 after a contentious four-way GOP primary for an open seat.
Nutt spent just one session in the Senate before doctors diagnosed him with the neurodegenerative disorder Alzheimer’s disease. The 60-year-old resigned to spend more time with family, including his three children, he said at the time.
Although Nutt’s stint in the Senate was brief, it was impactful, Senate Majority Leader Shane Massey said Tuesday. The list of legal rights for nursing home residents was the first bill Nutt introduced, which is a rare feat, Massey said.
“Not only did it become law, but it is very meaningful,” the Edgefield Republican said.
Among other protections, the law requires that nursing homes allow residents up to three designated family members who can visit during an emergency. The proposal, which passed both chambers unanimously, was in direct response to the COVID-19 pandemic, when social distancing rules kept loved ones locked out of nursing homes for over a year.
Under the law, nursing home residents can also choose their own doctors, have privacy during medical screenings, share a room with their spouse and attend religious gatherings as long as their health allows.
The law took effect in April, but Gov. Henry McMaster ceremonially signed it Tuesday. Nutt’s work to get the bill through showed  initiative on an important issue, McMaster said.
“This man did something good, and he did it in a hurry, and it was well needed,” McMaster said.
That’s the sort of work the Order of the Palmetto is meant to celebrate, McMaster added. Recipients are nominated and then screened by a committee to determine whether their work had a statewide impact.
“You fall squarely within that, with your service to our people, making our state better,” McMaster said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: US Department of Energy awards up to $1.9B loan for nuclear plant restart
description: PALO — The U.S. Department of Energy has closed on a loan of up to $1.9 billion to support the restart of Iowa’s only nuclear energy station, Duane Arnold Energy Center.  U.S. Deputy Secretary of Energy James Danly said Tuesday in Palo the “unmothballing” of sites like Duane Arnold are part of a larger strategy […]
text:
NextEra Energy staff are working to upgrade systems at Duane Arnold Energy Center, pictured here on Sept. 8, 2026, as the plant seeks to be recommissioned. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)  PALO — The U.S. Department of Energy has closed on a loan of up to $1.9 billion to support the restart of Iowa’s only nuclear energy station, Duane Arnold Energy Center. 
U.S. Deputy Secretary of Energy James Danly said Tuesday in Palo the “unmothballing” of sites like Duane Arnold are part of a larger strategy from President Donald Trump to “quadruple” the amount of nuclear energy in the nation by 2050. Danly called this effort a “nuclear renaissance.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Duane Arnold, which ceased commercial operation in 2020 and is slated to be back online by early 2029, is a 615-megawatt nuclear facility near the city of Palo now owned by NextEra Energy Resources. 
Danly said Duane Arnold is a “significant anchor facility” for Iowa and for Linn County. According to a study on the facility’s restart, Duane Arnold Energy Center is projected to have a $9.1 billion economic impact to the state of Iowa over a 25-year span. 
U.S. Deputy Secretary of Energy James Danly speaks at Duane Arnold Energy Center in Palo, Iowa Sept. 8, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
“It’s something that is going to help us achieve the objective of energy dominance,” Danly said. “… The loan that the U.S. Department of Energy provided is going to pay dividends for years and years and years. You couldn’t have a wiser use of money.” 
Once operational, the plant itself will offer more than 400 permanent jobs. According to spokespeople for NextEra, about 40% of the staff who have come on with the plant’s restart are “returnees” or people who worked at the facility while it was operational between 1975 and 2020. 
Some of the staff members, like Paul Hansen, retired after the decommissioning, but have come back to work at the plant again. Hansen started at Duane Arnold in 1985 and now serves as the engineering director for the facility. 
Hansen, while giving a tour of the nuclear energy center, said the control room is one of several areas NextEra is upgrading at the facility as part of the restart. 
The control room features a semi-circle wall full of levers, green and red buttons, lights and meters. Hansen said most of it is “’60s technology” and while it still works, there are pieces of the control room that are going to be upgraded to better, integrated computer systems and touchscreen controls. 
A view from inside the plant
The control room at at Duane Arnold Energy Center, pictured Sept. 8, 2026, is one of several areas that will be upgraded as the nuclear plant recommissions.  (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)  Looking down at the nuclear reactor at Duane Arnold Energy Center, Sept. 8, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)  Duane Arnold Energy Center in Palo, Iowa, began operations in 1975 and shut down in 2020. Now, the plant is seeking to restart. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)  Steam generated by the nuclear reactor powers turbines, pictured, to generate electricity at Duane Arnold Energy Center. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)  
In addition to the upgrades to the control room, Duane Arnold will also have a new training facility onsite, storage facilities, a maintenance building and new cooling towers that will be slightly larger to accommodate the greater power generation of the restarted plant.
Brian Bolster, CEO and president of NextEra, said the DOE loan will help to “facilitate” the restart at Duane Arnold, which in turn works to fulfill an “all of the above” energy strategy, improve energy security and “keep energy costs affordable for everyday Americans.”
“Duane Arnold can strengthen the grid while helping to ensure Iowa families and businesses are not asked to bear the cost of growth,” Bolster said during Tuesday. 
Around 90% of the energy produced by the nuclear facility will go to power Google systems, per an early agreement between NextEra and Google. A spokesperson with NextEra said Tuesday that 50 megawatts of the energy generated at the plant will go to Central Iowa Power Cooperative, or CIPCO. 
Danly said that when more electricity is added to a system, it’s also beneficial to have a lot of load to serve, because more customers, like the big purchase agreement with Google, will help drive down the fixed costs of an electricity system.
“Every time you build a new facility to serve a new load, you have downward cost, downward price pressure on rates,” Danley said while speaking with reporters. 
A recently released report from Gov. Kim Reynolds’ Iowa Nuclear Energy Task Force listed nine recommendations for nuclear energy expansion in the state. Most of the recommendations centered on state action to expand nuclear energy by exploring or creating local incentives and workforce development options. 
The last several recommendations directed the state to coordinate with the federal government on nuclear incentives and programs and to “consider” the state’s role in managing spent nuclear fuel. 
When asked about long-term solutions for nuclear waste, Danly said the DOE hopes to “encourage” the reuse of “spent fuel” which he said has historically been deposited after just one fuel cycle. 
“The objective is not just to ensure that it’s safely stored, which is obviously the primary concern, but also that we get as much out of it as we can,” Danly said. 
NextEra has not said publicly the estimated total cost to bring Duane Arnold back online. Bolster said the company hopes to be “well inside” the $1.9 billion loan confirmed with the DOE. 
“You can gather from that loan sizing that we’re talking about multiple billions of dollars here to bring this plant back online,” Bolster said.

title: US Supreme Court denies GOP effort to revive gerrymandered Missouri congressional map
description: U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh on Tuesday rejected Missouri Republican officials’ last-chance appeal to salvage a congressional district map favoring the GOP, closing out the months-long legal saga over the referendum that will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot as Proposition A. Kavanaugh’s ruling upholds a Missouri Supreme Court decision that enjoined[...]
text:
Supreme Court Associate Justice Brett Kavanaugh attends the State of the Union address during a Joint Session of Congress at the U.S. Capitol on Feb. 24 in Washington, DC. (Win McNamee/Getty Images).U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh on Tuesday rejected Missouri Republican officials’ last-chance appeal to salvage a congressional district map favoring the GOP, closing out the months-long legal saga over the referendum that will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot as Proposition A.
Kavanaugh’s ruling upholds a Missouri Supreme Court decision that enjoined Secretary of State Denny Hoskins from using the gerrymandered congressional map drawn during a 2025 special session. The Missouri court ordered Hoskins to use the map in place in 2022 and 2024 because the bill creating the new map, now subject to a statewide vote, had never legally taken effect.
Other cases are pending over side issues. But Kavanaugh’s decision leaves the 2022 map in place as Tuesday’s ballot deadline arrives, dealing a potentially final blow to efforts to use the 2025 districts in November. While opponents of the plan lost most major decisions, they won the ones that counted most — whether a redistricting plan is subject to a referendum and whether a legal referendum petition stops enforcement of a new state law.
The ballot to be finalized at 5 p.m. Tuesday will have the referendum as Proposition A and a congressional election based on a map drawn in 2022 that is expected to return a delegation of six Republicans and two Democrats to Washington.
Kavanaugh did not elaborate on his decision. 
In turning down the emergency application for a stay, Kavanaugh created no precedent on the issues raised by the state. But the decision does show that he did not find enough convincing argument that the state would likely prevail in a hearing by the full court or that the state would suffer “several irreparable harms” as claimed in the application.
People Not Politicians, the political action committee that submitted the referendum petition, on Sunday urged Kavanaugh to reject the state’s application and uphold both parts of Thursday’s ruling from the state Supreme Court.
People Not Politicians is represented at the Supreme Court by attorney Abha Khanna of Seattle, working with a six-member team that included the four Jefferson City attorneys, led by Chuck Hatfield, who represented People Not Politicians in the state court actions.
In the opening paragraphs of the filing, the attorneys write that the only reason the case is at the nation’s highest court now is the decisions to delay made by Hoskins during the signature verification process.
Hoskins “waited as long as possible to manufacture the present dispute” and held the congressional primary using the 2025 map, they wrote, “in the hopes of running out the clock on the judiciary’s tolerance for a last-minute reversion to the 2022 districts.”
Now, they wrote, Hoskins wants “this court to deliver him the political victory to which he was never entitled under the Missouri Constitution. This court cannot and should not reward the secretary’s scheme to outsmart Missouri voters, Missouri law, and the Missouri Supreme Court by granting applicants the extraordinary relief they seek.”
A key point made by Missouri Solicitor General Lou Capozzi in the state’s appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court was that the mechanism for changing between districts is too time consuming and difficult to complete before ballots must be delivered starting Sept. 19.
County clerks, however, told the Missouri Supreme Court that switching voters to the map used in 2022 and 2024 is a relatively simple process. And the Jackson County Board of Elections told the Kansas City Star it would be ready to hold the election in the 2022 boundaries. 
There was no decision as of late Tuesday afternoon in a separate case filed in St. Louis federal court by U.S. Rep. Bob Onder, state Sen. Rick Brattin and two voters.
The redistricting story began in the summer of 2025, when Onder, of Lake St. Louis, got the ear of President Donald Trump to tell him that Missouri, like Texas, could provide additional GOP seats to bolster the party’s thin majority in Congress.
Since Missouri lost a seat after the 2010 census, it has sent six Republicans and two Democrats to the U.S. House each election.
Onder won his seat in 2022, the year he and other members of the state Senate’s conservative caucus were outmaneuvered as they tried to force a congressional map that would tilt the 5th District, based in Kansas City, to the GOP.
And, despite initial misgivings, Republicans got in line behind Trump. Gov. Mike Kehoe called a special session inflamed with partisanship, including a state Senate rule change that effectively silenced Democrats, that forced through what the GOP majority wouldn’t do in 2022.
The legal and political backlash that followed has not yet spent its full force. It began when People Not Politicians began circulating the referendum petition and intensified as it became clear there would be more than enough signatures to qualify for the ballot.
Legally, the battle has upended the consensus on the effect that filing a referendum petition has on legislation as well as delivered strong new precedent upholding the governor’s power to select subjects for a special session and the General Assembly’s power to redistrict at any time.
Politically, the climax will be written in November, when voters decide on both the referendum and the congressional candidates selected in the primary.
The flurry of filings over the weekend shows the intense national interest in the outcome of the Missouri case.
Republican attorneys general from Florida, Texas and 18 other states filed in support of Missouri, arguing it is not legal to change voting districts between the primary and the general election. 
Meanwhile, in Texas, that state’s Supreme Court is deciding whether local voting districts can be changed after the primary to dilute voting strength of minorities.
The American Center for Law and Justice also sent a brief to the court urging it to rule for Hoskins.
On the other side, the Campaign Legal Center, the American Civil Liberties Union of Missouri Foundation and the American Civil Liberties Union Foundation joined forces to file a brief supporting People Not Politicians, as did the two Missouri voters who tried to get the 2025 map suspended while signatures were being checked.
A key point made by Missouri Solicitor General Lou Capozzi is that the mechanism for changing between districts is too time consuming and difficult to complete before ballots must be delivered starting Sept. 19.
County clerks, however, told the Missouri Supreme Court that switching voters to the map used in 2022 and 2024 is a relatively simple process. And the Jackson County Board of Elections told the Kansas City Star it would be ready to hold the election in the 2022 boundaries. 
This story will be updated.

description: Special Olympics Delaware announced that the 2026 Special Olympics Delaware State Bowling Tournament will be held at Mid-County Lanes in Middletown, Delaware, on September 12.   Special Olympics Delaware’s State Bowling Tournament will make its return to Mid-County Lanes in Middletown, Delaware, on September 12, according to a press release distributed on Se[...]
text:
Special Olympics Delaware athletes compete in the 2025 State Bowling Tournament at Mid-County Lanes. Photo Credit: Special Olympics Delaware.
Special Olympics Delaware announced that the 2026 Special Olympics Delaware State Bowling Tournament will be held at Mid-County Lanes in Middletown, Delaware, on September 12.
 
Special Olympics Delaware’s State Bowling Tournament will make its return to Mid-County Lanes in Middletown, Delaware, on September 12, according to a press release distributed on September 3. 
Mid-County Lanes will host the 2026 Special Olympics Delaware State Bowling Tournament throughout the day, starting at 8:30 a.m. This year’s event will bring together over 470 Special Olympics athletes and unified partners from all five Special Olympics Delaware areas across the state, according to the release. 
“There’s something special about seeing the lanes filled with athletes giving their all, cheering on their teammates, and celebrating every strike, spare, and personal best,” said the Director of Sports & Area Engagement for Special Olympics Delaware, Kylie Lavelle. “As one of the largest bowling tournaments ever held by Special Olympics Delaware, this event reflects the incredible growth of our program and the enthusiasm our athletes have for competition. We’re proud to bring together so many athletes and Unified partners for a weekend that highlights achievement, sportsmanship, and inclusion.” 
The event will feature competitions in singles, doubles, unified doubles and ramp and bumper divisions. There will be three timeslots for competition — 8:30 a.m. until 11:00 a.m., 12:30 p.m. until 3:00 p.m. and 4:30 p.m. until 6:30 p.m. — and each timeslot will begin with an opening ceremony and close with the distribution of medals and ribbons, according to the release. The awards will be presented by law enforcement.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana public defenders struggle to cover expenses, audit report says
description: Twelve of Louisiana’s 42 local public defender offices spent more money than they received in fiscal year 2024, highlighting the long budget struggle of public defense overall.
text:
Louisiana public defender districts continue to struggle with deficit spending. State Public Defender Rémy Starns has attributed these financial problems to an unreliable funding source. (Photo by Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch)More than a quarter of Louisiana’s 42 local public defender offices spent more money than they received during fiscal year 2024-25, highlighting the yearslong budget struggles of public defense overall. 

The 24th Judicial District office, which covers Jefferson Parish, had the largest cost overrun, spending $1 million more on public defense than it took in during the fiscal cycle that ended June 30, 2025, according to a Louisiana Legislative Auditor report released Monday.
While 12 public defender districts overspent in the fiscal cycle, they had enough reserves to cover the losses, according to the auditor’s report.

Still, the public defender system has strained for years to meet its financial demands and has required more state funding to stay afloat than many elected officials are comfortable giving. 
State Public Defender Rémy Starns has attributed the system’s financial problems to unreliable funding sources at the local level. 

“The unstable, inadequate and insufficient nature of our primary funding stream has always resulted in ‘deficit spending’ by several districts each year,” Starns wrote in an Aug. 20 written response to the auditor’s report.
Starns did not immediately respond to a call and text message made to his cell phone Tuesday.
The state provided close to half of the $79.8 million public defenders spent in fiscal year 2024-25, according to the report. The other half came mostly from local sources, including conviction and user fees. In Louisiana, a large portion of local public defender revenue has traditionally come from a $45 fee assessed when a defendant is convicted of a crime or pleads guilty. This includes convictions for traffic offenses.
Revenue from these fees has declined and can fluctuate drastically from year to year.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 
District attorneys in several jurisdictions have also set up diversion programs for traffic citations, which allow violators to bypass conviction and not pay the public defense fee. Instead, they pay prosecutors to take part in an alternative program that might keep the offense from affecting their auto insurance rates or help them avoid a more substantial fine. 
Starns pushed legislation earlier this year that would have provided more stability to the public defense system’s finances. It would have ensured public defenders’ funding increases every time district attorneys’ state funding goes up. 
The measure stalled over concerns that legislators would lose control over the amount of public defense funding the state provided every year. 

Starns said in his response to the auditor that he would press for legislative change again in 2027. 
In the report, the auditor suggested the Office of the State Public Defender monitor local offices closely to make sure their reserve funds don’t dip to under 15% of their annual expenditures. 

Starns agreed to do so and said he had hired more staff to track district office spending. 
Other public defender offices that spent more than they made for 2024-25 include those that cover the following parishes: Allen Caddo, Bienville, Bossier, Cameron, Claiborne, East Feliciana, Evangeline, Franklin, Iberia, Jackson, Richland, St. Bernard, St. Martin, St. Mary, Webster, West Carroll, West Feliciana. Some of the offices cover more than one parish.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

title: Trump doesn’t have the power to limit mail-in voting, lawmakers tell US Supreme Court
text: The hotly contested U.S. Postal Service rule restricting mail-in voting usurps Congress’ authority, as well as states’ power to administer elections, more than 250 current and former members of Congress said in a filing to the U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday.All 47 members of the U.S. Senate Democratic Caucus, 199 current House Democrats and 15 former House Republicans signed the friend-of-the-court brief opposing President Donald Trump’s policy to add several requirements to mail ballots. The U.S. Constitution “is unambiguous” in empowering states to run elections, while Congress can enact laws to oversee elections generally, they argued.“Congress has passed several laws regulating federal elections—though it has always done so surgically, deliberately leaving the States with considerable room to maneuver,” they wrote.The executive branch has no role, they said. The Trump administration has argued the rule, published last month, requires only “modest” technical specifications for mail ballots and that states transmit lists of eligible voters to receive the ballots. The rule is a targeted measure affecting mail delivery, not elections, the administration says.But the lawmakers say that argument fails. The agency cannot take action related to elections without a congressional directive, they wrote. Congress never wrote a law asking for the requirements included in the USPS rule, they said. Executive orderIn this case, Trump spurred the Postal Service to write the rule in a March executive order, based on the unsubstantiated premise that vote-by-mail is vulnerable to fraud. That shows the rule is meant to address Trump’s concerns about election administration, not mail specifications, the lawmakers said.“The integrity of our constitutional system depends on each branch keeping to its assigned role,” they wrote. “The Framers set up a two-part system that gave States default authority to regulate federal elections subject to Congress’s authority to override the States. The Framers did not provide the President with any authority to interfere in that system, nor has Congress imbued the Executive Branch with any such authority by statute.”Spokespeople for the White House, USPS and the Department of Justice, which is representing the Trump administration in the case, did not immediately return messages seeking comment Tuesday.In a separate brief, the legal advocacy group the Society for the Rule of Law made a similar argument, saying the federal postal law the administration has cited provides only broad language that does not empower the agency to regulate election mail.“The non-election, boilerplate … provisions on which Applicants rely are not a secret, alternative way for the USPS to bar ballot mail, conditionally or otherwise, on the eve of election day,” the group wrote. “Under the federalism presumption and the major question doctrine, the USPS needed a clear statement of statutory authority.”Rushed deliveryThe rule would require technical elements such as unique barcodes on ballot envelopes. Elections experts say those requirements are unworkable in time for the fall’s midterm elections because states have already designed, printed and — in some cases — begun sending ballots.The rule would also require states to send to the federal government lists of eligible voters, which would be checked against a Department of Homeland Security database to verify citizenship. The rule bans the Postal Service from delivering ballots to registered voters who are not verified through that method.The online portal that the rule says states should use for this process has still, less than two months until Election Day, not been introduced to states. A whistleblower last week reported the rushed development has led to myriad problems with the tool, which could result in legitimate ballots being rejected.Opponents, including more than 20 Democratic state officials and voting rights groups that sued to challenge the rule, say it would risk disenfranchisement for the millions of voters, including Trump, who vote by mail.High court ruling pendingThe rule has been the subject of rapidfire legal fighting over the past several weeks, and the Supreme Court is now weighing whether to overturn a Massachusetts federal judge’s order pausing the rule while litigation continues, after the Trump administration filed an appeal over the weekend.Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson on Sunday asked the states and voting rights groups challenging the rule to file their response to the application by Wednesday at 4 p.m. Eastern.That district court injunction from Judge Indira Talwani, who was appointed by President Barack Obama, held that the rule was likely unconstitutional and unlawful for reasons the members of Congress articulated Tuesday: The Constitution grants states and Congress the power to oversee elections and states would be harmed if they are forced to comply with the regulation before courts can determine its legality.

title: Planned Parenthood of Montana clinic to open in Bozeman
description: Planned Parenthood of Montana announced Tuesday it is opening a new clinic in Bozeman in summer 2027. In a news release, Planned Parenthood said it is proud to be expanding when sexual and reproductive care infrastructure is shrinking across the nation. It said the clinic will provide procedural abortion, which is only available in Missoula, […]
text:
(Thomas Barwick/Getty Images)Planned Parenthood of Montana announced Tuesday it is opening a new clinic in Bozeman in summer 2027.
In a news release, Planned Parenthood said it is proud to be expanding when sexual and reproductive care infrastructure is shrinking across the nation.
It said the clinic will provide procedural abortion, which is only available in Missoula, Helena and the Flathead in Montana.
The organization has health centers in Billings, Helena, Great Falls and Missoula, plus “a robust telehealth program.”
In an interview, Planned Parenthood of Montana CEO and President Martha Fuller said the organization is locating its new health center in Bozeman for several reasons. Bozeman is one of the fastest-growing cities in Montana and has a young population, she said, and it has not had a consistent abortion provider for a long time.
She said the need already is demonstrated there.
“We, every year, see about 1,400 patients coming from the Bozeman area to our other areas not just for abortion care but other services,” Fuller said.
Bozeman also has a busy airport, and she said at least once a month, out-of-state travelers fly into Bozeman and drive to Helena for care.
The Guttmacher Institute, a nonprofit research and policy organization with a mission to advance sexual and reproductive rights, said 200 people traveled to Montana for abortion in 2025. Fuller said many come from Idaho, which has a total ban on abortion. The Guttmacher Institute counts 13 states with complete abortion bans.
A news release about the health center said the $2 million renovation started Tuesday with $1.5 million raised to date with help from Bozeman volunteers, and the project will transform a professional building “into a high-caliber medical space.”
The center will have around seven rooms, including space for consultations, smaller-sized exam rooms, and larger rooms for procedures.
The organization said it aims to raise an additional $1.5 million to support operations for its first year. Fuller said some donations are coming from out-of-state supporters, but the project has seen “an incredible response” from donors in Bozeman and across Montana.
In a statement, Planned Parenthood of Montana Chief Medical Officer Dr. Samuel Dickman said many patients prefer to have an abortion procedure instead of a medication abortion, whether they’re farther along in a pregnancy, have a condition that requires a procedure, or “want the certainty of not being pregnant when they walk out the door.”
“That choice is what our patients deserve, and they shouldn’t have to drive long distances for it,” Dickman said in a statement.
The Montana Constitution protects abortion, but the government may regulate abortion after fetal viability. In a 1999 decision, the Montana Supreme Court said the constitution’s strict right to privacy covers choices in medical care, including abortion. In 2024, voters approved a constitutional amendment that says people have the right to make decisions about their own pregnancy, including the right to an abortion.
Fuller said lawmakers can do many things to increase access to sexual and reproductive health services, but she does not anticipate seeing such legislation from the 2027 Montana Legislature.
The Montana Legislature has attempted to restrict abortion in the past, but legislation has not withstood court challenges.
In the 2025 session, Fuller said Planned Parenthood saw a “significant decline” in the number of bills that aimed to curtail abortion, and no litigation came out of it. However, she said Planned Parenthood of Montana is the largest provider of gender-affirming care in the state, and she anticipates restrictions proposed in the 2027 Montana Legislature.
A spokesperson for the Legislative Services Division said Tuesday no draft bill requests are specifically related to abortion access or gender-affirming care so far, although some requests seek to make general revisions to health care laws.
The new health center is supported by peer providers including Bridgercare, the news release said. It said the new clinic will co-locate with Good Medicine Wellness Center, which will provide mental health care and community programming to Bozeman’s Indigenous community.



Statements from Bridgercare, Montana Family Planning, Planned Parenthood of Montana
Statement from Stephanie McDowell, executive eirector, Bridgercare and Montana Family Planning:
“We have enjoyed a strong, collaborative relationship with Planned Parenthood of Montana for decades, and we have tremendous respect for the work they do to advance reproductive healthcare across our state. Abortion is healthcare, and people have the right to make their own healthcare decisions with safety, dignity, and support. We’re excited to welcome them to Bozeman and look forward to continuing that partnership as we work together to ensure people have access to the care, information, and support they need.”
Statement from Dr. Samuel Dickman, Chief Medical Officer, Planned Parenthood of Montana:
“Bozeman will soon have a new Planned Parenthood health center that offers primary care, medication abortion, and procedural abortion services. Many patients either need or prefer to have an abortion procedure rather than a medication abortion, whether that’s because they’re farther along in a pregnancy, because they have a medical condition that means they need a procedural abortion, or they simply want the certainty of not being pregnant when they walk out the door. That choice is what our patients deserve, and they shouldn’t have to drive long distances for it. Building new abortion access in Bozeman, which is a key access point for much of Montana, Wyoming, Idaho, and Utah, and which has the busiest airport in Montana, will make it that much easier for our patients to get abortions and other critically important medical services. We’re looking forward to meeting that need.”
Statement from Martha Fuller, CEO & President, Planned Parenthood of Montana:
“For over 55 years, Planned Parenthood of Montana has served Montanans and their families, and we are proud to provide care across four health centers and via telehealth in every corner of our state. Everyone — no matter their zip code — deserves access to affordable, quality reproductive, preventative, and primary health care. We will always do whatever we can to ensure our communities have access to the care and resources needed to live healthy, thriving lives.  In the face of relentless political attacks on sexual and reproductive health and rights and Planned Parenthood’s mission, we are not backing down. That is why we are proud to be in the process of opening a new health center in Bozeman to serve more of our community members with the care and information they need.  We are grateful for the support from our generous donors and community leaders.”

name: VTDigger
title: State regulators say Vermont Lt. Gov. John Rodgers grew weed at unlicensed site
description:
Rodgers, who is running for reelection this year, downplayed the allegations as “a routine and common administrative matter.” He faces a $5,000 fine.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  State regulators say Vermont Lt. Gov. John Rodgers grew weed at unlicensed site.
text:
Lt. Gov. John Rodgers follows along as the Senate discusses a bill at the Statehouse in Montpelier in March 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Vermont Lt. Gov. John Rodgers is facing a $5,000 fine from state regulators after an inspector found him growing at least 100 cannabis plants at a site in Glover where he did not have permission to do so.
The Cannabis Control Board issued Rodgers a formal notice last month that he had violated state rules dictating how and where marijuana can be grown, according to records obtained by VTDigger. Rodgers has permission to grow cannabis on a different property, but not at the one in question, according to state regulators.
Rodgers — who is currently running for reelection — is pushing back on the board’s decision and plans to formally contest it, according to records VTDigger obtained. 
State regulators have set a meeting about the situation for Wednesday morning, at which they will “explore resolutions that are acceptable to (Rodgers) and the Board,” records state. The meeting is not open to the public, according to Patrick Crowley, a spokesperson for the control board.
In a statement to VTDigger Tuesday, the lieutenant governor called the situation “a routine and common administrative matter.”
“I’m working through the normal process with the CCB to get it resolved,” he wrote, adding that as lieutenant governor he has “prided myself on having one of the most open and transparent administrations in recent years.”
Rodgers has long been a vocal advocate for Vermont’s cannabis industry. He has said he grew weed on a small scale before it was legal and later set up a business in the regulated market. He’s had a license to cultivate cannabis at an address on Rodgers Road in Glover — which is named for his family — since 2023, according to regulators.
But the violation charges that Rodgers was also growing cannabis at an address about a mile away on Daniels Pond Road, even though he had not submitted the necessary documentation with the state to do so there. The latter address is also in Glover.
State rules adopted in July 2025 allow license-holders to cultivate cannabis at two “non-abutting” addresses — as regulators said Rodgers was doing — but they have to prove both sites meet certain requirements and that the sites are close by, according to the violation notice.
The violation says a state inspector visited the growing operation on Rodgers Road in October 2025. During that inspection, Rodgers said he planned to use a greenhouse located on Daniels Pond Road to cultivate cannabis plants in 2026.
In June, the agent conducted another inspection on Rodgers Road and asked to see the site on Daniels Pond Road. At the latter location, the agent “observed an unlocked greenhouse containing vegetable starts and approximately 200 cannabis seedlings.” 
The property “has never been authorized as a site of cultivation activities,” the notice states, because Rodgers never formally submitted information required to cultivate cannabis at an address other than the site on Rodgers Road. 
In a brief written response to regulators last month, Rodgers said that he has since moved the plants in question to the location where he has permission to grow. He declined to speak about the details of the situation on the record in an interview Tuesday.
The Aug. 13 notice came, notably, just days after Rodgers easily won this year’s Republican primary for lieutenant governor. He will face Democrat Molly Gray, who won her party’s primary, in the November general election.

title: Lawsuit filed to stop Oklahoma Constitutional Convention vote
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – A former Republican lawmaker has challenged Gov. Kevin Stitt’s power to call a constitutional convention. Former Rep. Mark McBride, R-Moore, on Tuesday asked the Oklahoma Supreme Court to rule that only the Legislature can submit a referendum to the people for a constitutional convention. Stitt last month issued an executive proclamation and[...]
text:
Gov. Kevin Stitt speaks at an event Oct. 29, 2025, at the Regional Food Bank of Oklahoma about the potential impacts of federal food assistance funding being cut off.  (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – A former Republican lawmaker has challenged Gov. Kevin Stitt’s power to call a constitutional convention.
Former Rep. Mark McBride, R-Moore, on Tuesday asked the Oklahoma Supreme Court to rule that only the Legislature can submit a referendum to the people for a constitutional convention.
Stitt last month issued an executive proclamation and called a special statewide election for April 6, 2027, to consider State Question 848. 
Stitt’s state question asks voters to determine if they want legislators to hold a constitutional convention that would give them the power “to propose alterations, revisions, or amendments” or even propose a new constitution.
Stitt, in a press release announcing the special election, said his ballot measure enforces state law which requires voters to have the opportunity every 20 years to request a constitutional convention.
Several bills over the years calling for a constitutional convention failed to get legislative support.
“The 20-year proviso fails to supply a sufficient rule specifying who must act, by what mechanism, at what election, or with what ballot language, all deficiencies that Oklahoma courts have consistently treated as indicators that a provision requires legislative implementation,” the lawsuit said.
The suit asks the Court to find Stitt’s action unconstitutional. It seeks to stay Stitt’s action until the legality can be determined.
“We believe only the Legislature, and not the Governor, can submit a referendum to the people of Oklahoma to call for a constitutional convention,” said Michael Burrage, one of the attorneys representing McBride.
Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond’s office and former Oklahoma Attorney General Drew Edmondson have said Stitt’s action was unconstitutional.
“Only the Supreme Court can decide who the Constitution authorizes to call for a vote regarding a constitutional convention,” said Bob Burke, who also represents McBride. “We have a wonderful Constitution that guarantees due process and equal treatment for all Oklahomans.
“We don’t want a handful of people deciding what our Constitution will look like in the future.”
Stitt’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Stitt, who is finishing his final year in office, and lawmakers over the years have clashed in court over which entity has the power to do what.

title: Utah inspected more than 9,000 watercraft for invasive species over Labor Day weekend
description: State agencies spent Labor Day weekend inspecting more than 9,000 boats, kayaks, paddleboards and other watercraft, almost half of them at Lake Powell, to prevent the spread of invasive species. The watercraft inspections are designed to keep harmful organisms like quagga mussels or Eurasian watermilfoil from spreading between water bodies. In all 9,418 wate[...]
text:
Boats leaving Lake Powell are required to undergo an exit inspection and a separate decontamination or cleaning process this summer after quagga mussels were detected. (Utah Division of Wildlife Resources)State agencies spent Labor Day weekend inspecting more than 9,000 boats, kayaks, paddleboards and other watercraft, almost half of them at Lake Powell, to prevent the spread of invasive species.
The watercraft inspections are designed to keep harmful organisms like quagga mussels or Eurasian watermilfoil from spreading between water bodies.
In all 9,418 watercraft were inspected — 440 of them at Lake Powell — and 154 decontaminated between Friday and Monday, according to a news release. Lake Powell is currently the only area in the state with a quagga mussel outbreak. 
New testing has Utah worried about zebra mussel spread in the Colorado River  

Invasive species technicians from agencies including the Utah Department of Natural Resources, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Utah State Parks, Arizona Game and Fish Department and the National Park Service performed the inspections at more than 40 inspection stations.
In their inspections, DNR officials recorded violations of Utah law looking to prevent the spread of invasive species, according to the news release, mostly from boaters who hadn’t completed the state’s mandatory mussel-aware boater program course, paid the aquatic invasive species fee or failed to remove drain plugs while transporting their watercraft.  
Quagga mussels can spread to water lines, clogging pipes and costing millions of dollars to remove, and damage boat engines. They remove plankton from water, disrupting food supplies for fish. Eurasian watermilfoil spreads quickly to form thick mats that block sunlight, harming native plants and fish, and can clog irrigation systems and tangle around boat propellers. 
DNA from invasive zebra mussels was recently detected for the first time in the Colorado River near Moab, and in neighboring Idaho, quagga mussels have been found for a fourth year in the Snake River.
More information about invasive species can be found at Utah’s STD of the Sea website, which includes a list of decontamination stations around the state and requirements for watercraft.
