title: Proposed data centers subjected to local approvals under Healey order
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service
description: The guardrails, which include expectations for securing tax breaks, stipulate that new data centers should directly procure or develop the energy resources to support their operations — without raising energy costs for ratepayers and straining the electric grid.
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY signed an executive order Tuesday subjecting proposed data center projects to local approval before developers can move onto state permitting, representing her administration’s latest crackdown on the facilities after halting tax breaks earlier this summer.
Pending data centers will now need to strike community benefits agreements with host communities that align with state standards before state permitting can get underway. The executive order also blocks the use of non-disclosure agreements between state agencies and data centers to “ensure a transparent and fair approval process,” Healey’s office said.
The governor in late June paused applications for data center tax incentives, as her administration also rolled out a framework for data center development to protect public health and the environment.
The guardrails, which include expectations for securing tax breaks, stipulate that new data centers should directly procure or develop the energy resources to support their operations — without raising energy costs for ratepayers and straining the electric grid. Data centers should also be situated where sufficient water supplies, wastewater and infrastructure exists, and they must minimize air emissions. Communities should also play a “meaningful role” in project planning and development, the Healey administration said.
Under the executive order, data centers projects with peak electricity demand topping 25 megawatts must show they are adhering to the administration’s framework to secure permits. The order also creates the “Ratepayer Protection Fund,” designed to give money back to customers.
“We’d like to have data centers be able to provide their own clean energy on day one,” Healey said at a press conference Tuesday afternoon. “And if they can’t, then they’re going to need to pay ratepayers for the energy that they consume until their own supply is in place.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Air National Guard members return home after extended deployment
description:
Air Guard members returned to Vermont on Sunday after being deployed for about eight months in both the Caribbean and the Middle East. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Air National Guard members return home after extended deployment.
text:
Vermont National Guard Sgt. Taylor Steele of Port Jervis, New York hugs his three-year-old son Jace at the end of a deployment ceremony at the Ethan Allen Firing Range in Jericho on Friday, May 29, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Vermont Air National Guard members returned home Sunday after a roughly eight-month deployment. 
Guard members from Vermont’s 158th Fighter Wing were deployed this winter on back to back missions to the Caribbean and the Middle East, though details of their exact role in those missions have been scarce.
“We are incredibly proud of what they represent, but today, more than anything, we are grateful to welcome them home,” said Adjutant Gen. Henry Harder Jr., in the guard’s announcement Tuesday. 
Just last month, Vermont guard members appeared to be overseas for one of their longest deployments in recent memory with no end in sight. And Gov. Phil Scott said during a press conference in late July that he had no updates on the deployment. 
“This is a federal issue and they don’t talk with us much about what they’re doing,” Scott said. 
A Vermont Air National Guard member returns home on Sept. 6, 2026. Courtesy of Vermont Air National Guard.
“I’m very concerned about the families of guard members who thought that they were just going to be away for a short period of time,” Scott added. He said at the time that Vermont officials were advocating to bring guard members home as soon as possible. 
The Vermont Air National Guard has about 1,000 members and a fleet of 20 F-35A fighter jets, which operate out of the Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in South Burlington. Joseph Brooks, a spokesperson for the Vermont National Guard, did not respond to requests for comment Tuesday about the details of the guard’s deployment and return. 
A June letter from Vermont’s congressional delegation called the 158th Fighter Wing’s deployment “unique,” explaining Vermont’s unit was the first of National Guard troops to transition directly to supporting in the war in Iran after aiding in the U.S. military operation to overthrow Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. 
While the Guard’s deployment stretched on, 27 veterans and guard family members signed a letter to Scott and legislators urging them to support a state law that would ban overseas deployment of the guard without congressional approval, according to the Brattleboro Reformer. 
Top military officials announced in early March that Vermont guard members would assist U.S. forces in the war in Iran. Although the U.S. has launched ongoing air strikes against Iran since February, Congress hasn’t officially declared war against the country. 
More than 7,800 people had been killed in Iran and Lebanon in late June, according to the BBC. And the Pentagon reports that 18 U.S. soldiers have been killed in the conflict, according to the New York Times. 
Members of Vermont’s congressional delegation have previously condemned both the Guard’s deployment to the Caribbean and to the Middle East. 

READ MORE

And in late June, Vermont’s congressional delegation sent a letter to U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asking him to resolve recordkeeping and payroll issues that they said guard members were experiencing. 
The Air Guard’s deployment comes during an especially tumultuous time for the U.S. military. At least 20 generals, admirals and civilian leaders have been fired or left their jobs since Hegseth took over at the beginning of President Trump’s second administration, according to CBS news. Just last week, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, the army’s top civilian leader, resigned from his post after clashing with Hegseth. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Air National Guard members return home after extended deployment.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Q&A: State Sen. Mike Reese, McNeese State president
description: Mike Reese is both a Republican state senator from Leesville and president of McNeese State University in Lake Charles, having taken on the latter role July 1. In a recent interview, he detailed his work chairing a study committee looking at Louisiana’s higher education funding formula.  This transcript of the interview has been edited for […]
text:
Sen. Mike Reese listens to debate on the floor of the Louisiana Senate on May 27, 2025. (Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)Mike Reese is both a Republican state senator from Leesville and president of McNeese State University in Lake Charles, having taken on the latter role July 1. In a recent interview, he detailed his work chairing a study committee looking at Louisiana’s higher education funding formula. 
This transcript of the interview has been edited for length and clarity. The full interview can be heard on Episode 67 of “The Light Switch” podcast. 

Piper Hutchinson: Why is the state studying the higher education funding formula? 

Mike Reese: I’m getting all these calls from institutions in my district or in other areas of the state that are saying if we don’t provide this additional funding, that they’re going to have a difficult time providing the service they provide. It has finally kind of built to this point where I think that the legislature has to kind of pause to say, “Well, wait a minute, we need to better understand what drives this formula.” 
I think that the legislature doesn’t want to be in the business of picking the winners and losers.

Hutchinson: What are the complaints that you’re hearing from the universities? 
Reese: Overall, it’s just it’s a total level of funding, right? They’ve said our portion of state support has diminished, and it’s more and more difficult to meet our mission with the amount of state support that we get. And we don’t have a lot of areas to go to, right? You have the state support, we have some scholarship support, we have some federal support in the way of Pell Grants, and a few other grants that we may receive. 
And then after that, it’s really the transfer of the cost to the students through tuition and fees. We’re very reluctant to continue to transfer more of that cost. 
Hutchinson: This task force is looking at how to allocate the funding that has been given to higher education. But you mentioned that there’s been a decrease in state support. Are there also discussions on the legislative end about providing more funding for the universities? 
Reese: I think that’s absolutely the case. So I think that you know part of this process is education to the rest of the legislators, as much as it is a review of how the formula currently works. Because the formula, if you actually stretched it out to what it would predict would be needed, it would be more like $2 billion, and we’re funding it more at the tune of about $700 million. So we know that it’s constrained. 
Higher education in Louisiana, short $800M, appears headed for a funding overhaul

Hutchinson: Being in the legislature, you’re very aware that there’s never enough money to go around. Can you tell us about some of the constraints contributing to that for universities and the state as a whole? 
Reese: There’s an anticipation that our state’s going to receive less in Medicaid funding from the federal government. In Louisiana, it’s not constitutionally protected — the funding responsibility of the state to higher education — and so when we have to start cutting the budget somewhere, typically one of the areas that has been the bill payer for other state responsibility has been higher education. We don’t want to be constrained by the lack of a qualified workforce. 
Hutchinson: One of the big questions that predicated this task force and some lawmakers’ interests in the funding formula was this “underrepresented minority” metric within the funding formula. That’s now been taken out, but can you tell me a little bit about what the concern was about that for lawmakers? Was it a concern about at least the perception that universities were continuing to fund DEI after lawmakers have made it clear that that was no longer a priority? 
Reese: Clearly the legislature had a position on that. Even the federal government had a position on that, and I think that it was meant to not be identified in the formula. 
Hutchinson: Do you think the task force report itself is going to include an overhaul of the formula or call for changes to the formula? 
Reese: I don’t know yet. Is it a matter of just that we need more money going into this formula that works pretty well, or do we need a little bit of both? Do we need some tweaks to the formula to address some of the problems that this commission is going to highlight, in addition to the legislature perhaps enhancing the amount of state funding going into the formula? 
Hutchinson: How are you managing two pretty big jobs? 
Reese: Right now we’re not in session. I very recently resigned from all of my committee assignments. I retained this higher education funding formula [task force] because I think it’s so important and timely right now in Louisiana’s growing economy, and then I’ve retained a couple of military-related committee assignments that don’t meet frequently but are vitally important to my district. And so I think this is vitally important work. It’s hard for me to do the work in higher education and the rest of my colleagues do the work in higher education if we don’t get this right in terms of the funding formula.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont, Fazio offer preview on coming debate over electric rates
description: The two candidates serve on CT's Bond Commission, which voted Tuesday to borrow $125M to offset the public benefits charge on electric bills.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont and his Republican challenger, state Sen. Ryan Fazio of Greenwich, practiced campaign talking points on electric costs Tuesday while seated together at a meeting of the state Bond Commission and then in back-to-back press conferences in the atrium of the Legislative Office Building.
The candidates are not scheduled to debate until next month, but Lamont chairs the Bond Commission and Fazio is one of two Republican lawmakers on the panel, which voted Tuesday to authorize $125 million in bonding to offset portions of what’s known as the public benefits charge on electric bills.
Lamont, a Democrat seeking a third term, was happy to share credit for the item that will contribute to lower electric costs, noting later it arises that from legislation that passed in 2025 with the support of Fazio and nearly every member of the General Assembly.
Fazio, the ranking Senate Republican on the legislature’s Energy and Technology Committee, mildly noted during the commission meeting electricity remains expensive in Connecticut.
“So I’d like to take the occasion just to say, while [this] will shift some of the costs in people’s electric bills temporarily, it’s a good time to remind ourselves that permanently we need to reduce many of these costs, both in the public benefits charge and the supply portion of our bill, as well,” Fazio said.
“Thanks, Ryan,”  Lamont replied.
The public benefits charge covers various state-mandated policy programs such as clean energy procurements and benefits for low-income customers, as well as a long-term contracts to purchase carbon-free electricity, such as the state’s deal with Millstone Nuclear Power Station. Those contracts cost consumers extra when natural gas used to generate electricity is cheap, but benefit them when prices are high, as they are now.
The gubernatorial candidates were less polite after the meeting in discussing Connecticut’s new status as a state with falling electric rates — they fell by 15% in May, a consequence of the largely disappearing public benefits charge from monthly bills and savings from the long-term contracts for electricity generated by nuclear power.
Lamont responded sharply when asked about Fazio blaming him for the cost of electricity.
“Then I’m the guy responsible for turning the public benefits charge into a credit, saving you about 15% on your on your bill as of, say, compared to a year ago,” Lamont said. “We’ve got a long way to go there. We’ve had the highest electric prices in the country going back 50 years.”
Lamont blamed President Donald Trump for destabilizing the economy with an erratic approach to tariffs and orders that briefly halted the completion of an offshore wind project, Revolution Wind. Lamont said Trump’s trade war with Canada eventually could affect the cost and availability of power.
“It’s no help when President Trump is talking about tariffs on hydro coming down from Quebec. It’s no help when he says he wants to pull the plug on Revolution Wind,” Lamont said. “Millstone, that contract is saving us money, with the incredibly high price of natural gas right now. Thank God we have that hedge because it’s saving our ratepayers hundreds of millions.”
Fazio said blaming the governor for the cost of electricity was justified by the Lamont administration continuing to pursue measures lowering greenhouse gases, including requiring a certain amount of power be purchased from renewable sources that typically are more expensive.
The current savings from the public benefits charge is temporary, Fazio said.
“I heard the governor take credit — ‘I’ve eliminated the public benefits charge’ — even though he just signed a bill into law that’ll increase public benefits charges for the next 20 years,” Fazio said. “We all know that the public benefits charge is very volatile. Sometimes it’s as low as zero. Sometimes it’s as high as 30%. But it averages 15% to 20% and will continue to in the future.”
The bill he referenced was House Bill 5340, a measure that extended Connecticut’s solar incentive programs over the objections of Republicans who argued that the proliferation of rooftop solar has become a costly burden on the rest of the state’s electric customers.
CT Mirror reporter John Moritz contributed to this story.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware governor signs biomarker testing coverage bill into law
description: New law expands insurance coverage for testing that can help doctors select treatments for cancer, Alzheimer’s disease and other conditions DOVER, Del. — Gov. Matt Meyer signed legislation Tuesday afternoon expanding insurance coverage for biomarker testing, giving more Delaware patients access to technology used to diagnose diseases and identify treatments[...]
text:
Photo: Photo courtesy of the Delaware Alzheimer’s Association
New law expands insurance coverage for testing that can help doctors select treatments for cancer, Alzheimer’s disease and other conditions
DOVER, Del. — Gov. Matt Meyer signed legislation Tuesday afternoon expanding insurance coverage for biomarker testing, giving more Delaware patients access to technology used to diagnose diseases and identify treatments tailored to their conditions.
Senate Substitute No. 1 for Senate Bill 120 requires more health insurance plans, including Medicaid, to cover medically appropriate biomarker testing. The legislation unanimously passed the Senate in June before receiving approval from the House.
The law is intended to close a growing gap between advances in precision medicine and insurance coverage for the tests needed to guide care.
What biomarker testing does
Biomarker testing examines genes, proteins and other characteristics that may provide information about a disease. Doctors can use the results to diagnose some conditions earlier, determine whether a patient is likely to benefit from a particular treatment, avoid treatments unlikely to work or identify potential clinical trials.
The testing has become especially important in cancer care and is increasingly used in diagnosing and treating Alzheimer’s disease and other conditions.
Supporters say expanded access can lead to earlier diagnoses, more effective treatment, less unnecessary care and better-informed decisions by patients and doctors.
Alzheimer’s advocates welcome signing
Representatives of the Alzheimer’s Association Delaware Chapter attended the bill signing.
Glen Gray, chair of the newly organized Delaware chapter, praised Meyer’s decision to sign the measure. He said the law represents another step toward diagnosing Alzheimer’s disease earlier, when patients and their families generally have more options for treatment, planning and support.
Gray also praised Sen. Spiros Mantzavinos for leading the legislative effort, calling the bill an example of effective leadership and thanking the senator for working to improve care for Delaware’s older residents.
A tool for cancer survivors
American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network volunteer Matt Wilson underwent treatment for pancreatic cancer more than 13 years ago, when biomarker testing was not as widely used as it is today.
“Though biomarker testing did not inform my initial treatment, it is a critical tool for ensuring my cancer stays in remission,” Wilson said. “It is also critical for ensuring continued progress in the fight against this disease.”
Wilson said greater knowledge about the characteristics of an individual patient’s cancer can help doctors choose more effective treatments.
“The more we know about cancer and the better we understand how to treat it, the closer we are to ending cancer as we know it for everyone,” he said. “Biomarker testing makes that possible.”
Coverage has lagged behind medical advances
Although the use of biomarker testing has expanded, supporters of the legislation said insurance coverage has not always kept pace with advances in medicine. That can leave patients unable to obtain testing that could identify the most effective treatment for their condition.
Mantzavinos sponsored the legislation, while Rep. William Bush championed the effort in the House.
“For thousands of patients in Delaware, biomarker testing has meant more effective care and better outcomes, offering renewed hope,” said Lance Kilpatrick, government relations director for the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network. “Yet too many people still struggle to access this testing due to barriers, including inadequate insurance coverage.”
Kilpatrick said the new law will help eliminate those barriers and give more patients access to testing that could improve their care.
To Go Box

What: Information about biomarker testing and precision medicine
Who may benefit: Patients whose doctors recommend biomarker testing to diagnose a condition or help select treatment
What the new law does: Expands coverage of medically appropriate biomarker testing through more health insurance plans, including Medicaid
Learn more: Visit fightcancer.org/biomarkers

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: New audit: NC Lottery sales up, but less is going to schools
description: North Carolina’s lottery is selling more tickets than ever – but it’s putting less of the money it makes into schools, says Auditor Dave Boliek. A new audit found that gross ticket sales for the state’s Education Lottery rose from $4.3 billion in FY 2023 to $6.6 billion in FY 2025. But the percentage of […]
text:
The rapid growth in ‘digital instant games’ and lower sales of traditional lottery games were the primary causes of the decrease in the percentage of lottery proceeds transferred to the North Carolina Education Fund. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)North Carolina’s lottery is selling more tickets than ever – but it’s putting less of the money it makes into schools, says Auditor Dave Boliek.
A new audit found that gross ticket sales for the state’s Education Lottery rose from $4.3 billion in FY 2023 to $6.6 billion in FY 2025. But the percentage of that money that went to public education fell each year from 23% in 2023, 20% in 2024, and just 16% in 2025.
Growth in gross ticket sales increased an impressive 51% over two years. Yet the annual transfers to the education fund essentially remained flat, increasing from $1.02 billion in FY 2023 to $1.09 billion in FY 2024, and dipping to $1.08 billion for FY 2025.
A key factor in the declining proceeds is the rise of digital instant games, which entice players by paying out more often than traditional lottery tickets. Because of that, the lottery’s net profit on digital instants is lower.
“Digital instant games are designed to have a payout rate of approximately 87%,” wrote  Boliek in the report. “They have gone from generating zero dollars in sales in FY 2023, to $2.60 billion in sales in FY 2025, which represented approximately 40% of total lottery sales that fiscal year.”
During the same time period, scratch-off tickets and the draw games saw a decrease in sales. And that’s a trend that seems to be continuing.
Greg Bowers, the lottery’s chief financial officer, told the North Carolina Lottery Commission in late June that digital instant sales saw a 22% increase in the first 11 months of the fiscal year compared to 2025. However, scratch-off sales dipped by about 3% for the year. As for those multi-state jackpot games, those are more unpredictable: consumers are not always motivated to play until the jackpot reaches a certain level.
Bowers said sales of scratch-offs and digital instants are projected to increase by 6.39% in 2027.
But the issue for Boliek is not whether people are buying more tickets or playing more often. It’s whether the lottery is meeting its statutory obligation to provide school funding – and he says it’s not.
Boliek said the Education Lottery’s statutory target is to transfer 38% of its net revenue to the Education Fund. When the lottery was established in 2005, the target was originally 35%. But the long-term average, according to the audit, is closer to 27%, and it’s been sharply lower in recent years.
“As lottery product offerings have evolved, the relationship between maximizing sales and maintaining a targeted transfer percentage has become less clear,” auditors wrote in the report.
The agency is recommending that lottery officials work with the General Assembly to clarify whether the lottery’s objective should be maximizing dollars transferred to education, maintaining a minimum transfer percentage, or balancing both objectives within a clearer policy framework.
In response, the lottery’s chief executive officer said the General Assembly should take another look at the statutory target, which is now over 20 years old.
North Carolina’s Education Lottery sets new records but faces headwinds

“If maintaining a minimum transfer percentage remains the primary objective, the General Assembly should consider whether the current 38% statutory target to transfer to the Education Fund remains appropriate given today’s lottery products and the competitive marketplace that has developed over the past few years,” wrote lottery CEO Mark Michalko.
Michalko said the Education Lottery is working to remain competitive and maximize returns because players have more places to spend their discretionary income.
And it’s not just North Carolina. A recent analysis by the U.S. Census Bureau found other state lotteries are in the same boat. More money is coming in, but they are paying out more to keep consumers playing.
Bettors in North Carolina legally wagered more than $7 billion on sports in 2025. And in July, the most recent month for which data is available, North Carolinians bet more than $566 million on sporting events, with $14 million in estimated tax revenue returned to the state.
While the Education Lottery supports education programs in all of North Carolina’s 100 counties, the revenue from sports wagering goes to the General Fund and university athletics with $2 million appropriated for gambling addiction treatment.

title: St. Mary’s nurses file charges against management with NLRB
description: Nurses at St. Mary’s Hospital in Madison have filed official charges with the National Labor Relations Board against the hospital’s parent company, SSM Health, for allegedly violating federal law by refusing to negotiate a contract with the recently established nurses’ union.  The hospital’s nurses voted by a landslide earlier this summer to establish a unio[...]
text:
Nurses at St. Mary's Hospital in Madison have petitioned for an election to vote on joining the Service Employees International Union. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)Nurses at St. Mary’s Hospital in Madison have filed official charges with the National Labor Relations Board against the hospital’s parent company, SSM Health, for allegedly violating federal law by refusing to negotiate a contract with the recently established nurses’ union. 
The hospital’s nurses voted by a landslide earlier this summer to establish a union — a result that SSM fought to prevent the NLRB from recognizing. The efforts of management to prevent the union recognition were rebuffed by federal officials. 
In a news release on Tuesday, the nurses argued that hospital administration is wasting time engaging in anti-union activities when instead negotiations on a labor contract should be getting underway. 
The nurses have complained that the hospital administration has reduced staffing to unsafe levels, putting patient safety at risk. Staffing levels at St. Mary’s are the lowest of Madison’s seven hospitals. 
“SSM should be investing in staffing, support and retention of nurses, not wasting time and resources fighting our union, which is our voice to speak up for our patients,” St. Mary’s nurse Hannah Joers said in a statement released by the union. “Our number one goal is to win a contract which better takes patients’ level of sickness into account for staffing, and makes sure that we keep nurses by the bedside. SSM executives in St. Louis are abusing our empathy, making us do more and more with less and less. We’ve had enough, and the time has come to transform the system so that our patients’ needs come first. We will never back down and we are 1,000% determined to win a strong contract to provide the highest quality patient care.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Former Kansas prison officials pressure governor to commute death sentences
description: TOPEKA — As Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly’s final term wanes, groups against the death penalty are pushing her to commute the death sentences of nine men convicted of capital murder in Kansas, favoring life in prison without the possibility of parole. Former prison officials were the latest to advocate for abolishing the death penalty in […]
text:
Roger Werholtz, former secretary of the Kansas Department of Corrections, talks about his opposition to the death penalty during a Sept. 2, 2026, appearance on the Kansas Reflector podcast in Topeka. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — As Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly’s final term wanes, groups against the death penalty are pushing her to commute the death sentences of nine men convicted of capital murder in Kansas, favoring life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Former prison officials were the latest to advocate for abolishing the death penalty in Kansas. They convened Sept. 2 at the Statehouse in Topeka to discuss the death penalty’s inherent risks and deliver a letter to the governor’s office, urging her to commute the outstanding death sentences in Kansas.
“The larger issue for me, in particular, is simply the abolition of the death sentence in Kansas and nationally,” said Roger Werholtz, a former Kansas Department of Corrections secretary, in an interview for the Kansas Reflector podcast. “In my view, it serves no useful purpose. It does not contribute to public safety. It does not serve as a deterrent, and there is too much opportunity for error and misuse of that particular consequence for heinous crimes, and it distracts from other public safety issues and distracts from families of victims of those crimes.”

             
Werholtz was one of three former state prison officials to speak at the press conference. He was joined by Robert Sanders, a Kansas Parole Board member from 2004-2011 and longtime employee of the corrections department, and Marilyn Scafe, a Kansas Parole Board member from 1995-2006 and Missouri parole and probation officer in the 1970s.
The American Civil Liberties Union of Kansas on the same day put out a call to action, encouraging supporters to send a message to the governor, urging her to commute all remaining death sentences. In 2024, the ACLU tried to abolish the death penalty in Kansas through litigation.
Commuting Kansas death sentences helps “confront the criminal justice system’s deep failures and stop further injustice,” the organization said.
In July, a group of faith leaders similarly called on the governor to commute all existing death sentences 
The group of former prison officials emphasized the trauma the death penalty can cause for corrections staff and its ineffectiveness as a deterrent of crime.
“The death penalty does not make us safer, not in our communities or in the correctional institutions,” said Sanders, who began working for the KDOC as a corrections officer in 1978.
Six former Kansas prison employees signed the letter to the governor that requested she commute the nine remaining death sentences in Kansas on the grounds that resurrecting the death penalty would be a “time-consuming and expensive process.” Plus, the letter said, the psychological toll on corrections personnel can have a devastating impact.
“Too often the death penalty is cynically used as a political ploy,” the letter said. “Too often we have seen examples of police, prosecutorial and judicial misconduct, even here in Kansas. There is too much uncertainty in our criminal justice system to allow an irreversible penalty to continue to exist.”
The death penalty hasn’t been carried out in Kansas since 1965, when two men were hanged. It has been banned, barred and reinstated multiple times in the state’s history, most recently in 1994. Nine men sit on death row today. Several of them have outstanding clemency requests with the governor, which state law enforcement officials, including the attorney general, oppose.
Werholtz said that life without the possibility of parole is favored because prosecuting the death penalty is costly, and the risk of a wrongful conviction and execution is too great.
Werholtz served as secretary of the Kansas Department of Corrections from 2002-2010, and as interim secretary in 2019 when Kelly took office. 
“I didn’t want any employees of KDOC to have to deal with the potential consequences of an execution in Kansas,” Werholtz said. “When you talk about it in the abstract, sometimes it’s very easy to deal with, and you can be pretty cavalier about what you think you will do until you’re confronted with the reality of what you might actually have to do.” 
He added: “Fortunately, I was never required to actually make a decision or participate in the killing of another human being, and I’m very thankful for that.”
The governor’s office declined to answer specific questions about its response to the letter and the risk of unequal application of justice in prosecuting death sentences in Kansas courts.
Olivia Taylor-Puckett, a spokesperson for the governor, said in an emailed statement: “Each request for executive clemency is reviewed on a case by case basis in a process that will continue as it has throughout Gov. Kelly’s time in office.”
Kelly’s term will be up in January. She has denied three clemency requests this summer from death row inmates: John Robinson, who was convicted of killing eight women, and the Carr brothers, who went on a violent crime spree in 2000 known as the “Wichita massacre.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC groups launch campaign to defeat two tax amendments on November ballot
description: Two North Carolina groups are launching a campaign against two tax-related constitutional amendments on the November ballot, touting plans to knock on 500,000 doors and collect 100,000 pledges from voters to oppose the measures.   Down Home North Carolina and the Carolina Federation, two progressive organizing groups focused on working-class voters, announce[...]
text:
(iStock / Getty Images Plus)Two North Carolina groups are launching a campaign against two tax-related constitutional amendments on the November ballot, touting plans to knock on 500,000 doors and collect 100,000 pledges from voters to oppose the measures.  
Down Home North Carolina and the Carolina Federation, two progressive organizing groups focused on working-class voters, announced the “Fund the Future” campaign Tuesday during a virtual press conference. Down Home organizes in rural and small-town communities, while the Carolina Federation works mostly in major metropolitan areas.  
NC voters set to weigh in on limiting state income tax and property taxes in November

One amendment will ask voters this fall whether to change the state’s constitution to prevent the income tax rate from exceeding 3.5%. The other would allow the General Assembly to limit the amount by which property taxes can be increased, though it does not specify how to do so or what the limits should be. 
Republican lawmakers who supported the amendments have argued they would protect taxpayers from future tax increases and rising property-tax bills.  
“These proposals reflect the tax and fiscal approach Republican lawmakers have successfully pursued in Raleigh and would protect those principles in the North Carolina Constitution.” the North Carolina GOP said in a statement to NC Newsline.
But the two groups say the proposals would restrict the ability of state and local governments to raise revenue as North Carolina grows and costs increase. 
Jenn Frye, co-director of the Carolina Federation, said current personal and corporate income tax rates are too low to adequately fund state services, and the amendments would keep future state leaders from remedying that problem. 
“It’s time that the richest people and corporations in our state pay what they owe, and these amendments do not fix that system. They actually double down on it and lock it into our state constitution,” she said. 
The Carolina Federation began talking with voters about the amendments in mid-July. As of Aug. 24, organizers had spoken with nearly 17,000 people, they say. The group said those conversations are part of an effort to build opposition before the Nov. 3 election. 
The campaign plans have more than 55,000 conversations with voters across seven counties. It will launch a website Wednesday with information about the amendments, voter pledge forms and digital organizing tools. 
Todd Warren, a former public school teacher and statewide campaign strategist for Down Home, said the groups are drawing on previous local campaigns over issues including school funding, affordable housing, parks and other community services. 
“These campaigns have been widely successful and have won real improvements for working people in rural and urban counties,” he said.

title: New Mexico lawmakers suggest expanding farm programs statewide to help address at-risk youth
description: New Mexico lawmakers meeting in Las Cruces Tuesday morning said they’d like to replicate an agricultural program that offers jobs to at-risk youth to the communities that need it most across the state. The discussion came as legislators evaluate how to address the state's 32,000 young residents who neither work nor attend school.
text:
New Mexico lawmakers on Sept. 8, 2026, discussed whether agricultural workforce programs could help fill critical gaps for young New Mexicans who aren’t working or attending school. (Photo by Santana Ochoa/Source NM)New Mexico lawmakers meeting in Las Cruces Tuesday morning said they’d like to replicate an agricultural program that offers jobs to at-risk youth to the communities that need it most across the state.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Representatives from the Anthony Youth Farm addressed state lawmakers on the interim Economic and Rural Development and Policy Committee about how they serve southern New Mexico’s children.
Leaders at the 25-acre farm train 20 to 25 young farmers annually and harvest more than 500 pounds of vegetables per week, they said. Those veggies fed nearly 38,000 students in the Las Cruces Public Schools and Gadsden Independent School District.
The presentation came as state leaders continue evaluating solutions to a statewide problem. About 32,000 New Mexicans between the ages of 16 and 24 neither work nor go to school, according to an April Legislative Finance Committee report. The report found that more than half of the state’s “disconnected youth” reside in Bernalillo, Doña Ana or McKinley counties, and largely attributed their unemployment to housing instability, a lack of skills or training and low wages.
Since that report first published, lawmakers throughout the summer have consistently focused on the issue.
Monique Hernandez, the farm’s program manager, told state lawmakers that she believes programs like hers can offer a lifeline to those young New Mexicans who aren’t employed or attending school.
“I started as an in-trouble youth myself,” Hernandez said at Tuesday’s hearing. “I was hanging out with the wrong crowd and my mom was like, ‘You know what? You’re not going to stay home, so get to work,’ and she sent me to Anthony Youth Farm. I loved it there and created my whole career out of it.”
State lawmakers on the interim committee were enthused about the financial support they’ve directed to the program. The state Legislature earlier this year allocated $200,000 toward well construction at Anthony Youth Farm in its annual capital outlay package.
House Minority Whip Alan Martinez (R-Rio Rancho) said he would like to see programs like this established in other communities statewide, particularly Albuquerque’s South Valley, Rio Rancho, Santa Fe and Española.
“I love that idea because it has a buy-in for the whole state,” he said.
Rep. Doreen Gallegos (D-Las Cruces), who serves as chair of the interim committee, recalled approving state funding for the farm in one of her first votes as a state lawmaker after taking office in 2013.
“When we first did the ribbon cutting, it was just this piece of dirt,” she said. “I’m always very proud to see the work that you’ve done. When you see the kids out there planting and it’s 103 degrees out there, it’s very, very hard work.”

name: VTDigger
title: An upgrade shouldn’t cost you your lifeline
description:
Phone companies can cut off landline service during an “upgrade” with no warning — a real danger where cell coverage and power can't be relied on.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  An upgrade shouldn’t cost you your lifeline.
text:
Dear Editor,
I want to raise a serious problem that isn’t getting the attention it deserves: phone companies abandoning landlines and their failure to warn you that your landline will be lost when you change your service level.
We have no cellphone coverage where we are. When my husband opted to upgrade to a higher-speed internet account, I only discovered that our landline was cut afterward, when the phone didn’t work. It was not because of a power outage: It was a failure in the internet relay for the local area, something I had no way of knowing about because I couldn’t call the phone company to ask why the phone wasn’t working. This happened the day after the upgrade.
Then I discovered that the panel that monitors for freezing, fire or break-ins, which worked on the landline copper wire, had to be rewired for internet connection, at a cost of $600. We also had to purchase a battery backup. Without it, a power outage would knock out our router relay box and with it our phone service. 
I felt quite endangered when I was cut off that day, not knowing what had caused it, and then furious when I learned that our landline had been cut. I called our internet supplier and other phone companies to try to get it restored — nothing doing, not even for a fee.
The landline worked when we were cut off by a blizzard in 2010 for four days, at a time when even the roads weren’t being plowed, a major emergency. I was taking care of my dying mother, and, though physically unreachable, we were never out of touch with the hospice workers by phone. I couldn’t walk to a house with a generator — the snow was too deep, and I couldn’t leave my mother. But we weren’t cut off.

READ MORE

When I learned that the “upgrading” had cut off my landline, a day of considerable anxiety followed. I couldn’t contact anyone and thought about what would happen if, alone at the house, I had an accident or emergency. Emergency buttons, pendants, watches and so on only work via the internet if you have no landline.
The phone company had no obligation to warn us when we opted to upgrade, and it didn’t. The company has no obligation to maintain or restore the copper-wire phone lines. California has made such maintenance mandatory in rural locations where cellphone reception and electricity cannot be relied on. Vermont should do likewise.
Anna ShapiroCavendish, Vt.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Defamation suit by GOP candidate Jonathan De Barros dismissed
description: He did not dispute he was convicted of shooting two men, but claimed he cannot be called a murderer due to an appellate decision and a pardon.
text:
A Superior Court judge has dismissed the defamation lawsuit brought by Jonathan De Barros against four Republicans he accused of undermining his congressional campaign by referring to him as a murderer when describing his fatally shooting one man and wounding another in 1996.
De Barros, a Republican, did not dispute that he shot the two young men outside a recreation center in Waterbury and was sentenced to life in prison after being convicted of murder, attempted murder and assault with a firearm. But De Barros claimed he cannot be called a murderer due to an appellate decision and a pardon.
Judge John Cordani wrote in his decision that De Barros failed to meet the high burden of proving that the “political speech” employed by the defendants during a campaign was defamatory, and that a pardon expunges De Barros’s criminal record without erasing the fact he killed one young man and wounded another.
De Barros, whose suit was filed before he lost a Republican primary last month, had sought damages and a gag order barring the defendants from further commenting on his criminal record.
“Political speech of this nature is at the very heart of our right to freedom of speech since it bears upon the public’s ability to make informed decisions on the operation of our republic and on their choice of representative,” Cordani wrote in a 10-page decision dated Sept. 4.
Cordani also wrote that “although a pardon can wipe away an official criminal record, it cannot wipe clean the public consciousness of what actually happened.” 
De Barros declined comment Tuesday. He lost a primary last month for the Republican nomination in the 5th Congressional District to Chris Shea, who now faces U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, a Democrat, in the general election.
The state Appellate Court overturned De Barros’ murder conviction in July 2000 and ordered a new trial, concluding the original judge had erred in barring evidence relevant to De Barros’ claim that he shot the victims in self-defense. A second trial ended in a hung jury. 
De Barros then pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of manslaughter under the Alford Doctrine, which allows a defendant to maintain innocence while conceding the state had evidence for a conviction. The plea deal resulted in a reduced sentence, and De Barros ultimately served 19 years in prison.
His lawsuit accused four people of defamation: Jeff Weiss and Pam Salamone, who were Shea delegates at the GOP nominating convention; and Steve Pedbereznak and Dawn Maiorano for comments De Barros says they made on a podcast. Maiorano was a  Republican nominee for mayor of Waterbury, and Pedbereznak is a former Waterbury police officer.
In his lawsuit, De Barros said Salamone referred to him as a murderer in conversations with other delegates at the Republican convention and that Weiss wrote on Facebook and Twitter that De Barros “claimed to be a victim in 1996 while murdering a man in cold blood.”
“It is clear, and the plaintiff has admitted, that the statements which form the basis of all of the plaintiff’s claims rest on the exercise of the defendants’ right to freedom of speech on matters of public concern,” Cordani wrote. “The complained of statements are commentary on the fitness of the plaintiff for federal public office and were made during an active political campaign.”
Cordani wrote that the defendants’ remarks — some of which they denied saying — were protected political speech, unless they acted with actual malice.
“In order to establish actual malice, the defendants must be found to have had actual knowledge of the falsity of the statements or reckless disregard towards the falsity of the statements,” Cordani wrote.
Rep. Craig Fishbein of Wallingford, a lawyer and ranking Republican on the legislature’s Judiciary Committee, had filed the original motion for a dismissal on behalf of Weiss. He called De Barros’ litigation a SLAPP suit, an acronym for a “strategic lawsuit against public participation,” the tag lawyers apply to frivolous actions filed to intimidate or silence critics.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: State auditor sounds alarm over $7.2M in Lincoln Fire and Rescue 2025 overtime pay
description: LINCOLN — Firefighters and rescue personnel in Nebraska’s capital city reportedly racked up $7.2 million in overtime pay last year, an amount the state auditor described as “staggering.” A 15-page report released Tuesday by Nebraska Auditor Mike Foley showed that the Lincoln Fire and Rescue Department’s top 25 overtime earners received an average of $72,247[...]
text:
State Auditor Mike Foley questions millions in overtime costs in the Lincoln Fire and Rescue department. Here, members extinguish a blaze at an apartment  complex in 2022. (Jazari Kual/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Firefighters and rescue personnel in Nebraska’s capital city reportedly racked up $7.2 million in overtime pay last year, an amount the state auditor described as “staggering.”
A 15-page report released Tuesday by Nebraska Auditor Mike Foley showed that the Lincoln Fire and Rescue Department’s top 25 overtime earners received an average of $72,247 in overtime during 2025, boosting their average total annual pay to nearly $190,000.
Nebraska Auditor Mike Foley speaks with reporters after a hearing before a legislative panel on a bill brought at his request earlier this year. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The top 100 overtime earners drew an extra $45,586 on average, bringing their total average salary to about $160,000. 
Ranking No. 1 was a fire apparatus operator hired in 2012. That firefighter’s overtime pay last year amounted to $164,176 — an amount higher than the individual’s gross base pay of $113,000, the auditor’s review showed. In 2024, the same employee received about $155,000 in overtime pay and, the year before that, about $115,000.
Meanwhile, Foley’s report said, the starting salary for a Lincoln firefighter last year was about $68,000. Total gross pay of the department for 2025 was about $45 million.
The report, which detailed individual salary and overtime pay for the entire department, was sent to Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird and City Council chair Brodey Weber. 
Call for ‘performance audit’
While Foley said he can’t recall ever hearing any citizen complaints about the first responders’ professionalism, he urged city officials to conduct a performance audit of the department’s personnel scheduling practices.
“More than $7.2 million in overtime pay during a single year is not chump change, and an objective performance audit of the department’s scheduling strategy might yield taxpayer savings,” Foley wrote in a news release.
Lincoln Fire Chief David Engler (Photo courtesy of Lincoln Fire and Rescue)
Lincoln Fire Chief David Engler, responding via an email statement, said several factors have contributed to increased overtime in recent years including the opening of new stations, placement of additional medic units into daily service, employee leave and required training and deployment obligations. He also cited contractually negotiated staffing requirements and pay increases.
Engler said his department has a responsibility to ensure reliable, around-the-clock emergency response while being a sound steward of taxpayer dollars. He said overtime is a “necessary part” of the operation. 
“In some circumstances, overtime is more cost effective than adding permanent positions or outsourcing specialized work,” the fire chief said. 
Foley at the same time admonished city officials for apparent inactivity of the city committee charged with auditing duties. He said the Lincoln Municipal Code requires the City Council to select at least one subject annually for a performance audit by the city committee. However, he said, no such audits have occurred in over a decade.
Furthermore, said Foley, the code requires the committee to hold  meetings at least quarterly, but it apparently had not convened in about five years, since summer of 2021. He called that a “special kind of neglect.”
Matters to property taxes
Lincoln Fire and Rescue serves as the city’s local fire department, operating out of 16 fire stations and providing emergency medical and rescue services, fire suppression and prevention and community support programs. 
Foley, in an interview, praised firefighters for their service but said also that most taxpayers likely are not aware of how much the first responders are paid. It matters to property taxes, he said.
Lincoln first responders answer a call. (Photo courtesy of Lincoln Fire and Rescue)
Foley’s team said the bulk of fire and rescue personnel, about 87%, are 56-hour-per-week employees who work a recurring 21-day cycle consisting of alternating 24-hour shifts on and off for 13 days, followed by eight consecutive days off duty.
According to the report, those firefighters automatically earn nine hours of overtime for working their “regular shifts.” Last year, that amounted to more than $2 million, about 28% of the total overtime paid for 2025.
“It is common also for department personnel to pick up extra shifts voluntarily on their regular days off, including during the eight-day ‘rest period,’ to increase either overtime compensation,” Foley said.
He noted that the department’s work schedule is the product of “complex” union negotiation ratified by the city, and that some of the overtime pay is “built into” the approved work schedule. 
But he said other firefighting companies around the nation use a variety of scheduling methods, and an “informed consideration of those different options might prove useful” when the city negotiates future labor contracts.
In commending Lincoln Fire and Rescue for “outstanding service,” Foley said “those courageous men and women deserve to be compensated well for protecting us — often at great personal risk.” 
But the auditor stressed also that a performance audit by the city would align with “previously neglected requirements” of the city code and also could help curb what he said appear to be inordinate overtime costs.
“Without an adequate study, such as through a performance audit, there would not be a way to determine which model may be more beneficial for the city and LFR staff,” the report said.
Audit panel reactivates 
Lincoln officials, in a response included in the report, acknowledged that the city’s Performance Audit Committee has been inactive for more than five years but said the city already had taken steps toward reactivation. The City Council on Aug. 31 adopted a resolution to initiate engagement with the committee.
The city’s response to the audit did not say specifically that the committee would review fire and rescue overtime practices. Foley said if it doesn’t happen, the city can expect to hear from him again. He said his office could conduct such a review, but the city would have to pay. 
Among the auditor team’s observations:

Lincoln’s Fire and Rescue total overtime paid in 2024 was a bit higher than in 2025, reaching $7.29 million. In 2023, reported overtime pay was $6 million.
After reviewing records of 10 select employees who earned overtime pay in 2025, the audit team highlighted one who was paid for eight hours of vacation leave on the same day she was paid nearly 10 hours of overtime. That resulted in $610 for overtime and $386 for vacation hours.

In their response, Lincoln officials agreed with that finding and said the city has collected the overpayment from the employee. 
The city, however, disputed Foley’s assertion that “inadequate documentation” was filed for that employee.
The auditor’s report reviewed overtime as it relates to the Urban Search and Rescue team, also referred to as Nebraska Task Force One. But Foley said in an interview that he did not see those missions as contributing to any problem.
Lincoln firefighters respond to an emergency. (Photo courtesy of Lincoln Fire and Rescue)
The US&R team is an expert group that responds to local, state and national disaster emergencies. Participating agencies provide people who have specialized skill sets. 
In 2025, 37 members of Lincoln fire and rescue department deployed with the US&R team. Various members were assigned, for example, to help with flooding in Texas and Washington states and with a severe weather situation in Tennessee. Some members were deployed to Nebraska emergencies such as a Custer County wildfire and a building collapse in Fremont. Not all 37 were deployed for each event.
Foley noted that labor costs of the US&R assignments are to be reimbursed by the Federal Emergency Management Agency or the appropriate agency responsible for addressing the emergency. Reimbursement includes the costs for those deployed as well as Lincoln employees needed to fill shift vacancies created.
Records show reimbursement during 2025 for about $1 million for costs related to US&R deployments and $200,000 for FEMA grants and training. The auditor team noted that full reimbursement takes an unpredictable amount of time. For example, funds for the July 2025 Texas assignment had not yet been received in full. 
Engler said fire officials recognize that consistently high overtime can signal a need for additional staffing. Since 2019, he said, the city has approved 33 new firefighter and firefighter-paramedic positions, including spots supported by federal grants, which have “significantly reduced overtime costs.”
The department continues to evaluate staffing and other strategies to reduce overtime “where practical,” he said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana marks National 988 Day with awareness event
description: State officials and mental health advocacy groups gathered Tuesday at the Capitol Gardens to spread awareness for Louisiana’s 988 mental health hotline, coinciding with National 988 Day.
text:
Speakers stand in front of the Huey P. Long statue in the gardens in front of theLouisiana State Capitol to spread awareness for the 988  988 mental health hotline. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator) State officials and mental health advocacy groups gathered Tuesday at the Capitol Gardens to spread awareness for Louisiana’s 988 mental health hotline, coinciding with National 988 Day. 
Southern University’s Human Jukebox Marching Band provided the event’s soundtrack, surrounded by colorful pop-up tents with stickers, buttons and miniature fans spreading the word about the 988 hotline and other behavioral health support programs available across the state. 
Three years ago, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline converted to a 3-digit shortcode from the previous 10-digit, 1-800 number established in 2005. The national network consists of more than 200 crisis centers supported by local, state and federal resources. The hotline provides 24/7 confidential support to people in suicidal, mental health and substance misuse crises.  
“Reaching out to 988 is not a sign of weakness. It is a sign of strength. It is a sign of caring for yourself, for your family, and for your community,” said Holly Howat, assistant secretary for the Louisiana Department of Health’s Office of Behavioral Services. 
Howat shared her own experience reaching out to 988 during a family crisis, saying the stigma around mental health services can be hard to overcome. 
“It’s not something that comes up in conversation, and I think sometimes people think ‘That’s for somebody else. That’s not for me,’” she said in a follow-up interview, adding that the event sought to “normalize” reaching out for help.  
National 988 Day events unfold as the Trump administration has said it intends to reverse course on changes made last year to hotline policy. In June 2025, the White House announced it would eliminate the “Press 3” option for LGBTQ+ youth in crisis, explaining that it had run out of funding. 
Congress has since allocated $33 million for LGBTQ+ youth in need of assistance, and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in April the original service will be restored to the hotline. An exact timeline for the return of the “Press 3” option remains unclear.
LGBTQ+ youth are up to four times more likely to commit suicide compared with their peers, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control. 
“This help is for all Louisianians, no matter your race, your age, your gender, your sexual orientation. This number is for everybody, and so we really want to emphasize that,” Howat said when asked about how Louisiana has handled removal of the “Press 3” option on the 988 line.
Quinetta Womack, Behavioral Services’ deputy assistant secretary, said the health department is trying new ways to reach people and spread awareness about its programs that support mental health. 
“We need to saturate Louisiana. We need to saturate the nation and help them understand,” Womack said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Federal judges revoke key permit for natural gas pipeline project
description: A appeals panel on Tuesday vacated a state permit that energy developer Williams needs to build its proposed Northeast Supply Enhancement pipeline.
text:
A appeals panel on Tuesday vacated a state permit that energy developer Williams needs to build its proposed Northeast Supply Enhancement pipeline. (Photo courtesy of the U.S. Department of Energy)A federal appeals panel on Tuesday vacated a key permit an energy developer needs to build a controversial $1 billion underwater natural gas pipeline between New Jersey and New York.
U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals Judge Jane Richards Roth, writing for a three-judge panel, said the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection acted in an “arbitrary and capricious” way last fall when it issued a water quality certification to energy developer Williams to build its proposed Northeast Supply Enhancement pipeline through the Raritan Bay.
State environmental officials failed to require Williams to prove it has adequately protected the bay from buried contaminants before it begins to dredge the seabed, Roth wrote.
“A key safeguard is missing: no prescribed NJDEP approval stands between the unfinished plans and dredging,” she wrote.
The state’s decisional documents also do not explain how the project complies with New Jersey’s water quality standards, she added.
“Technical expertise does not relieve an agency of its obligation to articulate the basis for its decision,” Roth wrote.
While the judges vacated the permit, their decision doesn’t kill the proposed pipeline altogether. Instead, it boots the project back to the Department of Environmental Protection for officials to fully explain why they approved the permit, or act otherwise.
“On remand, NJDEP remains free to supplement its explanation, require additional submissions or analyses, issue a new or revised certification, or reach a different result. We leave those specific choices to NJDEP,” Roth wrote.
Larry Hajna, a department spokesman, declined to comment.
Williams spokeswoman Cherice Corley said the company is reviewing the court’s decision, adding that the project “remains critical to strengthening energy reliability and meeting the region’s growing energy demand.”
Critics have complained the project would not directly benefit New Jersey residents because it would link gas supply between Pennsylvania and New York City.
Environmentalists also have warned it would endanger marine habitats, expose toxins buried in the bay floor, threaten wetlands in Somerset County where Williams plans to build a compressor station, and degrade the environment in Middlesex and Monmouth counties, where a new pipeline would be built to connect existing lines.
They celebrated Tuesday’s ruling, noting that state officials had rejected the project in 2019 and 2020 in part over concerns about its impact on water quality before approving the water quality certification last November. Another state environmental panel in May approved the final permit Williams needed to proceed with the project, which Williams subsidiary Transcontinental Gas Pipeline Company first proposed in 2017.
Attorney Jackson Garrity represented the Natural Resources Defense Council in a lawsuit it filed in November challenging the water quality certification. He called Roth’s ruling “a win for the waterways of New Jersey, the people who rely on them, and the rule of law.”
“This pipeline would not only have destroyed wetlands across New Jersey, but also would tear up the sea floor of Raritan Bay. The DEP’s approval of the water quality permit failed to address key water quality concerns that the public has been raising for years,” Garrity said.
Another group of environmentalists, including the New Jersey League of Conservation Voters, New York/New Jersey Baykeeper, and Food & Water Watch, filed a similar lawsuit the same day as the National Resources Defense Council, and the appellate court consolidated those challenges.
Allison McLeod, who heads the New Jersey League of Conservation Voters, called Roth’s decision “a monumental victory for New Jersey’s environment, public safety and working families who are tired of paying higher prices to further enrich billionaire oil and gas executives.”
She urged state officials to reject the project altogether and commit to renewable energy.
“This project would represent a capitulation to Donald Trump’s extreme fossil fuel agenda — sacrificing our public health and driving up costs to make billionaires even wealthier,” McLeod said. “As today’s decision demonstrates, New Jerseyans’ right to clean water is not negotiable. Now, the state has a prime opportunity to deliver a major win for affordability, public safety and clean air and water.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC to rebuild 169-year-old slave cabin destroyed by Hurricane Helene
description: SC is preparing to rebuild 169-year-old slave cabin on the Redcliffe Plantation destroyed by Hurricane Helene.
text:
A former slave quarters on South Carolina's Redcliffe Plantation was destroyed by Hurricane Helene. Nearly two years later, the state is rebuilding the 169-year-old structure. (Photo courtesy of SC Parks and Recreation)For more than a decade, the descendants of sharecroppers and people once enslaved on South Carolina’s Redcliffe Plantation gathered each year inside the former slave quarters on the property — now a state historic site — that their ancestors once called home.
Two remaining buildings out of four, arranged in a square, that served as the slave quarters at Redcliffe stood in the shade of a more than 200-year-old cherry bark oak.
But on Sept. 27, 2024, when Hurricane Helene reached the Palmetto State as a tropical storm with drenching rains and 75 mph winds, the tall oak fell. It leveled the nearly 170-year old building that had hosted so many annual gatherings, where descendants shared meals, conversations and read through historic documents about how their ancestors had lived.

“At the height, there were folks traveling from New York, Minnesota, California, probably close to 100 people,” said South Carolina State Parks Director Joy Raintree.
“With that building damaged and gone, you only have the one,” added Raintree, who started her career at Redcliffe. “It’s hard to recreate that open square that would have been the yard where enslaved housekeepers and gardeners would have lived and worked.”
Now, two years after the storm, the state park service is preparing to reconstruct the destroyed building, which the agency called “a rare and essential resource for understanding the site’s history.”
A legislative panel that oversees state spending last month approved using $755,000 in federal historic preservation grant funds to rebuild it, restoring the clapboard-sided structure as close to its original construction as possible.
Redcliffe’s history
Redcliffe, in present-day Aiken County, was one of four plantations owned by former South Carolina governor, congressman and U.S. Sen. James Henry Hammond. In all, the attorney and politician owned 14,000 acres of prime cotton-growing land along the Savannah River.
Hammond enslaved some 300 men, women and children across his properties. Between 20 and 50 of them lived at Redcliffe, his non-working estate in Beech Island. The freed descendants of the five or six families of slaves continued to live on the property until the 1990s.
South Carolina’s Redcliffe Plantation, located in the community of Beech Island in Aiken County, was among sites hit by Hurricane Helene in September 2024. Now the state parks agency is rebuilding a 169-year-old slave cabin destroyed by the storm. (Photo courtesy of SC Parks and Recreation)
Hammond’s great grandson, John Shaw Billings, donated Redcliffe to the state in 1973. Two years later, the state park service opened it to the public as a historic site.
When people, including about 2,000 school children on field trips each year, come to Redcliffe, they start at the visitor center with a small exhibit about all of the properties Hammond owned from the 1830s until his death in 1864 — Redcliffe but also Silver Bluff, Cowden, and Cathwood plantations. From there, they may explore the property and two-story Greek Revival mansion on their own or participate in a guided tour.
Park employees take those who opt for the tour to the slave quarters to begin. The last of the buildings that still stands today contains an exhibit, which opened last year, about the lives of its former inhabitants.
“Hammond was a prolific writer. He kept crop notes, plantation manuals, overseer’s manuals,” Raintree said. “Of course, all of that is from his perspective, but if you read it and study it you learn about how people were impacted by the things he was saying and the things he was doing.”
“We’re using James Henry Hammond’s words, but we are using them for the purpose to tease out what life was like for the people that lived there and lived under those rules and guidelines,” she added.
In all, Redcliffe has about 4,000 artifacts.
“We use all of those things as vehicles, as lenses,” Raintree said. “But at the end of the day, it’s the modern day conversations about what happened in the past that are important and Redcliffe provides space for that.”
Rebuilding
The building destroyed in the storm started out as slave quarters but was converted into a garage in the 1930s, with living space for a driver. While the outside changed, the inside remained largely the same, Raintree said.
“You could still see all of the original framing and the original sills were exposed,” she said, so visitors could get a sense of how the building was made.
As the park agency rebuilds the 800-square-foot structure, it plans to salvage as much of the original material as possible. The work will include timber framing, pine siding, doors and windows, brick piers and pine tongue and grove flooring. The park will reuse for exhibits that which workers can’t salvage.
“It is important to us to to preserve that tangible memory that allows us to tell the stories that we want to tell,” Raintree said.
Completion is expected by June 2029.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Death row men lose personal tablet access after advocate shares their stories online
description: Within two hours of Mississippi Today publishing a story about death row men's stories being posted online, prison officials took away their personal tablets.
text:
For the past year, men from Mississippi’s death row have been able to share with the public who they are and their experiences while incarcerated through an online platform.
The nonprofit organization Humans Remain, which several of the men formed a year ago with England-based advocate Liz McCann, hosts the platform. McCann runs the website, creates the videos and shares them on the group’s social media pages. Personal tablets enabled users to make video calls and send electronic messages. 
On Aug. 7, Mississippi Today published a story about the group’s first anniversary, purpose and work with the 34 men from Unit 17 at the Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman. The story quoted McCann and a death row prisoner and included one line about the use of tablets that helps the group do its advocacy and educational work.
Within two hours of the story’s publishing, the death row men lost access to their tablets, according to advocates, leaving two communal phones, mail and in-person visits as their available forms of contact with people outside the prison. 
A month later, the tablets have not been returned. The death row men continue to wonder about why it happened, how the decision was made and whether they can get the devices back. A spokesperson from The Mississippi Department of Corrections did not respond to a request for comment. 
“There’s literally a wall of silence,” McCann said last week. 
The restriction has prompted some of the men to speak out through an unpublished editorial that McCann shared with Mississippi Today. 
“The application of ‘mushroom censorship’ is absurd and as outdated as the death penalty itself,” they wrote in the editorial. 
Lisa Jo Chamberlin, the only woman on Mississippi death row, had a similar communication restriction at the beginning of the year shortly after Mississippi Today published a story about her. 
As with the men, she was not able to use her tablet, but her restrictions also included phone use. Chamberlin was blocked from making phone calls, and advocates who had regular contact with her were met with silence until April. She has since regained phone privileges, according to other advocates working with her.
MDOC did not provide Mississippi Today with a comment explaining why the tablets were removed.
Prison staff gave the death row men reasons why the tablets were taken away, according to the editorial, including that Unit 17 is a restricted area, that McCann has used the devices to contact them and that Mississippi Today published the story about their efforts. 
The editorial pushes back against those justifications. Unit 29, death row’s previous location, was also a restricted area and is where they first got access to the tablets. Advocacy from death row in the form of published videos predates the formation of Humans Remain. 
McCann said she takes some responsibility for what happened because she operates the organization. 
While the death row men criticized the prison officials’ actions, they gave credit to Chief of Institutions Marc McClure, the former Parchman superintendent. Under his leadership, the men said that their quality of life has improved, including freedom of movement within the unit.
According to McCann, Corrections Commissioner Burl Cain and McClure visited Unit 17 on Sept. 4 and talked with the men. The prison officials did not explain why the tablets were taken away, including when they would be restored or whether any prison rules were broken, she said. 
McCann said she has been transparent about using tablets to communicate with the men and to show people the advocacy group is being run legitimately. 
“We’ve never tried to hide any of this advocacy stuff,” she said.

title: Former Arkansas lawmaker pleads not guilty to felony domestic violence charges
