name: West Virginia Watch
title: Treasurer Pack says Mingo parents’ anger is ‘misdirected’ in Hope Scholarship lawsuit
description: State Treasurer Larry Pack said his office will “aggressively oppose” any attempt to block universal expansion of the Hope Scholarship following a recent lawsuit from parents seeking to block new applicants.
text:
West Virginia State Treasurer Larry Pack addresses reporters about his 2026 legislative priorities during a news conference Nov. 17, 2025, in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)State Treasurer Larry Pack said his office will “aggressively oppose” any attempt to block universal expansion of the Hope Scholarship following a recent lawsuit from parents seeking to block new applicants. 
Several parents of Mingo County students sued the state Treasurer’s Office last week over the Hope Scholarship’s recent expansion to all K-12 students. 
The parents have asked a judge to stop new applications to the state’s education voucher program who are eligible under universal expansion. 
Their students attend Dingess Elementary, which is expected to close next year. In the lawsuit, parents said the school district has been impacted by public schools’ financial distress while the state spent millions of dollars expanding the Hope Scholarship. 
Pack said the parents’ “anger is misdirected.”
“It is unfortunate that the Hope Scholarship is still being used as a political football, distracting from the urgent issues facing our public schools,” Pack said in a statement Tuesday. 
“While parents in Mingo County are right to demand solutions for public education, their anger is misdirected,” he continued. “We will aggressively oppose any attempt to reverse the universal expansion approved by the Legislature and signed by the governor. As Chairman of the Hope Scholarship Board, I am committed to ensuring every student in the program receives the unique educational opportunities they deserve.”
The lawsuit was also filed against the Hope Scholarship Board and West Virginia State Superintendent of Schools Michele Blatt. According to the lawsuit, Blatt was sued in her official capacity only because the state Department of Education transfers funding to the county school systems. 
The Hope Scholarship opened up to all West Virginia students in grades K-12 for the first time this school year. Up until this year, the program was restricted to incoming kindergarten students or public school students enrolled for at least 45 days during the current school year.
The Hope Scholarship gives students around $5,400 this school year to pay for in- and out-of-state education outside of public schools and other eligible expenses.
Mingo County parents said that while their school is set to close, there is no Hope Scholarship education service provider offering a full-time school program within a reasonable commuting distance of their homes. 
The lawsuit, filed in Kanawha County, asked that a judge ban further disbursement of the Hope Scholarship to new, first-time applicants who only became eligible under the universal expansion. It also asked the judge to mandate that defendants provide information on Hope Scholarship disbursements by county and recipient type so the court can evaluate the financial impact on public schools. 
Mingo County parents noted in the lawsuit that lawmakers expanded universal eligibility for the Hope Scholarship while leaving the school funding formula unaddressed. 
Lawmakers already allocated around $277 million for the Hope Scholarship to account for any student who chooses to use the program in the 2026-27 school year under universal expansion. 
Meanwhile, lawmakers’ bills aimed at updating the decades-old school funding formula to better account for declining enrollment didn’t make it through the Legislature. The price of those funding formula bills was often a sticking point for lawmakers. 
A school funding study commissioned by lawmakers ahead of the legislative session had recommended against universal expansion of the Hope Scholarship, saying, “that such an expansion would inefficiently subsidize private school tuition for many families who would have chosen private schools regardless.”
Pack has been vocal about public school funding and called on the Legislature “to act quickly and confront the urgent challenges in our public schools.”
“Our schools are demanding help, and the time for action is long overdue. We must cut burdensome regulations so teachers can focus on teaching,” he said. “But let’s be clear: improving public schools does not require sacrificing educational freedom. We can — and must — strengthen public education and uphold school choice at the same time. We are ready to partner with policymakers to deliver real change. The future of our students depends on it. Let’s get to work.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Uthmeier wants penalties for corporations whose AI chatbots contribute to crimes
description: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier called Tuesday for legislation imposing criminal penalties for corporations running chatbots that engage in criminal activity. Acknowledging you “can’t lock up a company behind bars,” the AG said in Tampa on Tuesday that his office is looking into the extent of involvement of corporate executives in chatbot behavior. “[...]
text:
A young woman asks AI companion ChatGPT for help in New York City. States are pushing to prevent the use of artificially intelligent chatbots in mental health to try to protect vulnerable users. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/Stateline)Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier called Tuesday for legislation imposing criminal penalties for corporations running chatbots that engage in criminal activity.
Acknowledging you “can’t lock up a company behind bars,” the AG said in Tampa on Tuesday that his office is looking into the extent of involvement of corporate executives in chatbot behavior.
“What designs? What intentionality was there? How aware were they of the behaviors of the crimes that took place? How involved were they?” he said.
Uthmeier’s comments came three months after he announced legal action against OpenAI and its chief executive officer, Sam Altman, alleging the company knowingly released and aggressively marketed ChatGPT to the public — including to children — while concealing “serious risks, suppressing internal safety warnings, and deceiving Floridians about the true nature and dangers of the product.”
That came after prosecutors reviewed chat logs between ChatGPT and Phoenix Ikner, the accused gunman in the April 17, 2025, shootings at Florida State University. Two people were killed, fathers who worked on that campus, and six more were shot.
Those chat logs revealed that in the hours and minutes leading to that attack, Ikner asked ChatGPT a series of probing questions, including what was the busiest time on campus, how Florida punishes school shooters, and how many victims are required to gain media attention.
Uthmeier said that while it was wrong for chatbots to provide specific information, at the very least those questions should have sparked a red flag to law enforcement, “to alert them to these very specific things that are being discussed, to alert our very brave men and women in uniform about what’s going on so they can make their own criminal threat assessment.”
The fact that did not happen despite the company’s employment of some of the smartest data scientists in the world “is wrong,” he said,
Uthmeier’s office expanded it investigation into OpenAI in April to include the murders of two University of South Florida doctoral students after learning the primary suspect used ChatGPT.
The proposed legislation has not been drafted yet, but Uthmeier imagines penalties could include heavy fines, payments to victims, court-ordered monitorship, and possibly suspension of business activity in the state.
He will call on the Florida Board of Medicine to investigate AL chatbots for unlawful practice of medicine by giving medical advice, he added.
OpenAI laid out a “commitment to community safety” in a statement issued in April. “We will continue to prioritize safety while balancing privacy and other civil liberties so we can act on serious risks,” the company said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Rapid tech expansion is outpacing Louisiana’s ability to govern it
description: These projects promise economic benefits, but they also expose a familiar weakness: Louisiana’s governing systems are not built for rapid, high‑stakes technological change.
text:
The marquee on Frank's Theatre in Abbeville welcomes SpaceX at an event to announce the company's Spacebase Louisiana project in Vermilion Parish on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo: Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)Louisiana is entering one of the most consequential periods of technological expansion in its history.

SpaceX’s plan to build a massive launch facility near Pecan Island is only the most visible example. Data centers, artificial intelligence infrastructure and advanced manufacturing facilities are arriving at a pace our institutions are not well prepared to manage.

These projects promise economic benefits, but they also expose a familiar weakness: Louisiana’s governing systems are not built for rapid, high‑stakes technological change.

State agencies, including the Department of Natural Resources and the Public Service Commission, and parish‑level permitting bodies are being asked to make decisions under conditions of speed, uncertainty and political pressure. These institutions were hardly designed for this dynamic environment, and their planning processes will be tested in trying to adapt to these demands.

State leaders have embraced data centers and AI‑related infrastructure with enthusiasm. These projects are promoted as evidence that Louisiana is becoming a central player in a new technological era. The narrative is familiar: new jobs, new investments and long‑term economic benefits.

But the assumptions behind this optimism are fragile. They shape incentive packages, permitting decisions and public expectations, yet these assumptions rarely undergo serious stress testing. When Louisiana Economic Development negotiates incentives or when parish officials approve land‑use changes, projections can often err regarding growth patterns, resource demands and stakeholder impacts.

Major technological shifts rarely unfold in smooth, linear trends. Early automation, computing, and internet adoption generated enormous optimism long before their costs and benefits were fully understood. AI will likely follow an even less predictable pattern. Energy and water demand add another layer of uncertainty.

Frontier AI models seem to require exponential increases in compute power, cooling capacity, and water usage, but actual requirements will depend on so many yet to be reckoned factors. Louisiana is already committing land, water and grid capacity to data‑center projects without fully knowing long‑term strains.

In Texas, local officials have raised concerns about data‑center water withdrawals during drought periods.

In Virginia’s “Data Center Alley,” Dominion Energy has warned in its regulatory filings that grid strain forced delays and modifications to planned infrastructure upgrades. These cases show how quickly early assumptions can break down.

Economic volatility presents additional risks. A recession, supply‑chain disruption or capital‑market shift could alter project timelines or viability. A COVID‑like shock could disrupt labor markets or infrastructure planning. Hurricanes or extreme weather events could force sudden reevaluations of coastal or inland development.

These are more predictable contingencies, yet how much are Louisiana’s institutions incorporating such scenarios into planning? Permitting process decisions are made based on certain explicit and often implicit assumptions about the future. Incentive agreements can lock in parish or state commitments without consideration of possible escape valves. Agencies can rush matters based on narrow or limited forecasts rather than scenario‑based analysis.

Contingency thinking, scenario planning, stress testing and stakeholder engagement are not exotic ideas. They are taught in business schools, public‑administration programs and strategy courses across the country. Yet these insights rarely migrate into the fast‑paced, politically charged environments where Louisiana’s public and private‑sector administrators operate.

This is the familiar theory–practice gap: Institutions know what they should do, but the pressures of time, politics and organizational culture lead them to rely on narrow assumptions and linear forecasts. The result is predictable blind spots.

Research in management and public‑sector planning shows that certain modest, structured approaches tend to reduce predictable failures. These include examining at least a small set of plausible futures, stress‑testing assumptions about energy, water, workforce, housing and emergency services, gathering input from key stakeholder groups who can identify blind spots early, monitoring early warning indicators such as grid‑strain metrics and water‑usage thresholds and periodically reassessing incentives, timelines, regulatory posture and infrastructure demands.

These practices do not require institutional or cultural transformation. They represent responsible steps in how major decisions are made, and Louisiana will eventually be studied in cases evaluating effective and ineffective actions by states facing rapid technological change.

The Gulf South is entering a technological crossroads. The question goes beyond whether data centers, AI infrastructure or launch facilities should be located here. Many of those decisions already have been made. The more important question now is whether Louisiana’s institutions can understand and govern the consequences as they unfold.

Contingency governance is required for institutional learning and performance under conditions of volatility. It anticipates diverse challenges rather than reacts to them after impacts become irreversible and harmful to affected stakeholders.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC inmate convicted of killing wife dies on death row
description: Louis Winkler was out on bond when he shot and killed his wife, then hid from police for two weeks, leading to his conviction in 2008.
text:
The state's death chamber in Columbia, S.C., is connected to a prison where an inmate died, leaving 21 inmates on death row. (Provided by the S.C. Department of Corrections)COLUMBIA — A death row inmate convicted of killing his estranged wife died in prison Monday morning after an extended illness, according to the state Department of Corrections.
Louis Winkler, a 66-year-old from Horry County, spent 18 years on death row. He was one of 22 men housed at the maximum security prison in Columbia.
Louis Michael Winkler, Jr., died Monday, Sept. 7, 2026, after an extended illness. (Photo courtesy of SC Department of Corrections)
The Department of Corrections did not give any more information about his illness or how long he was sick. Winkler will receive an autopsy, according to the agency.
Winkler was convicted in 2008 of killing his estranged wife two years prior, then causing a two-week manhunt.
Winkler and Rebekah Grainger Winkler, also known as Becky, spent less than two years married when Grainger Winkler ended the relationship and moved out in September 2005, according to court documents.
A month later, Winkler was charged with kidnapping, assaulting and raping his estranged wife. He was released on bond and allowed to leave his house every evening to search for a job.
In March 2006, while Winkler was still out on bond, he broke into 50-year-old Grainger Winkler’s Little River condominium, splintering the door in the process. After throwing Grainger Winkler’s 14-year-old son to the floor, he shot his estranged wife in the face, killing her instantly, according to court records.
For two weeks, Winkler evaded police, hiding in the woods near the condo. He was captured after a golfer spotted and reported him. When police found him, Winkler had a pistol, ammunition, a knife and a newspaper clipping about the shooting.
A jury convicted Winkler in 2008 of murder, burglary, and assault and battery, and recommended a sentence of death.
Winkler’s case remained in the appeals process at the time of his death.
A circuit court judge overturned Winkler’s death sentence in 2012, saying his attorneys made mistakes during his trial. The state Supreme Court reinstated his sentence four years later, sending the case back to the circuit court for further consideration.
Last month, his attorneys asked the state Supreme Court to again intervene, this time to stop a circuit court judge from dismissing Winkler’s claims of having brain damage that could make it illegal for the state to execute him. The state’s highest court had not yet taken up the case.
SC’s longest-serving death row inmate dies of natural causes

Winkler’s death leaves 21 inmates on death row in South Carolina. Another is imprisoned in California for crimes committed there.
Executions resumed in the state in September 2024 following an unintended 13-year hiatus, caused in part by prison officials’ inability to source the drugs used in lethal injections.
The state has put seven men to death since then. Three chose to die by firing squad, and four selected lethal injection. None have picked the electric chair, the state’s default method.
No inmates are scheduled for upcoming executions as several wait on last-ditch appeals to save them from the death chamber.

name: Michigan Advance
title: What Trump’s new study says about support for trans rights — and why experts are worried
authors: Orion Rummler - The 19th, Jasmine Mithani - The 19th
description: This story was originally reported by Orion Rummler and Jasmine Mithani of The 19th. Meet Orion and Jasmine and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. A new study from the Trump administration is sending alarm bells through pro-democracy groups for its potential to fuel a crackdown on Americans who support LGBTQ+ […]
text:
President Donald Trump imposed new import taxes on products from dozens of top U.S. trading partners on Friday, July 24, 2026. In this photo, Trump spoke before a friendly crowd at Wheeler High School near Marietta, Georgia, on July 22, 2026. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)
This story was originally reported by Orion Rummler and Jasmine Mithani of The 19th. Meet Orion and Jasmine and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
A new study from the Trump administration is sending alarm bells through pro-democracy groups for its potential to fuel a crackdown on Americans who support LGBTQ+ rights — or anyone with left-leaning views.
Last week, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) released a study that reaches a dramatic conclusion: Those who support transgender people may be more likely to justify political violence. The study also claims that those who agree with statements like “all political conservatives are fools” or “anyone who opposes gay marriage must be homophobic” may also be more likely to support political violence.
Experts have serious doubts about the study’s findings and major ethical objections to its methodology. They say that it builds on previous pseudoscience about trans people and, ultimately, they are concerned about how the Trump administration plans to use it. 
“I have rarely read a report that has come out of the government that is so clearly politically biased,” said Hanah Stiverson, director of policy at the Chamberlain Network, a pro-democracy nonprofit that fights political polarization. This report is clearly meant for political weaponization, she said.
This report is continuing the anti-trans campaign laid out by the Trump administration by moving the conversation beyond youth and sports, said Heron Greenesmith, a policy attorney who has researched anti-trans advocacy networks. It goes beyond past arguments by administration allies linking transgender people to increased capacity to violence, Greenesmith said: “It seeks to explicitly connect support for trans people to violence by actors on the left.”
The study, commissioned by HHS, was done by researchers with Rutgers University, as well as the conservative think tank Manhattan Institute and the Network Contagion Research Institute, a nonprofit studying extremism and online rhetoric from QAnon to the Democratic Socialists of America.
None of the authors responded to The 19th’s multiple interview requests. HHS and Rutgers also did not respond to a request for comment.
The HHS report notes that there is more work to be done, and “additional research questions will be addressed in subsequent analyses.” The authors shared their design on an open-source academic research site in June, hinting at directions of future reports and what else the government may use this research for.
 The study

The report released by HHS, titled “‘Where the Clinic Meets the Movement: Does Gender Ideology Arm Left-Wing Authoritarian Psychology?” analyzed the responses of 1,208 adults to questions about support for transgender people and other topics related to political violence and democracy.
The researchers considered the responses in terms of eight metrics. One was their own creation: the “Clinical Gender Affirmation Scale,” or CGAS, meant to measure support for trans people based on clinical guidelines from major medical groups. It asks respondents how much they agree with statements like “people should be supported in expressing their transgender identity” and whether using a trans person’s chosen name and pronouns is necessary.
The other metrics the researchers looked at included left-wing authoritarianism — a concept that has been controversial for decades — the justification of political violence and anti-democratic attitudes. On left-wing authoritarianism, the questions gauged support for statements including: “America would be much better off if all of the rich people were at the bottom of the social ladder” or “to succeed, a workplace must ensure that its employees feel safe from criticism.” On political violence, it asked about opinions on high-profile assassination attempts, damaging the property of wealthy people and setting fire to ICE buildings.
The authors of the study write that, based on their research, supporting trans people is linked to “left-wing ideological extremity that independently predicts support for coercive and violent political action.”
“Together, these findings support the paper’s core claim: gender ideology may function as an ideological accelerant, telling left-wing authoritarian psychology who the enemy is, why the situation is urgent and — in those already disposed toward force — that violence is legitimate,” the study authors write.
 Ethical and methodological concerns

Experts are baffled by such far-reaching conclusions.
“Correlation is not causation. The authors jump to a lot of implications based on a correlation,” said Jami Taylor, a professor of political science and public administration at the University of Toledo. “It kind of looks like a fishing expedition to me.”
Nuance is missing throughout the research, Taylor said, including on respondents’ beliefs that could impact their views of transgender people, like where they stand on equal rights, social norms and traditional gender roles. She also took issue with the sampling techniques and said that the findings couldn’t be extrapolated to the general population.
“If I was on the review board for the institution, I would have certainly raised some concerns about asking people about their attitudes on political assassination, particularly of the president of the United States. To me, it is pretty unethical,” Taylor said. In her view, asking about opinions on assassination attempts — including on President Donald Trump — is unethical because it invokes harm and can also put the respondents at risk of being targeted by the administration.
Stiverson, from the Chamberlain Network, found the HHS report’s conclusion — and the research that led to it — both unethical and misleading.
“It is, from my reading, misrepresenting data and creating a false equivalency,” Stiverson said. Affirming a marginalized group does not equal oppression, she said. And, she added, the study is built on a fundamental flaw: It misuses the term “authoritarianism.”
Stiverson, a scholar of fascist movements in the United States who has studied authoritarianism and extremism, said authoritarianism requires a focus on concentrating power, an almost blind adherence to that power and a rejection of anything outside the norms of society. That’s not what the study is asking about, though, she said.
She believes left-wing authoritarianism exists, but she doesn’t think it is adequately defined in this research — and that makes the premise flawed.
Left-wing extremism is generally well-documented, but the concept of left-wing authoritarianism is controversial. At least one study has argued that scales like the one used in the HHS report actually just measure rebelliousness, sadism or political leanings  — not authoritarianism.
“What they’re actually talking about is a radicalization towards political violence. Authoritarianism is more nuanced than that,” Stiverson said.
Experts had other issues with the study; some called the questions biased and poorly crafted. Greenesmith pointed out controversial statements within the report that were not adequately cited, such as the assertion that the killing of right-wing activist Charlie Kirk in 2025 — which respondents were asked if they viewed as justified — is “a case widely covered and publicly perceived as connected to gender ideology.”
Researchers had more questions: How was the study funded? Was it peer reviewed? Did the authors get approval from the Institutional Review Board, which provides ethical and regulatory oversight of research involving human subjects?
The 19th reached out to Rutgers with these questions and has not yet heard back.
 The politics

“I would call it pseudo-science,” said Wendy Via, cofounder and CEO of the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism, a nonprofit that opposes far-right movements. “They commissioned a report to support the conclusion they had already drawn, which is that transgender people or people who support transgender people are more likely to be violent.”
The nonprofit has released a full report detailing its issues with the study, saying it lacks independent validation or peer review for the CGAS scale and that it appears to be built with bias against gender-affirming care for trans people.
This study fits into a larger effort by the Trump administration to target anyone seen as anti-American or who has nontraditional views on gender, Via said. The architects of Project 2025, authored by the conservative Heritage Foundation, have urged the government to monitor and label transgender people — and those close to them — as terrorists. She sees this new study as a stepping stone toward that goal.
“When I first saw this report, the first thing I thought was that the administration is trying to build its case to finally designate ‘transgender ideology’ as a category of domestic terrorism,” Via said.
There is actually an abundance of evidence that attitudes about gender are tied to violent extremism — but that it’s misogyny, not acceptance of trans people, that fuels hateful violence. Experts like Cynthia Miller-Idriss at American University have pushed for the government to take misogynistic violence seriously as a precursor to mass violence and extremism, but instead the White House has emphasized left-wing violence, which is less prevalent than that motivated by right-wing beliefs. Misogyny exists everywhere, but is more in line with conservative values around patriarchy and gender roles. In her book released last year, Miller-Idriss documented how hateful rhetoric about how LGBTQ+ communities go against the “natural order” is prevalent in radicalization pathways, particularly among the manosphere.
Last year, a White House memo detailed viewpoints that the government sees as common recurrent motivations for violence and domestic terrorism and included “extremism on migration, race and gender” and “hostility towards those who hold traditional American views on family, religion and morality.”
This year, in the U.S. Counterterrorism Strategy unveiled by the White House, the government said that it would “prioritize the rapid identification and neutralization of violent secular political groups whose ideology is anti-America, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist.”
And more recently, Donald Trump Jr. — who does not work in the administration but who has a following on the right — put it more bluntly: “The radical transgender movement is per capita the most violent domestic terror threat if not in America, probably the entire world.”
All of this rhetoric raises fears that trans people, or anyone who supports them, could be labeled as anti-democratic, violent or prone to terrorism and pursued by federal authorities.
The transgender community is one of the most marginalized and victimized in America, Via said. Trans people are over four times more likely than cisgender people to be victims of violent crime, according to the Williams Institute at the UCLA School of Law. Over and over again, experts have debunked the claim of widespread violent threats coming from trans people.
“They continue to target this community as if it is the biggest threat this nation faces, and on its face it isn’t. But they do it because they can demonize the community and use them as a weapon to scare and threaten people into accepting a restriction of rights that will not end with trans people,” Via said.
 The authors

The Rutgers scholars who worked on the study are part of the university’s ​​Social Perception Lab, which is directed by psychology professor Lee Jussim. On Substack, he has written on topics including “there’s little or no anti-Black discrimination today” and “no evidence for workplace sex discrimination.”
Several researchers who produced the study also work with the Network Contagion Research Institute (NCRI), which has previously studied what it describes as a growing “assassination culture” within “the extreme left” in the United States. The nonprofit, founded in 2018, has produced reports about extremism across the political spectrum, including how the far-right conspiracy theory QAnon poses a threat to democracy. More recent work includes reports like “Democratic Socialists Of America: Policy Advocacy And Narrative Convergence With Hostile Foreign States,” “Beijing’s Dark Money Pipeline Into U.S. Higher Education,” and “Permission to Kill: How Candace Owens Built a Digital Assassination Culture Targeting Erika Kirk.” NCRI’s research on foreign gifts to universities has been cited by Congress.
The conservative Manhattan Institute has a track record of criticizing medical authorities on gender-affirming care, like the World Professional Association of Transgender Health (WPATH) and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP). The study claims that these medical groups are “ideologically structured” in their treatment of and support of trans people, and that that structure “can arm authoritarian psychology.”
Of the five authors, one declined to be interviewed, one was traveling and unable to comment, and the other three did not reply to emailed interview requests.
The country’s most prominent medical groups have been under considerable pressure from the Trump administration and Republican attorneys general over healthcare for trans youth. The government sued WPATH this summer and has made sweeping demands for internal communications from other medical groups that endorse gender-affirming care.
In a statement, WPATH criticized the new report as a “blatant attempt to villainize transgender and gender-diverse Americans” and said that “healthcare decisions should remain between the patient and their physician, free from fear of political or governmental interference.”
Ultimately, experts see this report from HHS as a political tool. What remains to be seen is how it will be used.
“I don’t doubt that they will try to act on this in some way,” Via said.
The authors note that the study has several limitations; namely, the causational direction of their findings: whether support for trans people apparently influences left-wing authoritarianism or vice versa.
The HHS report was preregistered through Open Science Framework, a platform where researchers can share their methodology and experimental plans to increase transparency and eliminate bias. The 19th viewed the linked submission, which listed some different co-authors and claimed no institutional affiliation.
Included there was a longer survey draft with questions beyond what was described in the HHS report, including whether the U.S. government is fascist and how likely a transgender person is to die by suicide if their gender isn’t affirmed. The 19th was unable to confirm whether this was the final survey shared with respondents.
“I think once this has more time to percolate in the scientific, academic spaces, it’s going to be torn apart,” Stiverson said.
A second study is being designed to address some of these limitations, the authors said in their report. The “experimental design” will “test whether exposure to CGAS-consistent content produces the patterns predicted by the present theory,” they write.

title: OSU announces sites for new veterinary hospital, agronomy center
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Locations for two major taxpayer-supported construction projects at Oklahoma State University were revealed Tuesday. A $330 million veterinary teaching hospital and a $50 million Agronomy Discovery Center will be built west of OSU’s Stillwater campus in a farmland area, the university announced.  The Oklahoma Legislature agreed to fund most o[...]
text:
A rendering depicts a future veterinary teaching hospital at Oklahoma State University in Stillwater. (Image provided by Oklahoma State University)OKLAHOMA CITY — Locations for two major taxpayer-supported construction projects at Oklahoma State University were revealed Tuesday.
A $330 million veterinary teaching hospital and a $50 million Agronomy Discovery Center will be built west of OSU’s Stillwater campus in a farmland area, the university announced. 
The Oklahoma Legislature agreed to fund most of the cost of both projects, but the university is still raising millions of dollars in private donations to cover remaining expenses. An OSU spokesperson did not immediately answer whether either project has an expected completion date.
State lawmakers dedicated $250 million in 2025 to build the veterinary teaching hospital. The 275,000-square-foot facility, to be built north of State Highway 51 west of South Western Road, will accommodate larger student enrollment than OSU’s current animal hospital, enhance educational opportunities and improve animal owners’ access to advanced veterinary care, the university announced.
Once finished, the hospital will serve large and small animals while also providing space for teaching and research. OSU College of Veterinary Medicine dean Dr. Richard Prather said the facility will help the university’s competitiveness in attracting top students, faculty and researchers.
“Our mission is to provide state-of-the-art veterinary care for every patient, from companion animals to livestock,” Prather said in a statement. “This care not only improves animal health and supports the people who depend on these animals, but also helps safeguard a strong and sustainable food supply for our state and nation.”
The future hospital will be built on a portion of the current OSU Agronomy Research Station in a part of Stillwater dedicated to farmland. Crop research will continue on the northern portion of the site, particularly the Magruder Plots, one of the longest-running wheat research experiments in the U.S., the university said.
The new OSU Agronomy Discovery Center will be constructed about half a mile away on the northwest side of the intersection of West Virginia Road and South Western Road.
A rendering gives an aerial view of Oklahoma State University’s future Agronomy Discovery Center to be built in Stillwater. (Image provided by Oklahoma State University)
The state Legislature appropriated $40 million this year for the agronomy center, which OSU said will be a “cutting-edge research and education hub that supports wheat breeding, crop science, soil fertility, forage and turfgrass research.” It also will expand OSU’s current agricultural research programs.
House Bill 4054, which provided the legislative funding, requires OSU to raise $10 million in private donations for the agronomy center by July 1, 2027, to receive state funds for the project. The university said 51 donors had pledged a collective $8.7 million as of Sept. 1.
“Together, these projects demonstrate OSU’s commitment to Oklahoma while positioning the university as a national destination for talent and leadership in agriculture and animal health,” OSU President Jim Hess said in a statement. “Most importantly, the discoveries made here will not stay on our campuses. They will reach pastures, farms, veterinary practices, businesses and communities across all 77 Oklahoma counties, turning knowledge into practical solutions that improve lives.”

description: LINCOLN — Enrollment across the University of Nebraska system is down 1.4% compared with this time last year, a difference of 700 students, according to NU data released Tuesday. Much of the decrease in fall enrollment to 48,948 students comes again from international students (an 11% decrease, or 318 fewer students) and graduate students (a […]
text:
Dr. Jeffrey Gold, president of the University of Nebraska system, gives his first "State of the University" address in the Nebraska State Capitol. Sept. 4, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Enrollment across the University of Nebraska system is down 1.4% compared with this time last year, a difference of 700 students, according to NU data released Tuesday.
Much of the decrease in fall enrollment to 48,948 students comes again from international students (an 11% decrease, or 318 fewer students) and graduate students (a 5.6% decrease, or 530 fewer students). NU said the drop in graduate enrollment mirrors national trends in reduced federal research funding.
NU also cited decreasing birthrates, both in Nebraska and in much of the United States, as a cause for the declining enrollment.
Enrollment figures are based on the sixth day of classes.
NU President Jeffrey Gold said the enrollment report “reflects national trends and an important inflection point for Nebraska.”
“Students are taking advantage of programs that allow them to move through college faster, and more quickly entering the workforce,” Gold said in a statement. “Across the NU system, more new students are choosing to pursue an undergraduate degree. These are positive developments that we should celebrate and encourage.”


Campus fall 2026 enrollment
University of Nebraska system: 48,948, down 0.2%
University of Nebraska-Lincoln: 23,577, down 1.6%
University of Nebraska at Omaha: 14,810, down 1%
University of Nebraska at Kearney: 5,477, down 3.9%
University of Nebraska Medical Center: 4,847, up 0.6%
Nebraska College of Technical Agriculture: 237, up 11.3%


Despite the declines, NU also highlighted points of pride, including:

More first-time freshmen, again, up 163 students to 7,987 (a 2% increase).
Relatively stable, “strong” total credit hours, at about 602,000 (a 0.7% decrease), indicating students are taking more courses and accelerating their path to graduation.
Increased enrollment at the University of Nebraska Medical Center and the Nebraska College of Technical Agriculture, a consistent trend for the campuses.

In fall 2025, NU’s enrollment dipped slightly, by 0.2%. NU, and particularly the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, had just broken a trend of declining student enrollment the year before, with a slight bump of 0.7% across the system and 1.7% at UNL.
NU is asking the Nebraska Legislature to increase its bottom line by $166 million in the 2027-29 budget cycle. That’s assuming NU’s share of tax dollars remains flat and lawmakers, or Gov. Jim Pillen, do not seek cuts.
Pillen, who is seeking reelection, has asked all state agencies to cut their budgets by 5% through the end of the current fiscal year. NU is included in that request.
“As Nebraska’s only public university system, serving the people and communities of our state is central to our mission,” Gold said Tuesday. “While I’m encouraged by our graduation rates and increasing numbers of first-time freshmen, we must continue our work to grow new programs that will support Nebraska’s workforce needs.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Donalds, Jolly say their camps are just beginning to discuss debates
description: TAMPA — Byron Donalds says David Jolly “isn’t doing much of anything” on the campaign trail, but Jolly is firing back that it’s Donalds who dropped out of what would have been the first one-on-one events between the two men running for governor of Florida. Those verbal exchanges took place over the Labor Day weekend, when […]
text:
David Jolly, pictured with his son while attending the West Central Florida Labor Council Labor Day Picnic in Tampa on Sept. 7, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix) TAMPA — Byron Donalds says David Jolly “isn’t doing much of anything” on the campaign trail, but Jolly is firing back that it’s Donalds who dropped out of what would have been the first one-on-one events between the two men running for governor of Florida.
Those verbal exchanges took place over the Labor Day weekend, when both men made separate campaign appearances in Tampa.
Donalds went first, speaking Saturday afternoon at an event with veterans near MacDill Air Force Base, where he accused his Democratic opponent of running a stealth campaign similar to what other Democrats have done in winning governorships and, in the case of Joe Biden, the presidency in recent years.
“Since the primary a couple of weeks ago, we have been doing events, rallies, Q&As, all over Florida,” Donalds said. “But I noticed that Jolly does not take questions. … He’s never around for the voters to ask him something.”
Donalds compared Jolly’s campaign to those of Arizona’s Katie Hobbs in 2022, Virginia’s Abigail Spanberger in 2025, and Joe Biden’s for president in 2020, complaining they ran “like potted plants, never saying anything.”
“[He] ran the very famous basement campaign,” Donalds said of Biden.
Jolly wasn’t having any of that when asked about it Monday.
“It’s fiction,” he told the Phoenix while attending the West Central Florida Labor Council Labor Day Picnic.
“We’re standing at a picnic talking about this. Last week, I was in Pensacola. Tallahassee. Jacksonville. Miami. All in about four days. If there’s one thing that our campaign’s been known for, it’s been the Lawton Chiles approach of the last 18 months. That’s the reality.”
(Then-state Sen. Lawton Chiles walked 1,000 miles from Pensacola to Miami on the way to victory in the 1970 U.S. Senate race.)
And Jolly says it’s Donalds who backed out of a scheduled event between the two at the Tampa Tiger Bay Club later this month.“I will tell you that he’s just cancelled on one we were going to do jointly at Tiger Tampa Bay,” Jolly said. “He pulled out of that, and now he pulled out of doing it solo and he’s sending Avila.”
A board member with the Tampa Tiger Bay Club Monday confirmed to the Phoenix that the Donalds campaign had initially agreed to appear jointly with Jolly. However, the board member continued, the campaign called later to say Donalds wanted to appear separately, and then reached out again to say he would not appear at all, but instead could offer his running mate, former Miami-Dade County Republican state Sen. Bryan Avila.
A source close to the Donalds campaign said it never confirmed Byron would attend.
“At no point was it on our calendar,” said the source, adding that that the campaign learned of the appointment “after the fact.”
Avila is now scheduled to appear at the Tampa Tiger Bay Club on Sept. 18. Jolly is scheduled to speak on Sept. 25.
Beginning stages
Both men said their campaigns are in the beginning stages of planning debates that definitely will happen sometime in the next eight weeks.
“I don’t think there’s been communication among camps,” Jolly said Monday. “We’re trying to get the logistics worked out on our side,” Donalds said Saturday.
Jolly says he hopes that, when the two do convene, the setup creates more light than heat.
“I have no interest in a debate for sports and to inject more toxicity into the conversation,” he said. “I really mean that. I don’t see any value in a format that puts in front of people that cheer and they boo and create memes and do whatever. That’s a social media game.”
“That’s why Tiger Bay’s a great format,” he added. “Let the people ask the questions. Give them an award for the hardest questions, right?”
Donalds said its important for the voters to know where Jolly stands on the issues, which is why he reiterated his request on Saturday for three debates before the general election. “We are looking forward to those debates.”
Jolly is as well, but says the charge he’s running a “basement campaign” reflects that “we’re seeing a campaign on their side that’s struggling to find their footing.”
“They’ve tried the culture war hits. They’ve tried tax hits. They’re trying guns and immigration. Now they’re trying the repeat of what Trump did against Biden, because that’s all they know how to do.”

title: Trump’s trade war with Canada escalates as new tariffs launch
text: WASHINGTON — Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on American goods kicked in Tuesday, escalating a trade war with one of the largest U.S. trading partners that President Donald Trump continued to antagonize over the holiday weekend.Trump posted an AI-generated cartoon image of himself Sunday evening in which he is depicted as a hockey player striking Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is shown down on the ice, with a hockey stick. “Get up, governor,” a speech bubble from Trump’s mouth reads, apparently referring to Canada as a U.S. state rather than a sovereign country. Nearly $28 billion in U.S. exports crossing the border to Canada now carry up to 50% tariffs, a dollar-for-dollar match on Trump’s taxes on Canadian goods imposed last month, according to Canadian officials. Among the 629 categories of products Canada has targeted are key outputs from U.S. states with hotly contested races in the fast-approaching November midterm elections, including Maine’s paper and lumber industry, Michigan’s vehicle manufacturing and Wisconsin dairy production.U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, a Maine Republican who’s in the midst of a tough reelection campaign, warned in late August roughly $170 million of her state’s goods will be impacted by the Canadian tariffs, with more than half of that coming from the forest product sector. Canada revised its tariff proposal Aug. 27 to exclude seafood, including Maine’s significant lobster industry. 5% of goods in questionThe United States and Canada’s dueling tariffs represent roughly 5% of the two countries’ massive and intertwined trading partnership, which totaled $879.9 billion in goods in 2025, according to the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.But the escalation has been accompanied by Trump’s near constant trolling of the U.S. northern neighbor, including threats since his days on the 2024 campaign trail to annex Canada as the 51st state. Over the Labor Day weekend, the president declared on his Truth Social platform “NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!”“If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank.’ BUY AMERICAN. FLY ON AMERICAN AIRLINERS. ENJOY AMERICAN LIQUOR AND BEVERAGES. SAIL ON LAKE AMERICA. AMERICA FIRST!” Trump wrote, referencing his executive order Aug. 27 renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America.The Canadian airline maker Bombardier has multiple manufacturing partners and facilities in the United States, including in Arizona, Florida, Indiana, Kansas and New Jersey, according to the company.“Bombardier aircraft create tens of thousands of U.S. jobs through the company’s growing American footprint as well as within its supply chain made up of approximately 2,800 American companies across 47 states,” according to a Bombadier statement issued Monday. “The company spends over $2.5 Billion with suppliers each year. This deeply integrated network and incredible growth stem from the company’s heritage in the business jet industry, dating back to the innovations of Learjet in Wichita, Kansas, and the first business jets to enter service,” the statement continued.U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran said in a post on X Monday evening that he contacted Trump “to make certain the President is aware of the significant contributions of Bombardier to Kansas and the importance of its presence in Wichita to many Kansas workers at Bombardier and in the Bombardier supply chain.”The company supports roughly 1,000 jobs in the state, according to the Kansas Republican.Executive ordersTrade talks between the U.S. and Canada collapsed Aug. 21. In days prior Trump had said he would delay new tariffs on Canadian goods while negotiations continued. Trump signed three executive orders for new tariffs on Canada in late July using a Depression-era law that has never been enforced. Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 authorizes the president to impose duties up to 50% of a product’s value in response to discrimination against U.S. commerce.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Nonprofit creates scholarship program fueled by federal tax credit for Kentucky students
description: A statewide nonprofit organization has been established to oversee educational scholarships for Kentucky public and private school students under a future federal tax credit program.  The Kentucky Education Fund “a statewide, nonpartisan option for administering qualifying contributions and scholarships under the new program,” a press release from the organi[...]
text:
A young boy walks down a hallway at Carter Traditional Elementary School in Louisville, Ky. (Jon Cherry/Getty Images)A statewide nonprofit organization has been established to oversee educational scholarships for Kentucky public and private school students under a future federal tax credit program. 
The Kentucky Education Fund “a statewide, nonpartisan option for administering qualifying contributions and scholarships under the new program,” a press release from the organization said. Earlier this year, the Kentucky General Assembly opted the state into a program of education grants for K-12 students promoted by the Trump administration and benefiting from a new federal tax credit. 
Republican state lawmakers said House Bill 1 would allow K-12 students and their families to benefit from a federal tax credit at no cost to Kentucky, but critics, including some Democrats, said the program is a way to support “school choice” options — at the expense of public schools — despite rejections by Kentucky voters and the state Supreme Court. 
Under the federal program, taxpayers can claim an up to $1,700 tax credit for contributions to approved Scholarship Granting Organizations, or SGOs, like the Kentucky Education Fund. The group said it received federal nonprofit recognition in July and approval from the Secretary of State Michael Adams’ office on Aug. 27 as a Kentucky SGO.  
Adams, a Republican, formally signed paperwork with the IRS to opt Kentucky into the federal program and signed a state regulation for the procedures to submit, review and process filings for SGOs. 
 The Kentucky Education Fund has partnered with Kentucky’s Area Development Districts to help with establishing the program in all 120 Kentucky counties and creating its governance. 
“For more than 50 years, Kentucky’s Area Development Districts have served as the conveners and planners across all communities, urban and rural,” said Senate President Pro Tem David Givens, R-Greensburg. “Having Area Development District leaders serve as the founding body of the Kentucky Education Fund is a natural extension of that work, bringing together regional knowledge, trusted partnerships and a shared commitment to creating greater opportunities for all Kentuckians.”
Will Hodges, a former superintendent of Green County Schools, is an adviser to the fund, and said in a statement that the organization plans to help students “from Paducah to Pikeville.” 
“The Area Development Districts brought regional knowledge from every part of Kentucky to the Fund’s formation, helping ensure that statewide reach was part of the conversation from the beginning,” Hodges said. 
According to its website, the Fund says K-12 students eligible for a scholarship may be “attending public or private schools.” Students who are “receiving a home-based education, provided the student and scholarship expense satisfy applicable federal requirements and Fund policies,” may also be eligible.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Judge tosses Newark mayor’s lawsuit against ex-prosecutor for arrest at ICE jail
description: A judge said Alina Habba, New Jersey's ex-top federal prosecutor, acted within the scope of her job when she bashed Newark Mayor Ras Baraka on TV and social media.
text:
Newark Mayor Ras Baraka speaks to a crowd of supporters outside the federal courthouse in Newark on May 15, 2025, after a conference on a trespassing charge he faces. (Photo by New Jersey Monitor)A federal judge has dismissed the libel lawsuit Newark Mayor Ras Baraka filed last year against Alina Habba, the former top federal prosecutor in New Jersey, over comments she made on social media and TV about his botched arrest outside Delaney Hall.
In a decision released Friday, U.S. District Judge Brian R. Martinotti said Habba was acting within her scope as acting U.S. attorney for New Jersey when she accused Baraka on social media and during a Fox News interview of illegal trespass and “grandstanding” during the May 9, 2025, visit to the federal migrant jail in Newark during which he was arrested.
“Making a public statement about potential criminal activity within a prosecutor’s jurisdiction falls within the ambit of a prosecutor’s employment,” Martinotti wrote. “Habba’s use of social media and her participation in media interviews to address criminal activity in New Jersey falls within the spatial limits of her employment as the interim United States Attorney for District of New Jersey.”
Baraka also failed to seek relief first from the Department of Justice, which the Federal Tort Claims Act requires, before filing his lawsuit, wrote Martinotti, an Obama appointee.
But the judge also said he wasn’t ruling on the merits of Baraka’s libel claims. He left the door open for the mayor to renew his claims, dismissing the case without prejudice. That means Baraka can amend and refile his complaint if he addresses the judge’s concerns, and Martinotti gave him 21 days to do so.
It’s unclear if he will. His attorney and city spokespeople did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
New videos capture tense moments surrounding arrest of Newark mayor

Baraka sued Habba and Ricky Patel, the special agent in charge of the Newark Division of Homeland Security Investigations, for false arrest and malicious prosecution in June 2025, a few weeks after Patel ordered armed, masked immigration agents to “take him down” during a tense visit Baraka made to Delaney Hall.
Three Democratic members of Congress — Reps. LaMonica McIver, Rob Menendez, and Bonnie Watson Coleman — also were there that day to inspect the prison, and McIver had asked Baraka to attend their post-inspection news conference.
After he arrived, a prison guard invited Baraka onto prison grounds past the fenced perimeter, where protesters had gathered. He waited there until Patel directed him to leave the fenced area about 45 minutes later, and even though he complied, the agents arrested him five minutes later, charged him with trespass, and held him in federal custody for five hours.
Ten days later, prosecutors dropped the charge and a federal judge scolded them for the “hasty arrest” and “embarrassing retraction” of the charge.
Baraka, a Democrat who was running for governor at the time of his arrest, accused Habba and Patel of political motivations. When Habba announced she was dropping the trespassing charge against Baraka, she filed criminal charges against McIver, accusing her of assaulting federal agents as they arrested Baraka. The U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals last month rejected McIver’s bid to avoid trial on two of the three charges she faces.
Habba resigned in December after another judge disqualified her from the post.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Andrea Fletcher tapped to lead Virginia’s government technology overhaul
description: Virginia is creating a team of technology specialists to improve state websites and computer systems while guarding against costly technology contracts and wasted taxpayer dollars.  Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Tuesday named Andrea Fletcher director of the new Virginia Digital Service, which will bring together engineers, designers and other technical experts[...]
text:
Andrea Fletcher will lead the new Virginia Digital Service, a team charged with modernizing state websites and computer systems and improving how the state purchases technology. (Courtesy of Virginia Governor’s Office)Virginia is creating a team of technology specialists to improve state websites and computer systems while guarding against costly technology contracts and wasted taxpayer dollars. 
Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Tuesday named Andrea Fletcher director of the new Virginia Digital Service, which will bring together engineers, designers and other technical experts to modernize state government operations and make public services easier to use. 
The team will also review how Virginia buys and uses technology, with an eye toward identifying problems before the state commits taxpayer money to poorly designed systems or contracts. 
“State government should work for the people it serves — and that means making sure Virginians can access the services they need quickly, easily, and reliably,” Spanberger said in a statement. 
Spanberger proposed establishing the Digital Service through an amendment to Virginia’s biennial budget after her administration said it discovered the state had lost $52 million on a failed IT project under former Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s administration. 
The project involved a two-year effort by the Virginia Department of Social Services to modernize APECS, the state’s decades-old child support enforcement computer system. The department had hired CGI Technologies and Solutions for the project, known as vCHAMPS, but abandoned the overhaul after what an internal report described as “significant issues.” 
Under Fletcher’s leadership, the team will work with agencies across state government computer systems, improve websites and speed up delivery of programs used by Virginia families, according to the governor’s office. 
“We also have a responsibility to make sure every taxpayer dollar is used as effectively and efficiently as possible,” Spanberger said. “At a time of unprecedented uncertainty and disruption out of Washington, Virginia can — and should — be a model of how we make smart, sound investments in technology.”
Fletcher previously served as the first chief digital officer at the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, where she led the agency’s Digital Service team. She also established what the governor’s office called the federal government’s first Open Source Program Office.
She began her tenure with the federal government through the U.S. Digital Service in 2021 after working in federal healthcare information technology policy, artificial intelligence governance and global health systems. Her work included projects in more than 20 countries and support for digital health systems responding to COVID-19, Ebola and HIV.
Fletcher received a Service to the Citizen Award in 2025 and was nominated in 2024 for the Samuel J. Heyman award for emerging government leaders. 
“Virginians should have an expectation that government services be intuitive and easy to use,” Fletcher said in a statement. “I’m excited to help deliver on that goal for the people of the Commonwealth and demonstrate that government can build great technology.”
David Wilkinson, Virginia’s chief transformation officer, said residents should be able to navigate state systems easily whether they are applying for a driver’s license, opening a business or seeking essential services. 
“In launching the Virginia Digital Service, the governor is bringing a proven approach to Virginia,” Wilkinson said. “Andrea Fletcher is a nationally respected digital leader with a track record of delivering results that save time and money.”
Originally from western Pennsylvania’s Appalachian region, Fletcher earned a bachelor’s degree from Washington & Jefferson College and a master’s degree in public health from Emory University. She lives in Alexandria with her husband and daughter. 
One of the new team’s early assignments will be helping state agencies respond to federal funding and eligibility changes under H.R. 1, the tax and spending reconciliation bill Congress passed last summer at the behest of President Donald Trump. 
The administration said the Digital Service will support efforts to maintain access to healthcare coverage and Supplemental Nutrition Access Program.
The move follows a separate legislative effort to modernize Virginia’s benefits system. House Bill 66, sponsored by Del. Michael Feggans, D-Virginia Beach, would have directed the departments of Social Services and Medical Assistance Services to develop a plan for updating technology used to administer federal medical and other benefit programs. The measure was continued to the 2027 session. 
Last month, Spanberger launched the “Keep Virginia Covered” policy directing executive agencies as they implement the federal law and seek to limit its effect on Virginians. 
Virginia is not the first state to create a government-run technology team. Similar programs elsewhere have been used to review contracts, simply applications for public benefits and rebuild government websites. 
In Colorado, the state’s digital team helped negotiate a grant-management system covering 17 programs and more than $60 million in annual grants before money was committed to the system.  
Pennsylvania used its team to haul over the process for appealing denied insurance claims, replacing what Spanberger’s administration described as a confusing form with a simpler system. 
Meanwhile, Maryland consolidated applications for Medicaid, SNAP, Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, the Special Supplemental Assistance Program for Women, Infants and Children, and energy assistance into a single process. More than 220,000 applications were completed through the new system in six months, according to the state’s Gov. Wes Moore. 
Maryland also redesigned its unemployment insurance website around a five-step process for claimants. The changes reduced the number of pages on the site by 40% and increased its completion rate by 15%.

name: National
title: The largest US school districts restrict student AI use
description: The country’s two largest school districts — New York City and Los Angeles — banned most student use of artificial intelligence in classrooms for this school year as anxiety over AI’s effect on learning intensifies. The Los Angeles Unified School District announced last week that it is barring student use of generative AI on school-issued […]
text:
Students work in a classroom. The nation's two largest school districts banned AI use for most students this school year. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The country’s two largest school districts — New York City and Los Angeles — banned most student use of artificial intelligence in classrooms for this school year as anxiety over AI’s effect on learning intensifies.
The Los Angeles Unified School District announced last week that it is barring student use of generative AI on school-issued devices for the current school year. Generative AI creates new text, images or other content following a user’s instructions. During the school year, a committee will produce recommendations for use of the technology in future years.
New York City Public Schools last week announced a similar but less broad approach. The district put in place a one-year moratorium on generative AI for children from pre-kindergarten through eighth grade. 
Schools spend billions on AI, but struggle to figure out what’s worth buying

High school students will have to complete 45-minute AI literacy modules twice a year. Some career-focused AI use will be allowed and some high schools will be permitted to test AI pilot programs.
The restrictions, which New York officials said will affect 600,000 students, will allow time to study the technology’s impacts. 
“The tech industry wants us to believe that A.I.-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a news release. “We do not see it that way.” 
Chicago officials may follow suit. About half the candidates running for the Chicago Board of Education this November have signed a pledge calling for a three-year moratorium on generative AI use in the public school classrooms.
Smaller school districts around the country have taken similar steps. Districts in Colorado, Kansas, Minnesota, Texas and Washington have blocked or limited tools such as ChatGPT, while some allow approved platforms under teacher supervision.
Stateline reporter Robbie Sequeira can be reached at rsequeira@stateline.org.
