name: Colorado Newsline
title: 14 measures will appear on Colorado’s statewide ballot in 2026
description: The Colorado secretary of state’s office on Friday certified the list of ballot measures going before voters in November 2026 — and once again, the list is a long one. A total of 14 measures will be decided by Colorado voters this year. The figure ties a record for the most questions put to voters […]
text:
Volunteers at the Denver Clerk and Recorder's office process ballots during the Colorado primary election on June 30, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)The Colorado secretary of state’s office on Friday certified the list of ballot measures going before voters in November 2026 — and once again, the list is a long one.
A total of 14 measures will be decided by Colorado voters this year. The figure ties a record for the most questions put to voters in at least the last 52 years, according to a state database. An equal number of measures appeared on Coloradans’ ballots in 2024, 2008 and 2006.
What sets this year apart, however, is the number of citizen-initiated measures, which are placed on the ballot through petition signatures. Thirteen of the questions on Colorado’s 2026 ballot are initiatives, while only one was referred to voters by the state Legislature. That’s compared to a 7-7 split two years ago. Coloradans haven’t voted on more than 10 citizen initiatives in any single election since 1974.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Nearly half of this year’s 13 initiatives are sponsored by Advance Colorado, a right-wing “dark money” group that does not disclose its donors. In recent years, as Republicans have fallen far short of competing for legislative majorities at the state Capitol, Advance Colorado has been highly active in attempting to pass conservative policies through the ballot box instead.
Ballot questions can either be statutory measures — which, if approved, become state laws that can be changed by the Legislature — or amendments to the state Constitution, which can only be changed by voter approval of a subsequent amendment.
Constitutional amendments face a higher bar for approval, requiring 55% of the vote to pass, rather than the simple majority required for statutory measures. An exception is that if a constitutional measure only repeals, rather than amends, language in the constitution, it only needs a simple majority.
Front Range cities will vote on tax measure to fund Colorado Connector rail service

To date, proposed initiatives have been numbered sequentially according to when they were filed with the state’s Initiative Title Setting Review Board, commonly known as the Title Board. More than 400 proposed initiatives were filed in the 2026 election cycle, the vast majority of which were denied a title by the board or withdrawn by proponents.
In addition to statewide ballot measures, voters in 31 Front Range municipalities will vote on whether to approve a 0.333% sales tax hike to fund the Colorado Connector passenger rail service. Many counties and other local jurisdictions will have ballot questions of their own.
Detailed information about the statewide measures prepared by nonpartisan staff at the Legislature will be mailed to registered voters in the 2026 Blue Book, which will also be available online. Ballots are scheduled to be mailed to voters beginning Oct. 2.
Constitutional amendments
Amendment 81 is a proposed constitutional amendment that would require Colorado law enforcement agencies to cooperate more closely with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and other federal immigration authorities. Current state law places strict limits on such cooperation. If the amendment were approved, police would be required to notify the feds when they file certain criminal charges against a person known to be “not lawfully present” in the U.S., or if “the status of the person’s lawful presence is unknown.” It’s sponsored by Advance Colorado.
Amendment 82, also sponsored by Advance Colorado, proposes a two-sentence change that would enshrine the right to buy and sell natural gas in the state constitution. “Consumers have the right to purchase natural gas for cooking or heating in homes or businesses throughout the state,” the measure reads. “Distributors and utilities have the right to sell natural gas for homes or businesses.”
Amendment 83 would establish a constitutional right to hunt and fish “by the use of traditional methods,” and declare that hunting and fishing is the state’s “preferred method” of managing wildlife populations. It would apply to species managed by the state, and wouldn’t include the right to hunt endangered species or species that are illegal to hunt under federal law. It’s backed by the Wisconsin-based International Order of T. Roosevelt, a right-leaning conservation group.
Amendment 84 would end Colorado’s signature-based mail ballot verification system, and instead require voters to provide the last four digits of their Social Security number or driver’s license number to ensure their mail ballot is counted. It’s backed by the Coalition for American Prosperity and Growth, a dark-money group.
Amendment 85 would require all future ballot initiatives and referred measures appearing on Colorado ballots to be written at an eighth-grade reading level. It’s backed by Advance Colorado.
Amendment 86 would require any mid-decade or “off-cycle” redistricting effort to be approved by both the state’s independent redistricting commission and the Colorado Supreme Court, and prohibit the approval of a map that “has been drawn purposefully to favor one political party.” It’s backed by Advance Colorado.
Amendment 87 proposes to enact a graduated income tax system with Coloradans earning over $500,000 a year — the top 3% of earners — paying higher rates, and those in lower brackets receiving a slight tax cut. It’s backed by Protecting Colorado’s Future, a coalition of progressive and liberal advocacy groups. Because it would only repeal, rather than amend, language in the constitution, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Canvassers received petition packets as they prepared to gather signatures in support of a graduated income tax ballot measure at a Protect Colorado’s Future event in Denver on July 18, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
Statutory measures
Proposition NN is the only legislatively referred measure to be considered by voters this year. Democratic majorities in the General Assembly voted to place it on the ballot in May. It would raise the limit on the tax revenue that the state is allowed to retain under the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights, increasing funding for K-12 education by about $500 million a year. Depending on state revenue growth in future years, it could reduce the amount returned to taxpayers as TABOR refunds.
Proposition 132 would substantially increase criminal penalties for the possession and distribution of synthetic opioids like fentanyl. The possession of any amount of fentanyl would be classified as a felony, and the distribution of any amount would require a mandatory prison sentence between 8 and 32 years. Options under current sentencing laws to reduce penalties and divert some offenders to treatment programs would be eliminated. The statutory measure is backed by Advance Colorado.
Proposition 133 would mandate that anyone convicted of child sex trafficking be sentenced to life in prison without parole, an increase from the current sentencing range of between 8 and 48 years. It’s sponsored by Protect Kids Colorado, a conservative anti-LGBTQ advocacy group also behind two other measures on the 2026 ballot.
Proposition 134 aims to prevent transgender children from participating in school sports. It would add language in state statute to define boys and girls based on physical anatomy, excluding transgender people. Sports teams sponsored by schools or athletic associations would be required to expressly designate those teams for men, women or co-ed. It’s backed by Protect Kids Colorado.
Proposition 135, the third measure backed by Protect Kids Colorado, would prohibit health care professionals from knowingly performing any surgery on a minor “for the purpose of altering biological sex characteristics.” The measure would also prohibit state and federal funding including Medicaid from being used to pay for gender-affirming procedures.
Proposition 136 is an Advance Colorado measure that aims to block the graduated income tax amendment. It would cap income tax rates at their current level of 4.4%, preventing Amendment 87’s higher rates on higher incomes from going into effect. If both measures are approved, their conflicting provisions would be resolved according to which measure received the higher number of yes votes.
Proposition 137 would boost state funding for conservation and wildfire mitigation projects by exempting tax revenue from sporting goods sales from constitutional limits set by the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights. It’s backed by The Nature Conservancy and a handful of other environmental groups.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Tommy Tuberville’s data center plan: Some good ideas, a lot of fatal flaws
description: Tommy Tuberville’s data center plan has some good ideas. The problem is that they’re good ideas for long-term constitutional reform, not the pressing challenges these large-scale facilities pose.  And even if he’s serious about giving communities the power to say no to data centers, his proposal lacks a key requirement to make those objections meaningful. […[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville speaking at the Alabama Republican Party's Summer Dinner on July 31, 2026, at the Renaissance Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama. Tuberville last week released a four-point plan for addressing data center development in the state. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Tommy Tuberville’s data center plan has some good ideas. The problem is that they’re good ideas for long-term constitutional reform, not the pressing challenges these large-scale facilities pose. 
And even if he’s serious about giving communities the power to say no to data centers, his proposal lacks a key requirement to make those objections meaningful.
But I will give Tuberville (or his handlers) credit. After weeks of belittling data center opponents and treating the facilities as inevitabilities, he has — for now — stopped mouthing the triumphalist rhetoric to hear what people are saying.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Data centers are about as popular as Tennessee in Tuscaloosa on the third Saturday in October. They’re loud, they consume a ton of electricity, and they threaten water supplies. In a state that already has some of the South’s highest residential electricity rates, you shake the pom-poms for data centers at your peril.
So at first glance, the approach Tuberville outlined in Alabama Political Reporter makes sense. Tuberville proposes letting communities decide whether they want a data center. He would extend an Alabama Power rate freeze past 2029 to prevent customers from subsidizing the facilities’ power consumption.
Tuberville also says that he wants data centers to pay full price for water and electric infrastructure, and to “replace the power and water capacity they take.” And he wants to place data centers “in Alabama’s highest property tax bracket, where they should be.”
This is all reasonable, though it’s less about addressing impacts than trying to make data centers more attractive. The Alabama Power rate freeze is fine, though extending it beyond 2029 would depend on a Gov. Tuberville appointing an energy secretary who does not uncritically accept everything the utility says.  
Data centers should pay for water and electric infrastructure, but it’s not clear how the state could force that outside a law or by leveraging economic incentives. The former couldn’t pass before next February at the earliest. Negotiations for the latter are opaque and usually revealed after the fact.
But two other points in the plan that cause problems.
Who resides in Alabama’s highest property tax bracket? Utilities providing utility services. Under that delightfully ruinous 1978 constitutional amendment known as the lid bill, the state taxes utility property at 30% of its assessed value.  
Putting data centers in this bracket could be politically and constitutionally tricky. But let’s assume you could.  
Take the $1.5 billion project Red Clay proposed in Lowndes County. (Tuberville in his op-ed wants you to imagine a $12 billion data center bringing in $150 million in revenue. There are no projects of that scale currently planned here.) Assuming the fair market value of Red Clay is $1.5 billion, Lowndes County would get about $17.3 million a year in property taxes under Tuberville’s plan.
I’m sure that money would be welcomed. Would the noise? Or the electricity and water consumption? Tuberville does not propose any regulation to mitigate the impact of data centers after they’re built. The Red Clay developers say they will pay for water infrastructure improvements, but I’m not sure how far that will go in the Black Belt, long plagued by problems with water supply.
And if you multiplied that by eight, to a $12 billion facility? Well, $150 million might not be enough. Amazon, which is building a $12 billion data center in Louisiana, is putting $400 million into local water infrastructure there.
Fine. A community could look at the proposal and say no under Tuberville’s plan.
Except Tuberville doesn’t say how he would do this. Alabama’s constitution severely limits county government powers. You can’t write a bill to reverse that. You need a constitutional amendment.
And that loud, angry gurgling you hear from Goat Hill is the custodians of Alabama’s top-down government contemptuously spitting out the phrase “home rule.” The Alabama Farmers Federation, arguably the most powerful interest group in the Republican coalition, has traditionally opposed anything moving powers from state government.
So you’d have to overcome their likely opposition. You’d have to marshal the votes in the Legislature. And then you’d have to send the amendment out for a vote, a vote unlikely to occur before 2028. (Also, the governor has no direct role in this process.)
That’s a lot of time for data centers to sink roots into communities as the constitutional process grinds on. And it assumes the Big Mules wouldn’t suffocate the proposal first.
To make community input mean something, you have to pause development long enough for local governments to get the power to decide. Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones has proposed a one-year moratorium on new data center construction. Tuberville blasted Jones for the proposal in his op-ed. But practically speaking, local empowerment means nothing if developers build their facilities before a county commission can say no.
It’s good to see Tuberville taking this issue seriously. But intentionally or not, his plan won’t let Alabamians decide whether a data center is a good fit. In fact, it could give developers a window to make local opinion meaningless.
If Tuberville is on board with constitutional reform, I’ll be there with him. But if he’s serious about addressing data center concerns, his plan needs more details, more safeguards and a lot more urgency.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama representative criticizes ongoing prison mental health litigation
description: An Alabama lawmaker and outspoken critic of the Alabama Department of Corrections said Thursday the Alabama Attorney General’s Office should have settled an ongoing lawsuit over mental health care in state prisons instead of continuing with litigation. Rep. Chris England, D-Tuscaloosa, said at the Contract Review Committee meeting Thursday that he wanted ans[...]
text:
A prison corridor in Holman Correctional Facility in 2019. An Alabama state representative last week said he wanted to know whether settling a long-running lawsuit over mental health care in state prisons would be cheaper than pursuing a settlement. (File)An Alabama lawmaker and outspoken critic of the Alabama Department of Corrections said Thursday the Alabama Attorney General’s Office should have settled an ongoing lawsuit over mental health care in state prisons instead of continuing with litigation.
Rep. Chris England, D-Tuscaloosa, said at the Contract Review Committee meeting Thursday that he wanted answers from ADOC about mounting costs in the lawsuit, known as Braggs v. Lovelace.
“I am just really sick and tired of giving more money to the Department of Corrections under this current administration and under this leadership, because clearly, we are just burning it,” England said in an interview with the media following the meeting. “There aren’t any real reforms, changes or anything meaningful happening, so we continue to dump millions of dollars into this thing and all we get are the courts and the Department of Justice telling us that, since ‘We came and told you that you were awful, you got worse.’”
Following a trial, U.S. District Judge Myron Thompson in 2017 ruled that mental health care in Alabama prisons was “horrendously inadequate” and ordered reforms. A three-judge panel of the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals issued a ruling in June that largely affirmed Thompson’s ruling, though it lowered some of the staffing requirements.
England made his comments while Mandy Speirs, an attorney representing ADOC at the meeting, presented committee members with a contract that the agency renewed with BBH CBMC, based in Talladega, for an additional $6.6 million to provide inpatient mental health services. The contract total has reached about $26.6 million.
“There is a level of healthcare required in Braggs, and this is how we meet that level of healthcare,” Speirs said.
The agenda states the contract aims to “discharge the State’s commitment to provide inpatient mental health care to State inmates in need of these services as required by the Braggs litigation.”
The contract reserves space for 10 people who will be referred to the offsite facility with another five as needed.
“The contract you have here says it is because of the Braggs litigation, $20 more million, (when) we have already paid our lawyers $27 million, you are asking for $6 million more after a court has told us we torture people and our mentally ill prisoners,” England told Speirs. “I think it is fair to try and find out if that legal strategy that we adopted, litigating and losing versus trying to settle, actually saved us money.”
England said he and other members received a cost estimate from ADOC that said the state saved money by litigating the Braggs case instead of settling it.
Speirs said she would provide settlement cost proposals to allow England and other lawmakers to compare the different outcomes.
This case is one of two significant lawsuits that ADOC will face in the coming months. England voted to delay a contract that ADOC awarded to Bill Lunsford to defend the ADOC in a lawsuit filed by the U.S. Department of Justice that alleges the conditions in Alabama’s prisons are unconstitutional.
ADOC is also scheduled to face a trial in November over charges from the U.S. Department of Justice that violence in the state’s prisons violates inmates’ Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment. Federal prosecutors Wednesday filed a motion for summary judgment against the state.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: New data center project coming to Mason County, WV spearheaded by Florida-based real estate group
description: The West Virginia Department of Commerce has approved and certified two separate high impact data center projects — one previously unannounced — for Mason County, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced at the state Chamber of Commerce’s business summit last week.
text:
A server room in a data center. (Photo by Getty Images)The West Virginia Department of Commerce has approved and certified two separate high impact data center projects — one previously unannounced — for Mason County, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced at the state Chamber of Commerce’s business summit last week.
One of those certifications is for the proposed Nscale Monarch Campus, in Point Pleasant. Developers for that project are proposing to build a data center complex that would potentially be powered by a biomass and carbon-capture facility that would generate electricity by burning wood chips as fuel. The power would not be made for sale on the grid. 
The data center and biomass facility — which received an air quality permit from the state Department of Environmental Protection earlier this year — are just part of the massive proposed campus.
The second project — announced by Morrisey for the first time at the annual business summit — would be located about 20 miles north of the Monarch Campus in Mason County. There, Morrisey said, Starwood Digital Ventures plans to invest $12 billion to develop a new data center complex. Starwood Digital Ventures — an arm of the Florida-based real estate firm Starwood Capital Group — currently owns data centers throughout northern Virginia and is working on developing a massive data center complex in Delaware. 
In West Virginia, Morrisey said the Starwood project (dubbed “Project Tamarack”) will require 2.16 gigawatts of power to operate, which it will receive from the existing grid. Morrisey asserted Thursday that the proposed project would not increase power rates for existing ratepayers, saying that Starwood will cover all necessary infrastructure costs.
The data center plans to run on a closed-loop cooling system, which generally uses less water than other systems. No specific source for the water was indicated during Morrisey’s announcement.
Morrisey said that the state began conversations with Starwood officials regarding the project over the last six months. Anthony Balestieri, Starwood Digital Ventures CEO, said that the company was “very excited” to pursue the project, which he said will be a “major contributor to a legacy of success here in West Virginia.”
Balestieri lauded the state law, House Bill 2014, that incentivizes data center developers to locate in West Virginia. He said that the passage of that law last year and the environment it created attracted the company to the Mountain State. West Virginia, Balestieri said, is “at the forefront of defining a clear set of standards for responsible development.”
That same law — which created the state’s certified microgrid and data center program — strips localities from having any power to enforce or create ordinances that would affect data center developments. That includes noise ordinances, zoning ordinances, public health policies and more. The law also diverts 70% of the tax revenue brought in from data center developments away from the county they are located to the state.
Over the past 18 months, residents across the state — from Mason, Mingo and Tucker counties up to the Eastern Panhandle —  have begun organizing against HB 2014, the rules it created and the developers who are looking to take advantage of it. They have spoken out against having their local rights and power stripped away in favor of developers. They worry that the consequences brought by data center developments — for public health, tourism, affordability and more — will drastically change their communities.
In Mason County already, a group — Mason United — has formed in response to the proposed Nscale Monarch Campus. They are concerned over the environmental impacts that the development could bring, especially as several neighbors in the area have already had their homes flooded due to construction occurring at the Monarch site.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Advocate files federal civil rights complaint against Kentucky school district
description: A special education advocate has filed a federal complaint against Warren County Public Schools on behalf of students and parents alleging the district overly refers students with disabilities to a local mental health facility.  Student advocate Mary Beth Patton filed the complaint with the Office for Civil Rights in early August and wrote that students […]
text:
An advocate says Warren County Schools are referring too many special needs students to a mental health facility. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)A special education advocate has filed a federal complaint against Warren County Public Schools on behalf of students and parents alleging the district overly refers students with disabilities to a local mental health facility. 
Student advocate Mary Beth Patton filed the complaint with the Office for Civil Rights in early August and wrote that students with disabilities “make up a disproportionate amount” of the school district’s mental health referrals for crisis and requested further investigation from the federal government. 
Citing records she obtained via open records requests, Patton wrote that 47% of 1,056 school-based mental health crisis referrals in the records involved students with disabilities. She added that students with disabilities make up about 16% of district enrollment. 
“When it comes to kids with disabilities, there are supposed to be considerations for their disability,” Patton told the Kentucky Lantern. “Children are not supposed to be referred for crisis to an institution or a psychiatric unit, when the behaviors that they are engaging in is a manifestation of their disability.” 
School officials may make the referrals in situations where a student needs immediate support from a mental health professional, usually after an assessment. A few Warren County parents who spoke with the Lantern said their children were given such assessments and they were notified afterward when a referral was made. They also said they felt pressured to take their child to Rivendell Behavioral Hospital, which is in Warren County and provides in-patient services. 
Rob Clayton, the superintendent of Warren County Public Schools, said in a statement that trained school employees “follow established procedures, communicate with the parent or guardian, and work to connect the family with appropriate professional resources” when a student may pose a risk to themselves or others or circumstances have a need for urgent professional mental health assessment. He added that WCPS “does not require families to utilize one particular mental health provider.” 
“School personnel do not diagnose students or make decisions regarding admission to a behavioral health facility; those determinations are made by qualified healthcare professionals,” Clayton said. 
The parents’ perspective
The Kentucky Lantern spoke with several family members who have elementary age children with identified disabilities who have been affected by this practice.
Keaton and Justin Johnson, who have a child in Warren County Schools, told the Lantern their child was given six referrals from the school within a couple of months last school year. They said they were told about assessments after they happened. 
“After his first one, we didn’t know any better. We took him to Rivendell because we thought that that’s what we were supposed to do. He ended up being admitted. He was there for a week,” Keaton said, adding that she spoke to her son on the phone a few minutes each day. 
Another parent, Jessica Sheene, said her child was given an assessment after an incident during school drop-off. She said Rivendell did not admit her child because he didn’t meet the criteria to be admitted and he returned to school the next day. 
“I do feel like my right to be his mom was taken away from me because there was no communication after simply the referral is being made,” Sheene said. “In my head I thought that that meant that, ‘OK, he will need to see his provider and talk with his provider about the incident.’ There was no explanation of how the crisis assessment needed to work. There was no explanation of anything other than he simply needed one. That the referral was being made.”
A fourth parent, Aurora Schrader, said her child has had 11 documented referrals from the school, but she wasn’t told each time what was the incident that escalated to an assessment. She said the process was “very traumatizing.” 
Schrader said school staff should have more training on how to assist students with disabilities. 
“That way, they can succeed in life and they can make it out of the school system and go into the real world. “
Keaton also said it is a “systematic issue” and said she would like teachers to have better information on helping students with disabilities. 
“Just because a child may present with certain behaviors doesn’t automatically make it a mental health thing,” she said. “It’s a special education thing, which is exactly what our case was.” 
A representative for Rivendell did not return a phone call seeking comment. 
Clayton said the school district has not been notified by the Office for Civil Rights about the complaint, but would cooperate with the review process and provide information if an inquiry is received. 
“The safety and well-being of our students will always remain our top priority. When a student is experiencing a potential mental health crisis, our staff work with the student and family based on the individual circumstances presented,” he said. “Decisions are not made simply because a student has a disability, nor does the district have a practice of referring students with disabilities to mental health facilities because of their disability.”
Privacy laws prevented Clayton from discussing particular cases involving students and confidential education and health information. 
“Because these situations involve individual students, confidential educational records and often sensitive health and disability information, federal and state privacy laws significantly limit what we can discuss regarding particular cases,” he said. “What I can say is that I strongly disagree with any characterization suggesting that WCPS routinely or indiscriminately sends students with disabilities to behavioral health facilities. Our staff members routinely work through difficult and complex circumstances with families while attempting to protect the safety, dignity and educational needs of every student.”
Warren County Public Schools regularly “evaluates its practices, works with families and community partners, and collaborates with the Kentucky Department of Education and other agencies to ensure we are serving students appropriately,” he added. 
Patton previously aided other families in filing IDEA State Complaints with KDE, she said. Those investigations typically review if a school district has violated the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). Patton wrote in her federal complaint that while KDE found that there were no IDEA violations regarding certain issues raised in the complaints, “those proceedings did not determine whether the district’s overall practices constitute disability discrimination under” Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act.
Patton said she’s received a letter of acknowledgment from the Office of Civil Rights after submitting the complaint. 
Jennifer Ginn, a spokesperson for KDE, said the department “does not have a policy regarding mental health referrals, as these are local decisions,” and it does have resources on school-based mental health listed online. 
“If a student’s mental health concern rises to the level of needing a threat assessment, KRS 158.4412(2)(b) outlines expectations for the district’s school safety coordinator,” Ginn said. “Districts are encouraged to create mental health referral pathways through their multi-tiered systems of support, but these are local determinations based on the resources available and the willingness of mental health providers to partner with them.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: College athletics lawsuit sheds light on Louisiana DAs with private law practices
description: Thirty of Louisiana’s 42 district attorneys who maintain a private practice on top of their government job,
text:
District Attorney Jason Williams, of Orleans Parish does outside legal work on top of his government jov. Most other district attorneys in Louisiana have a similar arrangement. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)A high-profile lawsuit over who can participate in college athletics led to an unusual showdown Thursday between two of Louisiana’s best-known prosecutors: Orleans Parish District Attorney Jason Williams and Tony Clayton, who leads criminal cases in Iberville, Pointe Coupee and  West Baton Rouge parishes. 

It also shed light on a fact not often talked about outside of legal circles. Most Louisiana district attorneys practice law on a private basis on top of public jobs holding criminals accountable. 
At the Baton Rouge court hearing that drew national attention, Clayton represented a group of athletes hoping to play in college again after running out of eligibility, after some attempted to go professional. Williams was on the other side, working with the Southeastern Conference, to block the athletes from rejoining college squads.  
Clayton and Williams are among 30 of Louisiana’s 42 district attorneys who maintain a private practice on top of their government job, according to a review of disclosure documents they have submitted to the state over the past two years. 
“They are litigating because they are both exceptional trial attorneys. What they are doing is not illegal or unethical,” said Rafael Goyeneche, president of the Metropolitan Crime Commission, a New Orleans-area group focused on exposing government corruption. 
Louisiana law allows district attorneys to maintain a private law practice outside of their public sector job as long as they don’t do any criminal defense work. Assistant DAs are also allowed to take on private law clients as long as the district attorney who leads their office allows them to do so. 
“It is just sort of traditional. It’s historically been done that way,” Attorney General Liz Murrill said Thursday. 
Wiliams’ decision to continue working as a private attorney has been scrutinized since he first took office in 2021. His job as New Orleans’ top prosecutor is considered more complex and demanding than most, if not all, other positions around the state. 

Clayton, whose rural judicial district has about a fifth of New Orleans’ population, is known for taking on prominent and sometimes controversial cases at his private law firm. He didn’t change that approach after becoming district attorney in 2020. 
For example, Clayton was part of the legal team who won $411 million, the largest personal injury jury award for an individual plaintiff in Louisiana’s history, last year. More recently, he represented Louisiana Supreme Court Justice Jefferson Hughes in a defamation lawsuit against The Times-Picayune and Advocate newspapers. 
“The ability to maintain a civil practice can supplement the comparatively low salaries provided by the state to prosecutors in Louisiana,” Zach Daniels, executive director of the Louisiana District Attorneys Association, said in a written statement Thursday. 

At least 13 Louisiana district attorneys make over more than $200,000 per year from their public offices, and at least 34 are paid more than $150,000, according to a review of their personal financial disclosure forms.

Williams and Clayton earn $192,000 and $183,000, respectively, as district attorneys, according to their records. 

But they are among a group of just seven DAs who garner more than $100,000 per year from their private law practices, according to the disclosure forms. Others in that category include Joel Chaisson (St. Charles), Paul Connick (Jefferson), Chris Nevils (Winn), James Paxton (Tensas, Madison and East Carroll) and Joseph Waitz (Terrebonne). 

Whether a district attorney decides to take on private clients in addition to their public work doesn’t necessarily correspond to the size or complexity of their district.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

East Baton Rouge DA Hillar Moore and Collin Sims, who prosecutes cases in St. Tammany and Washington parishes, run two of the largest offices in the state and don’t maintain private law practices on the side.
Dane Ciolino, an ethics law expert and professor at Loyola University New Orleans, said the college athletes’ lawsuit is unlikely to create conflicts of interest for Williams or Clayton at their day jobs. 
“There’s no potential criminal prosecution in this SEC suit,” Ciolino said. 
However, district attorneys can run into problems if one of their private clients becomes a suspect in a crime. 
That scenario played out when former St. Tammany District Attorney Walter Reed recused his office in 2011 from the criminal prosecution of a truck driver who was charged with killing two women. Reed, who was later sent to prison for political corruption, was representing the family of the victims in a wrongful death claim as a private attorney. 
Williams has been accused of having a similar conflict of interest this year. He is on the legal team representing John McQueen, a wealthy New Orleans resident who has been sued by his former wife, Anne McQueen. As part of an ongoing legal battle, the McQueens have each accused each other of engaging in criminal activity, which Anne McQueen’s legal team alleges creates a conflict of interest for Williams. 
“Prosecutorial action or inaction involving either side will affect Mr. Williams’ private clients as well as his ability to continue his representation,” attorney Mark Montiel, who is representing Anne McQueen, wrote in a legal brief on the matter in July. “The conflict cannot be ignored merely because no charges have been filed at this time.”

The issue of whether Williams should have to step away from that case is now pending before the Louisiana Supreme Court, though lower courts have ruled in Williams’ favor and said he can stay on the case.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Fired Virginia State University professors file civil rights complaint with AG’s office
description: The Virginia State University Board of Visitors will meet on Friday, roughly a week after the legal team representing six professors fired late last year filed discrimination complaints against the university with the Virginia Attorney General’s Office of Civil Rights. Faculty leaders have recommended the instructors, dubbed The Fired Six, be reinstated and[...]
text:
A person holds a sign stating "reinstate the fired six now" outside of Virginia State University on Feb. 24, 2026. The university fired six faculty members from its agricultural research station in December 2025. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)The Virginia State University Board of Visitors will meet on Friday, roughly a week after the legal team representing six professors fired late last year filed discrimination complaints against the university with the Virginia Attorney General’s Office of Civil Rights.
Faculty leaders have recommended the instructors, dubbed The Fired Six, be reinstated and cited policy violations in the “reorganization” process that led to their terminations.
Virginia State University faces questions after firing six agriculture research experts

VSU’s firing of the Agricultural Research Station faculty members drew heavy criticism and prompted questions about how the institution could remove tenured faculty members from their offices.
In May, a VSU Faculty Senate subcommittee found that the terminations, carried out by deans and human resource managers, violated the university’s termination authority policy, making them unauthorized and illegitimate. 
The policy states that only officials at the vice presidential level or higher have the legal authority to dismiss staff and notify them of their release.
The committee has since determined that the university should restore the professors’ jobs and pay them lost wages.
VSU did not respond to questions about the findings or if it would act on the subcommittee’s recommendation.
Vitalis Temu, one of the fired professors, said VSU’s Board of Visitors, which is responsible for formally discussing and approving any major academic restructuring of university departments, had yet to respond to or take up the findings or recommendations made by his former colleagues, nearly four months after they were published.
“This is a shame for the university,” said Temu.
The controversial VSU dismissals followed federal government changes to agricultural research funding, policy priorities, and USDA operations..
In 2000, VSU was also the subject of another investigation involving the treatment of faculty members by the American Association of University Professors (AAUP). 
Following that investigation, AAUP concluded the university violated academic due process and principles of tenure in dismissing two professors when it improperly changed and applied post-tenure review procedures, and placed the burden on the professors to prove they should be retained.
The school also failed to provide the faculty participation and procedural protections required for dismissal of tenured faculty, the AAUP probe found.
 Background on the firings

The six faculty members were cut from VSU starting Dec. 16, after being called into individual meetings to discuss the research station’s transformational efforts. 
Instead, at the meeting they learned their research programs were being sunset and their jobs were ending immediately.
The former professors said they declined to sign severance agreements at the meeting, largely because they didn’t have sufficient opportunity to review the documents. They said university personnel warned them they would lose any severance if they refused. 
Vitalis Temu, an agricultural research expert, speaking to reporters outside of Virginia State University, which fired him and several faculty members from the institution’s agricultural research station on Feb. 24, 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)
When they refused to sign, they were escorted off campus, required to surrender all items belonging to the university like equipment, identification and keys, and issued trespass warnings.
In February, following a rally for the fired faculty members, a university spokeswoman said VSU made “programmatic adjustments” in the College of Agriculture to align research and operations with the university’s strategic goals.
She said personnel matters are confidential and that the institution does not comment on individual employment actions.
 More details of the Faculty Senate subcommittee’s findings

In addition to determining that the deans and HR staff who notified the professors of their terminations weren’t qualified to do so, the school’s Faculty Senate developed several recommendations for recourse and future action. 
The group’s subcommittee recommended that the institution issue a formal apology, provide financial compensation if the institution cannot return overdue pay, and engage in a conversation with the faculty members to discuss the situation.
Joshua Erlich, the attorney representing the fired faculty members, said his clients are proud to have been vindicated by the faculty committee. 
“VSU used this false reorganization as a pretext to terminate respected members of the VSU academic community, marching them out without time to pack up their offices, say farewell to their colleagues, or transition their research,” Elrich said. 
“VSU’s conduct was illegal, destructive, and disrespectful. The Fired Six greatly appreciate this first step towards vindication and look forward to being made whole by VSU, whether through settlement or in court.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Beyer criticizes ‘Republican price tag’ ahead of November midterm elections
description: U.S. Rep. Don Beyer, D-Alexandria, joined a recent call with small business owners from around the country to discuss economic challenges Americans are facing due to rising healthcare, food and fuel costs, which he said are the result of President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans not meeting their promise to lower costs.  Beyer — one […]
text:
Incumbent U.S. Rep. Don Beyer, D-Alexandria, faces three challengers in this fall's congressional midterm elections. Beyer is sharpening his campaign's focus to highlight voters' financial strains under Republican leadership. (Photo by Andrew Kerley/Virginia Mercury)U.S. Rep. Don Beyer, D-Alexandria, joined a recent call with small business owners from around the country to discuss economic challenges Americans are facing due to rising healthcare, food and fuel costs, which he said are the result of President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans not meeting their promise to lower costs. 
Beyer — one of the richest members of Congress — said everything he does is informed by his “small business background” that keeps him attuned to the public’s fiscal frustrations. He is seeking a seventh congressional term.
“I spent 46 years running the family car dealership,” Beyer said. “So fixing cars, selling cars, selling parts. You know, having an anxiety attack on the 10th of every month, wondering whether we made money, whether we lost money.”
How 8th Congressional District Democratic primary reflects party’s shifting identity and priorities

Unrig Our Economy, a left-leaning organization that advocates for economic reforms and policies such as “tax the rich,” organized the call. The group released a figure detailing the “Republican price tag,” the average extra amount Americans have paid for healthcare, groceries, utilities, clothing, gas and basic household expenses since Trump’s second term started. 
Their original estimate was $3,500, but that number has since grown to $3,800. The report cites data from a report by Democrats in the Congressional Joint Economic Committee, of which Beyer is the senior House Democrat.
On the state level, Virginians have paid about $3,200 more for goods and services under the Trump Administration; about $686 on housing costs, $310 for groceries, $702 in gas and $107 for electricity, according to Democrats’ report. 
New polling shared by the Democratically-aligned research group Navigator showed three out of four Americans view the economy negatively. Three out of five said they are feeling “uneasy about their personal financial situation over the next few months.”
 Beyer, opponents weigh in on affordability struggles

Beyer has spoken this year about how people in and around his Northern Virginia district have suffered due to federal workforce cuts — an issue that defined the five-way primary election he overwhelmingly won in August.
Now, the longtime congressman is refining his message to focus on the extra costs for consumers on Republican’s watch. 
The GOP’s passage of the “largest healthcare cut in American history” in their “big ugly bill,” Trump’s renewed reliance on global tariffs and his “illegal” war with Iran that has costed billions in defense spending and driven up gas prices are the root cause of the nation’s economic woes, Beyer said.
“Republicans have done almost nothing to lower prices,” Beyer said. “They have total control of government. They have the House, the Senate and the White House, and they’re using it to give Donald Trump his rubber stamp for everything he does to make the problem worse.”
Beyer is asking voters to elect Democrats to Congress, who are focused on lowering prices for the American people, his deputy chief of staff Aaron Fritschner stated in an email. 
“Our leadership, including Congressman Beyer, have identified specific, substantive steps that they intend to take early in their majority, including repealing health care cuts from Republicans’ one big ugly bill, restoring trade authority to Congress and stopping President Trump’s destructive trade wars, and ending Trump’s illegal war with Iran,” Fritschner stated.
In the race to represent Virginia’s 8th Congressional District, which includes Arlington, Alexandria, Falls Church and parts of Fairfax, Beyer is facing three challengers.
Republican Tony Sabio is a “Reagan-style conservative” who served in the military, Secret Service and the CIA. Libertarian and “Fairfax warrior mom” Shelly Arnoldi and independent candidate Tim Sharman are also on the ballot.
Sabio has raised $21,917 according to the Virginia Public Access Project. Sharman has raised $25,000 and Arnoldi does not have any finances reported. Beyer’s fundraising dwarfs the competition’s, with over $2.1 million raised and $860,000 cash on hand as of July 1.
In a statement provided to the Mercury after Beyer’s press call, Sabio acknowledged the financial strains many are facing, but said “Northern Virginia families don’t need another Washington blame game.”
“These issues did not appear overnight. Families in Northern Virginia have been struggling with affordability for years, and I do not believe Congressman Beyer’s record has delivered enough improvement in the everyday lives of the people he serves,” Sabio stated.
Sabio said a more “strategic” use of tariffs could provide solutions, as well as expanding American nuclear energy efforts, creating home ownership incentives for essential workers and building out a private-sector jobs ecosystem in the region centered around technology and cybersecurity that is less dependent on Washington.
Sharman said the answer to beating rising costs is not “simply to tax and spend more.”
“We need greater efficiency, smarter regulation, an end to abusive corporate practices, higher wages, and economic growth that reaches more Americans,” Sharman stated.
Congress “cannot fix every price overnight,” Arnoldi stated, but  can stop driving costs up through reckless spending, bad energy policy, unnecessary wars, tariffs, taxes and red tape.”
“My approach is simple: peace, affordable energy, lower taxes, less regulation, less spending and no hidden taxes on the things Virginians need every day,” she stated.
 Election Day on the horizon

Having cleared his primary hurdles, Beyer appears to be in a strong position heading into the midterms in his Northern Virginia district, a Democratic stronghold. He has not won a general election by less than 70% since 2014. 
Beyer — a major fundraiser for his party — has acted to shore up other Democratic races down ballot and in other congressional districts. He said he’s also looped in with candidates in swing districts across the country. 
He also maxed out his donations to Virginia’s 1st Congressional District Democratic nominee Shannon Taylor, 2nd District nominee Elaine Luria, 5th District nominee Tom Perriello and 6th District nominee Beth Macy.
Early voting in Virginia starts on Sept. 18. The deadline to register to vote or apply for a mail-in ballot is Oct. 23. Election Day is Nov. 3.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: ‘Priceless to me’: Valley Link transmission line threatens generational farm in Orange County
description: “It started November 5th, 1910. My great-great-grandparents purchased this property for $722.50,” Michael Carter Jr. said at a picnic table outside the Orange County home where generations of his family have been born and died.   As insects chirp in the grass and cows mull around the pasture, Carter points to the tree line at the […]
text:
Michael Carter Jr. stands on his family's 116-year-old farmland in Orange County, Va. One of the proposed routes of the Valley Link transmission line will encroach on the property, Carter says. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)“It started November 5th, 1910. My great-great-grandparents purchased this property for $722.50,” Michael Carter Jr. said at a picnic table outside the Orange County home where generations of his family have been born and died.  
Michael Carter Jr. walks through a pasture on his family’s farmland in Orange County, Va. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
As insects chirp in the grass and cows mull around the pasture, Carter points to the tree line at the back of the property, on the other side of the creek that separates the property from his neighbor’s. That is where a portion of the proposed 115-mile, 765 kilovolt Valley Link transmission line will slice through, if state regulators approve the project. 
While the final route preferred by the company is yet to be determined, all three of the current iterations of the route all converge on this spot bordering Carter’s family’s land. The line will send surges of power to Northern Virginia, where most of the state’s data centers are clustered.
“This was considered to be kind of the black and poor side of town.”
Carter has used the land for farming for years, specializing in growing organic African crops. 
“This was considered to be kind of the Black and poor side of town,” he said of the historic acreage.
He has taught courses on these farming techniques at multiple Virginia universities and recently became a consultant to help others make their farms financially viable. 
The Valley Link line line, which is a joint venture between Dominion and two other companies, will stretch from Lynchburg to Culpeper County to bring more power to Northern Virginia where the demand is greatest – largely due to the world’s largest concentration of data centers being housed there. 
Cows graze in the pasture of Carter Farms in Orange County, Va. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
The line would be the biggest transmission project in Dominion’s territory. But Carter said it would infringe on land that is immeasurably valuable to his family and community.
“You know, births, deaths, joys, and pains have all been experienced here, and you’re trying to rob me of that because you want to provide more electricity to the data centers,” Carter said.
The project was identified by the regional grid operator PJM, which manages the power grid for 13 states and D.C., as  crucial to maintain grid reliability. Valley Link will be able to carry 6.6 gigawatts of power from Joshua Falls in Campbell County to a new substation in Culpeper. 
Depending on which route makes the final cut, the transmission line could cut through nine counties: Campbell, Appomattox, Buckingham, Fluvanna, Louisa, Orange, Goochland, Spotsylvania and Culpeper.
Carter had been planning a major farm expansion to create a nature-based health resort and rural retreat for city dwellers and had purchased nearby property to facilitate that vision when he first got word of the planned transmission line. Now, the future of his dream is uncertain.
“It’s beyond frustrating. It’s disheartening,” Carter said. “We’ve been fighting for this land for the last 116 years. I’m the fifth generation (and) now I have to continue to fight to just maintain peace of mind.”
Transmission lines are built within a wide berth of the trees, which would mean that the trees lining Carter’s homesite would likely have to be cut down. He also worries the creek would be damaged during construction.
Carter is extremely concerned about how exposure to the Electromagnetic Field (EMF) from the lines could impact human health. Research on potential links between EMF exposure and certain cancers is inconclusive, according to the National Cancer Institute. Carter said it’s still too risky.
“I’m old enough to remember the class action lawsuits related to asbestos. It was 100% safe and then, 20 years later, ‘have you or your family ever been exposed to asbestos?’”  I love my health too much … to put my grandchildren in jeopardy of harm because (they) wanted to make sure that (they) can build another 700 to a 1,000 data centers in Virginia,” he said.
A view of proposed transmission lines in relation to Carter Farms. (Map courtesy Valley Link Transmission Line project)
Valley Link’s developers said they are studying the EMF impacts and are aiming to design lines that reduce EMF exposure. 
The concern is so great that Carter has discouraged his children from continuing the farm if the transmission lines are built near the property. 
He said he is willing to walk away from the land his ancestor acquired over a century ago, where a marker nestled in trees still marks the place where an uncle died in a farming accident — and where Carter envisioned generations of his family would continue to live and work.
Michael Carter Jr. stands next to the marker where his great-uncle, Lewis Carter, died in a farming accident. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
“How do we get back to the indigenous understanding of making a decision for seven generations? We’re constantly making decisions for seven figures, and it’s costing us our lives,” Carter said. “It’s costing us our future because we’re not looking at seven generations. Our future is not in our children anymore. It’s money.”
Photos hanging inside the ancestral home of Michael Carter Jr., which he said will be severly impacted by the Valley Link Transmission project. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
Before she was governor, Abigail Spanberger visited the farm during her time in Congress, a nod to the role the property plays in Virginia history. U.S. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., has also visited the historic house that Carter had slowly been turning into a museum.
Inside, a commemorative letter by Spanberger hangs on the walls next to pictures of his grandmother, an aunt’s diploma and news clippings that show the evolution of a Black Virginia family who dared to chase the American dream in the nadir of the Jim Crow South.
A letter from then-Congresswoman Abigail Spanberger sent to Michael Carter Jr. in commemoration of his family’ Black farming legacy in 2021. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
“I’m fighting for the legacy of my great-grandmother, for my great-great-grandparents, for all those who have sacrificed to make sure that we had this,” Carter said. ”I can’t, as much as I know I may have to walk away, I can’t walk away without a fight.”
Others are also opposing the power line, with grassroots efforts to reject the project mobilizing across the nine impacted counties. 
The line’s developers are still determining their preferred route and back up options for the State Corporation Commission to consider. Virginians interested in learning more about the project may visit its website. 
Michael Carter Jr. stands near greenhouses and water tanks on his historic farm in Orange County, Va. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Nixing Black hero’s name from Va.-built aircraft carrier is offensive, affront to military members
description: It’s not just that the administration of President Donald Trump, who’s proved repeatedly that he’s racist, wants to remove the name of Pearl Harbor hero Doris “Dorie” Miller from an aircraft carrier under construction at Newport News Shipbuilding – and name it for Trump, according to a published report.  The USS Doris Miller would be […]
text:
U.S. Navy Sailor Doris “Dorie” Miller ws killed in action during the Pearl Harbon attack by Japanese bombers in 1941. His name deserves to remain on an aircraft carrier currently under construction in Newport News, columnist Roger Chesley writes. (Photo courtesy US National Archives and Records Administration)It’s not just that the administration of President Donald Trump, who’s proved repeatedly that he’s racist, wants to remove the name of Pearl Harbor hero Doris “Dorie” Miller from an aircraft carrier under construction at Newport News Shipbuilding – and name it for Trump, according to a published report. 
The USS Doris Miller would be the first carrier named for a Black person. No carrier has been named for a sitting president, CNN reported recently. 
Nor is it that Trump dodged military service himself during Vietnam with repeated deferments. (He was like many other men from rich, influential families who avoided conscription.)
Let me make it plain: How could any congressperson or military official countenance such a special honor for Trump, who has called American troops who died in war “losers” and “suckers”? 
During Trump’s first term, the service announced the Ford-class vessel would honor Miller. Sources told CNN that internal conversations have discussed renaming it for Trump. The carrier is scheduled to be delivered to the Navy in 2034.
It would be a stunning betrayal to celebrate a man who’s requested that wounded veterans be prevented from participating in military parades where he attended. Trump’s disdain for the sacrifice of military men and women is reprehensible – especially in a commander in chief.
A Pentagon spokesperson told me by email last week there was “nothing to announce” right now about the issue – but notably didn’t deny the CNN report.
This is a huge insult to Miller’s legacy, African-Americans and service members in general. Miller, from Waco, Texas, enlisted in the segregated Navy in 1939, when Black people were limited to support roles. He completed boot camp in Norfolk, and he then was assigned to the battleship USS West Virginia.
Miller was a mess attendant at the time of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941, but he proved his skill and love of country – at a time when the country didn’t love Black people back.
During the onslaught that killed or wounded more than 3,500 Americans, Miller rescued wounded sailors. He also wielded an anti-aircraft gun – for which he had no training – and fired on enemy planes. It’s unclear whether he downed any, though Miller said he thought he hit one, according to Navy records. He earned the Navy Cross, the service’s second-highest honor.
Miller was killed in action in November 1943 when a Japanese submarine sank the Liscome Bay in the Pacific. 
CNN reported the Navy is now referring to the new aircraft carrier internally only by its hull number, CVN-81.
From the Kennedy Center to the Great Lakes, Trump has become downright pathological about nomenclatures and edifices. His sycophants may care about the name changes, but many Americans see his campaign as childish.
The Navy could rename another warship after Miller, CNN reported, and recommend him for the Medal of Honor. It’s the highest decoration for military valor and, likely but for racism, was denied decades ago.
Miller deserves both honors – including his name on the carrier. A ceremony in January 2020 at Pearl Harbor announced the recognition.
“In selecting this name, we honor the contributions of all our enlisted ranks, past and present, men and women, of every race, religion and background,” said Thomas Modly, then-acting secretary of the Navy.
More than 70 Democrats in Congress, including several from Virginia, have urged the U.S. secretary of defense and acting secretary of the Navy to keep Miller’s name on the carrier.
“When he served, segregation restricted the roles available to Black sailors and servicemembers,” the Aug. 26 letter says. “Yet, when his country came under attack, Miller did not hesitate for one second to put himself in harms’ way to defend his fellow sailors and his nation.
“This story embodies the finest traditions of the United States Armed Forces.”
I asked Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Virginia Beach, and a former Navy helicopter pilot, why she didn’t sign the letter. Her spokesperson didn’t respond to my emails. She’s in a tough campaign rematch against Elaine Luria.
Her decision to stay mute is craven. 
That Trump is relegating someone who is African-American is no surprise. His racism toward people of color – and Black people in particular – is well-documented and decades old. Here are several examples:

In 1973, the U.S. Justice Department sued Trump and his father for racial bias at Trump housing developments in New York. The case was eventually settled in which the Trumps promised not to discriminate. Testers for the New York City Human Rights Division said Black people who went to Trump buildings were told there were no apartments available, while white people were offered units.
 He ran newspaper ads calling for the return of the death penalty in New York state following the arrests of five Black and Latino boys dubbed the Central Park Five, at a time of heightened emotions in the city. They were charged in the 1989 rape and pummeling of a white woman. They were convicted and served prison time, but those convictions were later overturned after another man admitted the rape. Trump has never apologized to them.
  Trump led the lying, toxic birtherism claims that Barack Obama wasn’t born in the United States. Obama became the nation’s first Black president in 2009.
 Trump has fought diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives that have provided Black and Latino people with a foothold into education and employment. He has said little about the centuries of discrimination and enduring governmental structures that prohibited Black people from a level playing field.
He put the brakes on efforts to place abolitionist and Underground Railroad conductor Harriet Tubman on the $20 bill.
He repeated false, racist stereotypes that Haitian immigrants were eating dogs and cats in Ohio during the 2024 presidential campaign. 
 In the wake of the Army helicopter-airline crash near Reagan Washington National Airport in January 2025 that killed 67 people, and with investigations just starting, Trump baselessly rushed to blame the collision on DEI policies to boost hiring of air traffic controllers. Nor did he acknowledge the crowded airspace around Reagan National and its shorter-than-average runways that have long been challenges for pilots.

Against this backdrop, the administration’s attempt to remove Doris Miller’s name should be seen for what it is: Racist. Usurping a real hero’s rightful honor. Sucking up to someone who denigrates military men and women.
Trump isn’t worthy of this recognition. Miller is.

title: Grieving children need more than our sympathy. They need a place to belong.
description: Children who lose a close family member grieve differently than adults, and their grief changes as they grow. A loss experienced at 8 can take on an entirely different meaning at 12, 16 or 25. A child can be deeply sad and still want to swim, make art, play games and laugh with friends. HopeHealth […]
text:
The needs of children and teens who have lost a loved one can easily go unseen. Camp BraveHeart brings them together for support and connection. (Photo by Emily Conde courtesy of HopeHealth)Children who lose a close family member grieve differently than adults, and their grief changes as they grow. A loss experienced at 8 can take on an entirely different meaning at 12, 16 or 25. A child can be deeply sad and still want to swim, make art, play games and laugh with friends. HopeHealth makes room for all of it at Camp Braveheart.
This summer, 100 grieving children and teens attended our day camp at Camp Hoffman in South Kingstown with another 75 experiencing the camp offered in North Attleboro, Massachusetts. Camp BraveHeart is a free, two-day grief support camp for youngsters ages 5 to 17 who have experienced the death of someone they love. 
Those 175 campers are part of a much larger population whose needs can easily go unseen. According to the 2026 Childhood Bereavement Estimation Model, 1 in 11 children in the United States —- about 6.6 million —- will experience the death of a parent or sibling by age 18. That number does not include children grieving the deaths of grandparents, other relatives, friends or other significant people in their lives. 
There is something powerful about a child discovering that they are not the only one. Being surrounded by peers who understand can replace some of that isolation with connection and belonging. Research suggests that this kind of setting can make a difference. A 2025 systematic review of 31 studies of grief camps found positive effects on participants’ grief and psychosocial functioning. This research reflects what I have witnessed firsthand watching our campers whisper to a horse, nuzzle a fluffy cat and gather together in a circle to lift up a colorful parachute.



Quotation







There is something powerful about a child discovering that they are not the only one. Being surrounded by peers who understand can replace some of that isolation with connection and belonging.


This summer, as we marked our 20th anniversary, Randi Gilmore returned with three of her five children — Jackson, Katie and Megan — who were among the youngsters who attended our inaugural camp after their family experienced tremendous loss. 
Megan was 9 when she first attended. She came back each summer until she aged out at 17, and two of the Gilmore siblings later came back as counselors, helping other children experience the same sense of belonging they found. Their story is shared in HopeHealth’s 20th-anniversary Camp BraveHeart story. 
Seeing the family again two decades later was deeply moving. Their return was a powerful reminder that grief does not follow a timetable.
Children grow around their grief, and new milestones can bring new emotions and questions. That is why support cannot end in the weeks or months after a death. For those of us who work in hospice and palliative care, bereavement support is part of caring for the whole family. But many grieving children never had a loved one in hospice, and families may not know where to turn. Strong connections among grief organizations, schools, health care providers and community partners can help families find support when they need it.
We see that broader approach in HopeHealth’s Weekend of Hope & Healing for grieving adults and caregivers and in community outreach, including our recent participation in a Cranston Public Schools Wellness Fair. 
U.S. Sen. Jack Reed and U.S. Rep. Gabe Amo joined Camp BraveHeart’s closing ceremony on Aug. 21, where they met campers and presented a proclamation recognizing HopeHealth and the camp’s 20th anniversary. Their presence was a welcome opportunity to share this work with leaders who help shape the resources available to children and families. 
None of this work happens without the people who carry it forward. Camp BraveHeart continues under the compassionate leadership of Marsha Ireland, HopeHealth’s manager of grief support services and camp director, alongside a dedicated team of staff and volunteers. 
Twenty years after our first camp, the lesson remains simple: We cannot take away a child’s loss, but we can surround them — and the people who care for them — with the support they need to find their way through it.

title: You still can’t smoke medical cannabis in Georgia, but you can vape it. What’s the difference?
description: Medical cannabis dispensaries are now selling the flower form of the drug in Georgia, but a new state law that took effect this summer has created some confusion over how it can be legally consumed.  Lawmakers passed a measure earlier this year that overhauled the state’s medical cannabis program by dropping the confusing “low THC […]
text:
Buds of marijuana on display inside Mother Earth Wellness in Pawtucket, one of eight retailers licensed to sell recreational cannabis. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Medical cannabis dispensaries are now selling the flower form of the drug in Georgia, but a new state law that took effect this summer has created some confusion over how it can be legally consumed. 
Lawmakers passed a measure earlier this year that overhauled the state’s medical cannabis program by dropping the confusing “low THC oil” branding, allowing dry-herb and oil vaporization, adding qualifying medical conditions and removing previous potency barriers. The changes quickly triggered significant growth in the number of patients enrolled in the program, with nearly 50,000 patients as of Sept. 2, according to the Department of Public Health.
But limits remain on how the raw cannabis flower can be used. Smoking it remains illegal under the new state law known as the Putting Patients First Act, which allows registered patients 21 and older to consume flower and oil at home strictly through vaporization.
“The law is very clear. You can vaporize flower and then of course vaporize the vape oil. So, the only thing that’s allowed in inhalables is vaporizing. That’s it,” said Newnan Republican state Sen. Matt Brass, the bill’s sponsor, in a phone interview.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Because flower is now being sold in Georgia’s dispensaries and independent pharmacies, retailers are finding themselves at the forefront of educating patients who incorrectly assume the availability of flower means the state legalized traditional smoking.
Enrollment jumps after lawmakers ease access to Georgia’s medical cannabis program

Priya Raje, the owner of Lotus Farmacy in Suwanee, an independent pharmacy specializing in medical cannabis, said she is frequently asked about the difference between smoking and vaping and said that a part of her role is to educate patients on what’s legal in Georgia. She said that most people are familiar with smoking flower because it’s the way cannabis has been historically consumed, so she spends that extra time educating patients about what is allowed under the law.
“I just tell them what the legality is and what the risks are if they choose to do anything else,” Raje said.
Yolanda Bennett, who is a patient and co-head of the Georgia Medical Cannabis Society, which is an organization that advocates for medical cannabis access and educates patients, said smoking and vaporizing flower form of cannabis are entirely different methods. She said that smoking flower burns all the particles and plant matter and creates smoke from the combustion, whereas vaporization using a device only heats up the plant matter to a certain temperature without burning it, only creating an inhalable vapor.
“When you take a flame and ignite the flower, that’s illegal,” Bennett said.
The bill did not originally allow Georgians to vaporize the flower, but Brass said he didn’t push back after the House amended the bill to include it because he figured that vaping flower could be a healthier alternative to oil vapes. 
“You’ve got different additives that are put in that oil to have it hit a certain percent, and the flower is grown and there’s nothing added to it, and so that was why I agreed to it. I don’t know if that’s why [the House] added it, but to me, that makes sense,” Brass said.
