name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri AG trashes state Supreme Court ruling in federal filing
description: Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s chief litigator on Sunday accused the state Supreme Court of adopting “a legal fiction” when it ruled that putting the state’s new congressional map to a referendum means Missouri must use its previous district lines in November. In a federal court filing, Solicitor General Lou Capozzi asked U.S. Chief Judge Stephen […]
text:
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway's office is attacking the legal reasoning of the Missouri Supreme Court in federal district court filings (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s chief litigator on Sunday accused the state Supreme Court of adopting “a legal fiction” when it ruled that putting the state’s new congressional map to a referendum means Missouri must use its previous district lines in November.
In a federal court filing, Solicitor General Lou Capozzi asked U.S. Chief Judge Stephen Clark of the Eastern District of Missouri, an appointee of President Donald Trump, to block the state Supreme Court order. Capozzi wrote that his client, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, agreed with the two GOP congressional candidates who filed the lawsuit that the map favoring Republicans drawn in 2025 should be the one used in November.
In the unanimous opinion last week, Missouri Supreme Court Judge Ginger Gooch wrote that People Not Politicians had submitted a legally sufficient petition referendum and the Missouri Constitution required that the legislation creating the new map can have no effect in law until a vote of the people. 
Hanaway appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court on Friday afternoon. Justice Brett Kavanaugh set a noon Monday deadline for other parties to weigh in on the application for an emergency stay. 
U.S. Rep. Bob Onder, state Sen. Rick Brattin, and two voters filed their lawsuit in the Eastern District court on Friday, with People Not Politicians seeking to intervene to have the case dismissed.
Like Kavanaugh, Clark set a noon Monday deadline for any other intervenors to file and for arguments on whether he had any jurisdiction. Both could issue decisions as early as Monday afternoon. 
Tuesday is the deadline for changing the Nov. 3 ballot.One state law prohibits local election authorities from adding or removing candidates or issues after that date and another extends that prohibition to the courts.
Solicitor General Louis Capozzi argues last week before the Missouri Supreme Court (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
In his Sunday filing on behalf of Hoskins in the Eastern District, Capozzi acknowledges that he cannot dispute last week’s decision on state law grounds.
“The Missouri Supreme Court’s decision rested solely on state law,” Capozzi wrote. “Indeed, the court suggested Secretary Hoskins was barred from even considering federal law in his certification decision.”
The referendum petition was filed Dec. 9. The bill that included the gerrymandered map intended to flip the 5th District — where Brattin is the GOP nominee — was constitutionally set to take effect on Dec. 11.
The provision on a referendum in Missouri’s Constitution, whether lawmakers put legislation on the ballot or it is done by petition, is that it does not take effect until approved by voters. Because the primary was conducted before the ruling that the petition was sufficient, Capozzi wrote, “the Missouri Supreme Court adopted a legal fiction that the (2025) map used in the primary election must be deemed retroactively invalid.”
In the motion to dismiss, attorney Chuck Hatfield argued on behalf of People Not Politicians that the federal district court should not second-guess the Missouri Supreme Court’s decision.
The court does not have jurisdiction, Hatfield wrote. He also questioned whether there was a true dispute between Onder, Brattin and the voters and Hoskins. 
Marc Ellinger, the attorney representing Onder and Brattin, argued side-by-side with Capozzi in the case decided by the Missouri Supreme Court. Now his clients have filed suit against Hoskins, who has told the court he agrees with their demands. 
“The hallmarks of collusion are unmistakable,” Hatfield wrote in the motion to dismiss the case.
The lawsuit is a true dispute, Capozzi wrote, because Hoskins wants to do as Onder and the other plaintiffs demand, but cannot because he would have to break the law to do so.
Ellinger, in his filing, echoed that argument.
“A defendant who lacks the power to grant the requested relief without a court order cannot collude to manufacture one; the very fact that plaintiffs need an injunction from this court, rather than a stipulation from the secretary, is proof the dispute is real,” Ellinger wrote.
In the motion to dismiss, Hatfield used an argument drawn on repeatedly by Ellinger and Capozzi to urge courts to allow the 2025 map to be used in the general election — it is too late to change and doing so would harm the election.
The Supreme Court appeal will decide all the important questions raised by Onder and the other plaintiffs, Hatfield wrote.
“A district-court injunction directing use of the (2025) map while the Supreme Court considers whether to stay the Missouri Supreme Court’s injunction against that map would create chaos for election officials, candidates, and voters,” Hatfield wrote.
He urged Clark to dismiss the case.
“The pending Supreme Court proceeding demonstrates an adequate alternative forum — the constitutionally designated forum — for plaintiffs’ federal claims,” Hatfield wrote.
One unusual aspect of the Eastern District case is that Hanaway is not defending the decision of the Missouri Supreme Court. Usually, when a Missouri state law or precedent is challenged in federal court, the attorney general’s office works to defend it as a correct application of the law.
Instead, through the state’s filings, Capozzi belittles the work of the state’s highest court. 
The decision ignored many of the arguments he made and accepted by the Cole County Circuit Judge Daniel Green, Capozzi wrote. On several occasions, he wrote, the court did “not mention” his effort to use a tie-in to the federal Constitution to block the referendum,
And the court, to his surprise, applied Missouri law to the case.
“Shockingly, the Missouri Supreme Court reversed and directly issued an injunction prohibiting the secretary — ‘and all those acting in concert with him’ — ‘from implementing, using, or mandating the use of the congressional redistricting in (the 2025 map),’” Capozzi wrote.
Capozzi also criticized the court for refusing to accept his version of facts, adopted by Green but disputed in filings directly to the court.
“Even more bizarrely, the Missouri Supreme Court entirely ignored the circuit court’s finding that changing congressional maps would be ‘impossible’ and force Missouri to violate the federal election calendar,” Capozzi wrote. “Instead, the court explicitly eschewed any consideration of the ‘confusion, expense, and practical difficulties’ that ‘may result’ from its injunction.”
Those issues Hoskins and Hanaway have with the court ruling means the attorney general’s office cannot defend the Missouri Supreme Court decision, Capozzi wrote.
“Defendants take their obligation to defend state laws seriously,” Capozzi wrote. “But under the extraordinary and unprecedented circumstances in this case, defendants believe their oath to comply with the U.S. Constitution prevents them from defending the use of a different congressional map for the general election.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Election 2026: New Mexico State Auditor
description: Incumbent Democrat Joseph Maestas faces write-in Republican Joshua James Ryan Lawrence in the New Mexico State Auditor race.
text:
The Nov. 3, 2026, general election features a race between incumbent State Auditor Joseph Maestas, left, and Republican write-in candidate Joshua Ryan James Lawrence. (Courtesy photos)The New Mexico Office of the State Auditor employs 35 people to root out financial fraud, waste or abuse in more than 1,000 public entities in New Mexico, from large state agencies to tiny political entities like acequias or municipal water systems.
The Nov. 3 general election for the office will feature incumbent Democratic State Auditor Joseph Maestas against Republican Joshua James Ryan Lawrence, a business owner and conservative activist who will appear on the ballot as a write-in candidate. 
Whoever wins will inherit an office Maestas says public employees are increasingly turning to with credible fraud complaints, and one he says is stretched to complete its mandate due to limited state resources and fewer certified public accountants in the workforce. 
The auditor earns a salary of $144,000 a year and oversees an office with a roughly $6.3 million budget. In the last year, the office has released high-profile audits of Mora County’s distribution of federal disaster funding and local governments’ failure to spend opioid settlement dollars. 
Source NM spoke to both candidates about their visions for the office and why they’re running. Their answers below have been edited for clarity and concision. 
Joshua James Ryan Lawrence
Joshua James Ryan Lawrence was born in Mesquite, Texas, but has lived in New Mexico since age 19, most recently in Tucumcari. He’s worked in or owned various businesses related to film or events over the last 20 years here and said the state’s COVID-19 lockdown policies cemented his turn from a “liberal Democrat” to a “constitutional conservative.” 
In 2022, Lawrence ran unsuccessfully in the Republican primary to become Bernalillo County sheriff, earning about 14% of the vote among four candidates. He also said he intended to run in this year’s Republican gubernatorial primary but dropped out when he saw the slate of candidates. 
“I decided to switch over to auditor because I believe that I can definitely jump in and bring transparency to the auditor’s office and audit everything and everybody,” he said. 
What makes you the most qualified to be state auditor? 
I truly care about the well-being and the prosperity of the people of this state, and I’m willing to find the best of the best of the people to work with, work with our federal government, work with the [defunct U.S. Department of Government Efficiency] to literally uncover and expose anything and everything, and I care about our Constitution and our founding documents.
What is the aspect of being state auditor that is most overlooked, in your opinion?
Corruption. I mean, nothing is looked at. Why are we the poorest state? Why are we the hungriest state? Why are we everything? Why has Epstein Ranch not been opened up? Why are elected officials multimillionaires while in service?
Is anybody looking into those things? Is our auditor, is our treasurer, our attorney general, is anybody looking into those things? No, they’re all fighting Trump. Trump’s not in New Mexico. We need to look into the people here in New Mexico and uncover everything because it could be instantly done. Instantly.
How effective has the fraud, waste and abuse hotline been for the office and how could it be improved?
Does anybody in the state know about that hotline? Does the auditor utilize his platform to inform the people of the state about what comes in through that platform? And do we see the results of it? No.
I will make sure that everything is loud. I will use our platform to expose and to show and to teach and educate everybody in the state what’s happening. You know how it’s been happening, why it’s happening, and how we can change it. I don’t hear any solutions from anybody in elected office right now, especially in the controlling party. And I think everybody has the same sentiments.
If elected, do you have any new initiatives you intend to implement in the office?
Oh, absolutely. We will spend as much time as we need, hopefully not longer than a month or two, overlooking how everything is run, what everybody is doing. We will vet everybody in the office. Ultimately, the plan is for small government. 
So I definitely plan on overhauling the entire office, minimizing it, putting the most qualified people in there, ensure that all auditors and everybody that we’re doing business with are as New Mexican as possible, because a lot of our money is our auditors and these companies are out of state, and I want to implement a New Mexico DOGE office.
DOGE utilizes AI, and they utilize qualified people to dig into everything and see where every penny is spent, and making it completely transparent so that people can see everything that’s going on.
What was the most significant audit that’s come out of the office in the last four years?
I would say absolutely nothing. We’re still in the same boat.
How prevalent would you say fraud, waste and/or abuse is across New Mexico state agencies?
I’d say that I believe that New Mexico is one of the worst in this country when it comes to fraud, waste and abuse.
Once again, we’re still 50th in education. [The state Children, Youth and Families Department] — only now are you seeing the issues. We should have seen auditors opening up those books a long time ago. The trafficking that comes out of the state and the missing children is insane, especially on our reservations. There’s actually no investigations. The auditor has the ability to audit and look into everything. Why haven’t we seen anything? Why now? And even what we see now is minute compared to the issues that we’re faced with.
What is the most common problem audits of state agencies identify?
I’ve not seen the fruit of anything that this auditor has put out. Yeah, you know the misappropriations of funds, the RICO and racketeering, the theft, fraud and extortion that is happening through every agency, through every county and municipality is through the roof.
Joseph Maestas
Joseph Maestas, the Democratic incumbent, was raised in Santa Cruz, New Mexico, and holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in civil engineering and is a certified fraud examiner.
He came to the State Auditor’s Office in 2022 after serving on the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission. Before that, he served as  Española’s mayor, and on both Española and the City of Santa Fe’s city councils. If re-elected, Maestas said he hopes to ensure the office has all the resources it needs from the state Legislature to continue its statutorily required duties and also to rebuild a pipeline of qualified accountants that the state sorely needs. 
What makes you the most qualified to be state auditor? 
I have almost four years of experience as state auditor, and I have led this agency through a lot of change and accomplishments, and we’re poised to do even more in the next four years if the voters of New Mexico will have me for a second term. 
I’ve dedicated my whole life to public service. I was able to get legislation passed, whether it was the City of Santa Fe or the PRC, so I think I have a solid record of elected public service.
What is the aspect of being state auditor that is most overlooked, in your opinion?
The function of it. I take every single opportunity to explain without geeking out what the state auditor does, but I think there’s a great lack of understanding of what the office does. I think that that is the most misunderstood. Audits, to most people, are boring. 
How effective has the fraud, waste and abuse hotline been for the office and how could it be improved?
We implemented a new case management system that has really helped to streamline the way we manage these cases, and so we can always be more efficient. However, we have experienced an incredible increase in our fraud, waste, and abuse complaints. 
In fiscal year 2025, we had 254 complaints that were credible, that we created cases for, and we had 452 in fiscal year ’26. That’s a 78% increase in fraud, waste and abuse complaints between those two fiscal years. Right now, we probably have a caseload of about 350 active cases.
So how can we improve it? We’re resource limited. We need to continue streamlining our case management system. We think that AI can play a role to help manage these cases.
If re-elected, do you have any new initiatives you intend to implement in the office?
We hired a contractor to develop a customized AI program to streamline our audit report review process reviewing audit reports that independent public accounting firms send in. We’re just that inundated, and we need help. We need more human resources, and we are going to ask for more human resources for our financial audit division in our fiscal year 2028 budget. I want the appropriators to know that I’m doing everything I can to make this office as efficient as possible, and I feel that this AI initiative is going to be very, very effective.
The other initiative that I have is that right now the accounting industry is experiencing a workforce crisis. Let me put it that way. There are fewer and fewer CPAs. A lot of the CPAs are baby boomers. I think 75% are already eligible to retire.
I am pushing legislation to create our own program to integrate accounting into [Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics curriculum], and this could vastly improve the awareness of accounting. I think it’s going to accelerate the integration of exciting technologies into accounting, like AI, like blockchain learning, data analytics.
What was the most significant audit that’s come out of the office in the last four years?
Doña Ana County [in May 2026]. I mean that’s the second largest county in the state. The audit revealed 42 findings and uncovered widespread dysfunctions throughout the county administration. This was a special audit, and it was an audit done at the request of the independent requests of the Doña Ana County Sheriff and the Doña Ana County administration.
We sent a referral to the Department of Finance and Administration, and the Department of Finance and Administration put Doña Ana County on restrictions. They cannot manage their own capital outlay. They have to hire a fiscal agent until they resolve each and every finding in that report. This is significant.
How prevalent would you say fraud, waste and/or abuse is across New Mexico state agencies?
It’s prevalent. There is a statute and it requires any entity that has any knowledge of apparent fraud, waste and abuse, they have to notify my office, and some of these entities forget. They forget to do that. We’ll read about this in the paper, you know, in some place in New Mexico, and we have to ding them in their audit for not notifying us. So there’s even a lack of understanding of the statute that requires folks with any knowledge of apparent fraud, waste and abuse that they need to notify our office.
What is the most common problem audits of state agencies identify?
I’d say a lack of internal controls and the lack of adherence of established policies and procedures.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Dordt University launches generative AI pilot program for tools access, community conversations
description: Dordt University students, faculty and staff this fall began participation in an artificial intelligence pilot program aimed at providing campuswide access to high-quality tools and together explore how AI can be used responsibly inside and outside of the classroom. Officials with the private, Christian university said that as AI and large language models (L[...]
text:
Dordt University students Cameron Grimes, left, and Daniel Garcia work on computers at Dordt University. The private institution has started a year-long pilot program to provide students with AI tools and discussions. (Photo courtesy of Dordt University)Dordt University students, faculty and staff this fall began participation in an artificial intelligence pilot program aimed at providing campuswide access to high-quality tools and together explore how AI can be used responsibly inside and outside of the classroom.
Officials with the private, Christian university said that as AI and large language models (LLMs) bleed into different areas of people’s lives, it’s important to help students understand how to interact with it rather than leave them without guidance.
“As we’ve seen throughout history, different technologies are created, invented, and people can use them to do beautiful things, and people can use them to do destructive things,” said Dordt Chief of Staff Rev. Aaron Baart. “And so, pretending like AI or LLMs (don’t) exist in our world today or in our future would not be equipping our students to be effective kingdom citizens in the world that they’ll be working and living in.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Sioux Center institution has partnered with AI platform BoodleBox for this yearlong pilot, Baart said. As many as 1,300 higher education institutions use BoodleBox products, he said, and Dordt has both received recommendations for it from other university leaders and a better negotiated price for the program through the Council for Christian Colleges and Universities.
BoodleBox provides Dordt with premium versions of AI tools including Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity, programs which some students and faculty were already using on their own time. Baart said the university’s AI policy boils down to “you can use AI to the extent in which your faculty tell you that you can,” and BoodleBox will also house assignments and course resources created with AI.
“We saw around campus students already using a lot of AI,” Baart said. “We saw faculty using it in some classes, and so you’ve got subscriptions all over the place to different different LLMs, and providing equal access for everybody on one single subscription seemed like a fair educational access move.”
Asking community questions of ethical AI use
Dordt is “really leaning into” faculty expertise as part of this pilot, Baart said, by including faculty like education professor Dave Mulder in the decision to run the program and to supplement it with discussions of AI through different lenses that can be more deeply explored in students’ classes.
Mulder, a self-described “techy teacher,” said AI has been “just over the horizon” in the education technology field for more than a decade. In an emerging technology graduate course he teaches every other summer, Mulder has watched as students started bringing up AI in 2021, ChatGPT becoming a focus of the class in 2023 then AI discussions being “almost a given” in 2025.
Mulder and Dean of Chapel Rev. Justin Bailey are working together to put on monthly campuswide discussions of AI, Mulder said, through lenses of both education technology and theology. Talks will focus on the ethical and responsible use of AI, with one hope of Mulder being that a common language around what “ethical” means in this context is created at Dordt.
“We’ve got a great set of tools here with the opportunities that (Boodlebox) affords for us,” Mulder said. “Let’s talk about what are ethical and responsible ways we can use tools like that.”
Baart said he’s heard from faculty that the more fluent they are in AI programs, the easier it is to catch AI-aided academic dishonesty from students. Mulder, who has published a book titled “Teach Like a Human: Playful Practice and Serious Faith in the Age of AI,” said he likes to remind people that cheating wasn’t invented with ChatGPT, but offloading work to a machine in this way is relatively new, and AI fluency can help faculty spot ideas output by a chatbot rather than a student.
Teaching when to use powerful tools
Baart has his own, personal concerns about how AI can infringe upon people’s creativity, saying his son told Baart that if he had used AI to do the assignments that prepared him for the LSAT, “there’s no way” he would have done as well as he did.
“There’s a lot of questions about ethics within it,” Baart said. “What does it mean to be human? How do humans appropriately interact with technology without it replacing them, understanding the difference and the biases that exist within different LLMs, these are all things that we can do when we’re working campuswide to explore it together.”
Many students are already personally exploring questions like those Baart posed, Mulder said, and he’s had the opportunity to work with students in different classes to try to pick through potential answers.
For the one-year pilot, Mulder said he hopes that the availability of these tools and the discussions surrounding them will “demystify” AI and make students and faculty “more critical consumers of technology.”
Humans have always used tools to their advantage, but sometimes with new technologies people can end up using the wrong tool for the job, which Mulder likened to using an excavator to plant radish seeds in his garden. He also wants the Dordt community to “reclaim a sense of the goodness of work,” saying he wants to push back against the idea that work is bad and should be avoided with tools like AI.
“I hope that, students, staff, faculty, that we’re encouraged to think about how we can use tools to the best way that we can to do the work that we’re expected to do really well, and to not try to avoid work, but to reclaim the sense of the the goodness of the work that we get to do,” Mulder said.

name: VTDigger
title: We chose this housing crisis
description:
Vermont didn't stumble into a market where work doesn't pay enough to live. We built it that way.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  We chose this housing crisis.
text:
Dear Editor,
I agree with Tray DuClos’ recent letter to VTDigger about Vermont’s housing shortage. It is definitely a huge obstacle to our growth, no matter how you measure it, right up there with our fantastically high costs and our fantastically low wages. Yet we need to look beneath the surface issues such as zoning and ask ourselves a far more uncomfortable question: How and why did we create a society where people cannot afford to live where they work?
This is not a natural phenomenon, like the 100-year floods that are hitting us every year or so now. We have deliberately done this to ourselves. We have deliberately made the math brutal. A typical working person makes somewhere around $15 to $20 an hour. It is not uncommon to see rents for a one-bedroom apartment around $1,200 to $1,500 a month. A $20-an-hour full-time worker earns about $3,467 a month before taxes. Rent of $1,500 consumes 43% of that gross income. At $15 an hour, rent consumes 58%. I am 71 years old and work two jobs. I still cannot afford these rental prices; were it not for public housing, I would be living on the streets.

READ MORE

We have created these problems through deliberate business, political and social choices that consistently favor capital over labor. We celebrate rising property values, investment returns and so-called economic growth while treating workers’ wages and housing as somebody else’s problem. Then we complain that businesses cannot find workers.
If we want to expand our economy to benefit all Vermonters, rather than the big donor class, we have to stop pretending that wages, rents, land prices and profits exist in separate worlds. This housing crisis is the predictable result of these deliberate choices.
The deep question underlying all this is: Do we really want this kind of society?
So far, the answer has been yes.
Walter Carpenter
Montpelier, Vt.

text:
Iowa Workforce Development manages unemployment claims filed on behalf of Iowans. (Photo by Getty Images, logo courtesy the State of Iowa)Several fired healthcare professionals were recently awarded unemployment benefits by Iowa judges who found the workers had not committed workplace misconduct.
One of the cases involves Garmai Rogers, who worked for the nursing home chain WesleyLife from September 2024 through March 2026, when she was fired.
WesleyLife alleged that over a two-week period in July 2025, there had been at least 14 instances of Rogers failing to answer residents’ call lights in a timely fashion.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State records show that in January 2026, Rogers was disciplined by WesleyLife for allegedly throwing a phone and call light onto a resident’s chest out of frustration. WesleyLife then concluded Rogers had failed to treat residents, visitors, and coworkers in a professional and courteous manner and fired her.
After a subsequent hearing on Rogers’ application for unemployment benefits, Administrative Law Judge Michael Lunn found Rogers credibly testified the state had found insufficient evidence to substantiate any allegations of abuse against her.
Noting that WesleyLife failed to submit into evidence a March 2026 incident report that it said led to Rogers’ dismissal, Lunn ruled the company failed to meet its burden of proving Rogers engaged in workplace misconduct. Rogers was awarded unemployment benefits.
Other healthcare workers whose unemployment cases were recently decided include:
Theresa Simpson, who worked for Terrace Hill Healthcare as a certified nursing assistant from June 2025 through June 2026, when she was fired for alleged gross misconduct.
Terrace Hill alleged that during a resident council meeting on June 15, 2026, multiple complaints were lodged about Simpson either not helping residents or making derogatory statements about them. The company fired Simpson shortly after the meeting, citing both the number of prior complaints against her and the nature of the more recent complaints.
Administrative Law Judge Elizabeth Johnson recently ruled Simpson was eligible for jobless benefits, finding that Terrace Hill had not established whether the complaints were found to have merit or were even investigated.
Heather Bartlett, who worked for Covenant Medical Center from 1991 until June 2026 when she was fired. During her last five years with the company, she was the nursing manager for acute in-patient rehabilitation at MercyOne hospital in Waterloo.
In the weeks leading up to her discharge, Bartlett had voiced concerns with a proposed change in the hospital’s dietary program that she believed had a disruptive impact on patient care. She also filed a complaint about her supervisor, alleging he created a hostile work environment through yelling, verbal abuse and the use of profanity. Prior to her dismissal, Bartlett had allegedly received positive performance reviews and high scores in patient-satisfaction surveys.
Administrative Law Judge James Timberland recently ruled Bartlett was fired for no reason that would disqualify her from collecting unemployment benefits. Covenant, he noted, had provided no evidence of workplace misconduct.
Chasity Kephart, who worked fulltime as a first-responder community health coach for Methodist Jennie Edmundson Hospital from May 2024 through April 2026, when she was fired.
According to state records, the hospital contracted with the City of Council Bluffs’ police and fire departments to provide first-responder health coach services, and Kephart was assigned to work for those departments for the duration of a two-year contract set to expire in June 2026.
On April 17, 2026, the city investigated an incident in which Kephart was alleged to have shared with others a photograph containing some sort of confidential information. Days later, the city notified the hospital, without explanation, that it was terminating the contract early and no longer needed Kephart’s services. The hospital then fired Kephart, citing the lack of available work for her, while challenging her subsequent application for unemployment benefits.
Administrative Law Judge Stephanie Adkisson ruled recently that there was no evidence to indicate Kephart had committed job-related misconduct and that she was entitled to jobless benefits.

title: Letting the river roam: Surveying the scars left by Irene 15 years later
description:
To river scientists and conservationists, a collapsing slope in southern Vermont is a case study in what happens when decades of flood‑control instincts collide with more recent extreme weather.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Letting the river roam: Surveying the scars left by Irene 15 years later.
text:
Jacob Fetterman (left), coordinator of Trout Unlimited Battenkill Home Rivers Initiative, and Jim Henderson (right), environmental program manager with the Bennington County Regional Commission, at the site of the Green River landslide in Sandgate. Photo by Danielle M. Crosier/Bennington Banner

This story by Danielle M. Crosier was first published in the Bennington Banner on Aug. 28, 2026.
SANDGATE — On a late summer morning along the Green River, the scars of Tropical Storm Irene are still visible on the landscape — even if they now appear to look more like “natural” features.
High above this Battenkill tributary, a towering slope of loose gravel continues its steady creep, collapsing directly into the river.
Locals just call it “the landslide,” but to river scientists and conservationists, it’s a case study in what happens when decades of flood‑control instincts collide with the kind of extreme weather that Vermont has seen since Irene hit 15 years ago.
“It really started letting go during Tropical Storm Irene,” said Jim Henderson, environmental program manager with the Bennington County Regional Commission, during a recent site visit. He noted that the storm’s saturated soils set off slope failures “all over the state of Vermont.”
Standing at the site of the town office, far away from the base of the slope, Henderson sized it up and put the drop at “close to around 300 feet or so.” Later, Jacob Fetterman, coordinator of Trout Unlimited Battenkill Home Rivers Initiative, checked Vermont contour maps and confirmed the slope failure is closer to 220 feet tall — still a deceptively massive wall of loose material hanging above the Green River.
Today, the Sandgate project unfolding below that landslide is part repair job, part course correction — a collaborative effort among the experts to give the river back its flood plain, rather than wall it off and hope for the best.
How a farm berm helped create a 220‑foot landslide
The steep actively failing slope above the Green River wasn’t carved by natural forces alone.
A previous owner spent years stockpiling excess fill along the edge of his hayfield — rocks, river cobbles, chunks of concrete, even car parts. The goal was simple and familiar to Vermont farmers: Keep the water out of the field.
“He built a berm along the edge of the hayfield to keep the water from going into the hayfield,” Henderson said, indicating the rise of the largest sections of the berm. “He wanted to try to contain the river so that his hayfield didn’t get flooded.”
The fix worked in the short term, but at a higher cost to the surrounding landscape and watershed. When Irene and later storms pushed high water down the Green River, the stream had nowhere to fan out. This inability to naturally spread out created a high speed, high intensity, high water, high velocity situation — a powerful, powerful force.
“The river wasn’t able to spread out and go through its natural flood plain during a high water event,” Henderson said, waving an arm along the narrow river channel. “It gets more powerful. It’s like a fire hose.”
Instead of spilling across the field and dropping its sediment harmlessly, the narrowed, supercharged river slammed into a sharp bend at the base of the slope.
“It was literally getting blasted into the base of what is now the landslide,” he said. “Because it’s all gravel, it’s easily erodible.”
Over time, the slide erased what used to be a farm road on the far side of the river — a road you could “drive a vehicle on.” Today, Henderson said, there is “absolutely no chance of that anymore at all.”
It’s all been washed away.
Irene, thousands of landslides and a shift in state policy
In the years after Irene, that eroding bank in Sandgate was just one of many.
“After Irene happened, landslides got started all over the state of Vermont,” Henderson recalled, wincing at the recollection. At the same time, he said, the state was reconsidering its approach to managing rivers that are increasingly hammered by intense rain.
A statewide “river corridor” initiative emerged, aimed at drawing lines back from streambanks and accepting that it is healthy for rivers to migrate over time. The idea is not just about flood control, but also about giving streams enough room to find what scientists call “natural equilibrium.”
“With the river corridor easements, it’s trying to give the river the space it needs to find natural equilibrium,” said Fetterman. “Rivers do migrate over time.”
That policy shift came with a hard truth for landowners living with unstable slopes.
“The Agency of Natural Resources decided we’re not going to stop landslides anymore,” Henderson said, citing both resource constraints and the new river corridor philosophy. “They just don’t have the money, the manpower — and because of new policies to try to stop them, my efforts of getting permits and a grant to do that work came to nothing.”
Instead of armoring the base of the slope — “putting a band‑aid on it,” as Fetterman described it — the state wanted to see projects that addressed the causes upstream: the channelized rivers, the human‑made berms and the flood plains cut off from high water.
That’s where Sandgate’s current work comes in.
Cutting holes in the berm, not fighting the river
Standing in a grassy field along the Green River, it’s easy to miss what has changed. The berm that once walled off the river from its flood plain is still visible in places — a low, rock‑studded rise along the field’s edge. But it is largely overgrown.
However, the machine work is obvious in two key spots.
“Up there was the first breach, and then this is the second one,” Fetterman said, pointing along the berm to where recent work has demolished it. “This was taller. We probably took 4 to 6 feet of height out of it.”
Inside that human‑made ridge, they found exactly what you’d expect from decades of ad hoc flood control. “It was mostly old river cobbles,” Fetterman said. “In most berms that we see, (they) are made just by the farmer picking rocks out of their field that were at one point deposited there by the river, and then stacking them up right next to the stream. Here, there was a lot of junk. And there’s chunks of concrete.”
Instead of scraping the entire berm down to ground level, the team strategically lowered it in places where the river wants to spread out during high flow periods.
“By cutting out sections of the berm under higher flows, it allows the river to spread out onto the flood plain,” Fetterman said. “We’re reconnecting where the river would have gone had the berm not been built.”
The goal is simple but counterintuitive: Invite the river back onto the field in controlled ways, so it can lose speed and drop sediment there, instead of continuing to hammer the base of the landslide and sending even more tons of gravel racing downstream.
“The big idea is that (the river) somewhat abandons this over time,” Fetterman said, gesturing toward the failing slope. Right now, as material sloughs off, he said, “every time we get a high flow event, the river just carries it downstream” rather than letting the toe build up and stabilize.
By reengaging old channels and historic “flood chutes,” the project aims to bleed off that energy before the river reaches the most vulnerable point, the base of the current landslide.
Trees, debris and the case for a messier river
The Sandgate work is not just about dirt and rock; it is also about what grows — and falls — along the river’s edge.
Over the next several years, project partners plan to plant more than 500 trees along this stretch of the Green River, extending roughly 50 feet back from the top of the bank in some places and tracing the full curve of a major bend.
“We’ll probably plant all the way out to where it starts to slope up, so 50 feet,” Henderson said, adding that the goal was to establish about 500-plus trees “on both sides of the river, but predominantly here.”
If the landscape were a work of art, the planting palette would be tailored to wet soils and areas of periodic flooding: sycamores and basswoods near the river, shrubby willows and dogwoods right along the bank, then silver and red maples, sugar maple, black cherry and oaks set farther back. Black walnuts, a favorite of both wildlife and woodworkers, will be tucked in as “investment trees” for the distant future.
“We specifically look to plant trees that would naturally grow in the flood plain,” Henderson said. “Trees that like wet soil and can handle being flooded.”
Downstream, where large trees are already toppling into the channel as the bank undercuts, Fetterman is quick to counter a common instinct to “clean up” the fallen wood. “People sometimes think of debris in the river as a bad thing,” he said. “But really, it helps slow down water.”
Standing together at the base of the landslide, beside a small drop where the river pours over a downed tree and into a deep pool, Fetterman described how that structure works.
“This is a great visualization of the ability for naturally recruited wood to dissipate energy,” he said. “You see, it’s kind of rapid. Then, it hits a spot and it’s able to release energy into a pool. So, instead of just flushing across a more consistent surface, it hits this break, releases energy down into a pool, and then it’s really slow coming out of it. So, you really want this diversity within a stream.”
As climate change drives more intense storms, that messy complexity — the woody debris, the side channels, the rough flood plains — is exactly what slows water down and spreads it out, reducing damage downstream.
“In instances like this, no infrastructure is at threat by a tree falling in here,” Fetterman said. “So then, it actually helps engage the flood plain, helps slow down water and promotes flow out onto the flood plain.”
Why flooded fields can be advantageous
For generations, farmers along Vermont rivers have responded to flooding with understandable instincts. They push the water away from crops, push rocks back toward the river, and mow right up to the banks.
The Sandgate team is trying to show that, in an era with storms of increased strength, working with the river may offer more durable benefits, even for agriculture.
“Even for farmers, the reason that a lot of farmers have really successful crops grown in a flood plain is because of the nutrients in those soils,” Fetterman said. “Even though there’s negatives to that field flooding for them, the positives would be that that river is bringing in nutrients that will sustain those crops instead of the man‑made fertilizers that are put on crops.”
“It’s a natural fertilizer produced by the river,” he added, “and organic material that it transports that is then able to make those soils so fertile.”
That doesn’t mean that the trade‑offs are easy. Letting water reclaim pieces of field “requires them to be far more adaptable in their farming practices,” Fetterman acknowledged. But, he argued, “it is better overall for the entire environment, including the food we eat.”
Conservation, ownership, funding and a long view
The Sandgate property itself has changed hands as Vermont’s conservation landscape has evolved since Irene.
The original family sold to a private owner, who later sold hundreds of acres — essentially everything but the house — to The Conservation Fund. From there, the land went to the Monarch Foundation, which now owns both sides of the river at the critical “choke point” where the project is focused.
“The Conservation Fund sold it to the Monarch Foundation,” Henderson said. “They’ve been very supportive” and have “endorsed this project to happen.”
On the Green River site, the Monarch Foundation has allowed the berm breaches and extensive tree planting. An adjacent landowner on the opposite bank has agreed to a more modest buffer, after some early miscommunication led to newly planted trees being mowed — twice.
“They are participating, just not to the extent that we would like,” Henderson said.
Funding for the design and implementation of the Sandgate project was provided by Watersheds United Vermont through the Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation’s Clean Water Initiative Program.
From start to finish, many partners have been involved in the project’s development and eventual implementation. These include the Batten Kill Watershed Alliance, the town of Sandgate, the Southwestern Vermont Chapter of Trout Unlimited, the Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation, the Fish & Wildlife Department, the U.S. Forest Service, the Bennington County Conservation District and landowners (currently the Monarch Foundation).
From Irene to what comes next
In Sandgate, the work along the Green River is one piece of a more broad post‑Irene effort to rethink how Vermont lives in harmony with its rivers.
The same partners are currently preparing a similar bank stabilization and flood plain reconnection project nearby, in Sunderland, and in cooperation with Ducks Unlimited. This Sunderland project will address a collapsing hayfield bank along the Batten Kill and the Batten Kill tributary known as Tanner Brook. Work there is expected to begin after Labor Day, with more tree and buffer planting to follow.
Meanwhile, the Batten Kill Watershed Alliance — which grew out of local resistance to restocking Vermont’s stretch of the Batten Kill with hatchery trout in the 1990s — continues to argue that restoring natural habitat and shade is a better long‑term strategy than pouring more fish into a stressed system.
“The main reason why the Batten Kill Watershed Alliance got created was to prevent stocking the Batten Kill in Vermont again,” Henderson said, arguing that the river “has all the elements of being a natural, self‑sustaining population” — if habitat is protected and repaired.
Fifteen years after Irene, the Sandgate project reflects that same philosophy on the land: Stop trying to pin rivers in place, and instead help them behave like rivers again, even when that means there will be an adjustment period.
Watching a 220‑foot slope slowly crumble does not seem natural, but it was the human-made berms that created the problem and helped to identify it. It is difficult to place trust in change, but those carefully cut berms and young sycamores will, in time, make things more stable, not less.
As Fetterman said while looking up at the loose gravel wall above the Green River, the height itself is “one of those sort of illusions.”
“It looks like it’s higher than it might actually be, when you’re standing close by,” he said.
But the deeper illusion might be what the Sandgate project suggests: the idea that we can hold rivers still in an era of highly variable and transitioning weather patterns, and that the safest place for high water is anywhere but the flood plain.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: The race for governor: Low stakes in New Hampshire’s gubernatorial primary on Tuesday
description: On Tuesday, Granite Staters will cast their votes in one of two gubernatorial primaries, but those votes are unlikely to have much impact. Former Executive Councilor Cinde Warmington is the only name on the Democratic ballot. And incumbent Gov. Kelly Ayotte does not face a serious primary challenge. Shaun Fife, of Gilmanton, and Bob Wayne […]
text:
Cinde Warmington (left) and Gov. Kelly Ayotte (right) are already looking ahead to the November general election. (Left: Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin; Right: Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)On Tuesday, Granite Staters will cast their votes in one of two gubernatorial primaries, but those votes are unlikely to have much impact.
Former Executive Councilor Cinde Warmington is the only name on the Democratic ballot. And incumbent Gov. Kelly Ayotte does not face a serious primary challenge. Shaun Fife, of Gilmanton, and Bob Wayne McClory, of Goffstown, have filed to challenge Ayotte in the Republican primary, but neither has mounted a campaign likely to make a dent in Ayotte’s chances.
This is Ayotte’s first reelection bid. She won election in 2024 over Manchester Mayor Joyce Craig with the endorsement of her predecessor, Gov. Chris Sununu, whom she has sought to emulate in many ways. Before becoming governor, she represented New Hampshire in the U.S. Senate from 2011 to 2017 and was the state’s attorney general.
Warmington served on the Executive Council, an elected body unique to New Hampshire that approves contracts and vets the governor’s appointments, from 2021 to 2025. She was the lone Democrat on the council. This is her second time running for governor. In 2024, she lost the gubernatorial primary to Craig.
Ayotte’s approval rating in UNH’s August Granite State Poll was 49%. In her first term as governor, she successfully pushed the Legislature to roll back a bail reform law that she believed was too lenient on pre-trial crime suspects. She signed a bell-to-bell public school cell phone ban into law. She harshened penalties for drivers who refuse a Breathalyzer test. She implemented premiums to some Medicaid enrollees and increased their copays. And she enacted a budget that made major cuts to agencies like the Office of the Child Advocate and the Department of Health and Human Services.
Warmington trailed Ayotte in an August UNH poll, 49%-39%. As an executive councilor she opposed canceling and denying contracts with Planned Parenthood of Northern New England, a measure her Republican colleagues on the council successfully pushed for. She was sometimes the only vote opposing Sununu’s nominees for governmental posts. She was regularly the most scrutinizing councilor of state agency commissioners during her tenure on the council.
Ayotte has sought to make the campaign entirely about Warmington’s work lobbying for the opioid industry. Before becoming executive councilor, Warmington worked as a healthcare attorney for Purdue Pharma and a clinic that was criticized for over-prescribing opioids. The incumbent governor’s campaign has spammed advertising spaces with commercials, billboards, and other ads labeling Warmington an “opioid lobbyist.” In terms of policy, she’s promising voters that in a second term a slate of housing legislation she signed into law will ease skyrocketing prices and that she’ll continue the tough-on-crime style policymaking she’s become known for.
Warmington has criticized Ayotte for her Medicaid premium plan and the cuts in the budget she signed into law. She’s also blamed Ayotte for an ongoing abuse and neglect scandal at the Sununu Youth Services Center, a juvenile justice facility in Manchester. Warmington and her Democratic allies have tried to tie Ayotte to President Donald Trump, who has historically low approval ratings and who lost New Hampshire in three consecutive presidential elections. Warmington argues Ayotte is not willing to “stand up to” Trump by speaking out or participating in lawsuits against the administration over federal funding being revoked from New Hampshire or other matters.
The general election is Nov. 3.
Getting to the polls and voting
The polls will open at varying times on Tuesday morning depending on the municipality. Voters can find out where their polling location is and which races will be on their ballot on the Secretary of State’s website at https://app.sos.nh.gov/pollingplacesampleballot. New Hampshire allows same-day voter registration. To register to vote on Election Day, voters will need to provide proof of their identity (driver’s license, government-issued photo ID, or passport), age (also driver’s license, government-issued photo ID, or passport), U.S. citizenship (birth certificate, passport, naturalization papers, or other proof), and domicile (government-issued ID or documentation with an address on it).

name: Mississippi Today
title: A complex jaw reconstruction surgery reaches Mississippi
description: Herbert Griffith shows the 3D-printed teeth he received at the University of Mississippi Medical Center School of Dentistry after double jaw surgery, the result of a cancer diagnosis, Thursday, July 2, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Since losing his teeth, Herbert Griffith has tried just about every smoothie on the market that his older sister could find for him. 

Thanks to a newly available surgery at the University of Mississippi Medical Center School of Dentistry, Griffith, a 65-year-old oral cancer survivor and fishing enthusiast living in Laurel, has graduated to mashed potatoes. 

Beverly Cole, left, and Herbert Griffith, right, stand with their late mother. Credit: Courtesy of Beverly Cole
Griffith lost most of his teeth after being diagnosed with oral cancer in 2022. Radiation treatment, which targets cancer cells but can kill healthy ones in the process, took the rest. 
“They just crumbled up,” said his sister Beverly Cole, who has helped manage Griffith’s care since his tooth pain first alerted them that something was wrong. Griffith has difficulty speaking, and Cole, a retired medical manager, often steps in to help him communicate. She has spent much of her career and retirement as a caretaker, first as a hospice worker, then for her mother, and now for Grffith. 
To her, he’s just “Herbie.”
Traditional dental implants require drilling into the jawbone to screw in individual teeth, but Griffith’s cancer-riddled bones made that procedure impossible. There wasn’t enough bone to support them. Instead, he became the second candidate in Mississippi for a double jaw subperiosteal, or “on-the-bone” surgery.
Over several months, doctors used advanced scanning techniques to map out the shape of the jaw. Then Griffith’s care team worked with a medical technology company to 3D print a robust scaffold made of titanium alloy that sits on top of what remains of his jawbone. After checking the scaffold’s fit, the team of plastic and oral surgeons can mount a full set of teeth, giving the patient a functional jaw in the same day. 
The medical center’s dental school is the only in-state center that performs this procedure, said Dr. Ignacio Velasco, an oral and dental surgeon at the medical school and one of Griffith’s doctors. It is among a handful of medical centers nationwide that have both the infrastructure to take care of patients and the multidisciplinary team of doctors who can perform it. 

The surgery isn’t for everyone, Velasco added. But for people who physically cannot undergo the traditional process, it is the only way to regain functional teeth, and thus the ability to chew and speak normally. 

With this capability, Velasco said he can keep seeing his oral cancer patients for the whole recovery process. Before, many of these patients endured without a working jaw. 
“Now, patients don’t need to leave Mississippi to get a full treatment for their cancer and finally the dental reconstruction,” he said.
A complicated procedure
Dr. Pasha Shakoori, a plastic surgeon who specializes in facial reconstruction, works on these surgeries at the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine in Baltimore. It’s a complex procedure to pull off, he said. For each patient case, Shakoori said he works with a dentist, an oral surgeon, and an ear nose and throat doctor. 
Patients benefit from the speed of the process, Shakoori said. For traditional implants, patients have to wait three to six months for the metal posts to heal before they can get each individual tooth screwed into place. For a full set of teeth, that is time-consuming and expensive, because insurance often only partially covers dental implants. 
In 2025, the dentistry school team started offering single jaw subperiosteal implants and completed their first double jaw case in February 2026. Double jaw surgery is more difficult, Shakoori said, because there are literally more moving parts. 

“What makes the bottom jaw a little bit more complicated is (that) it moves,” he said. The top jaw is attached to the skull which makes it easier to operate on, Shakoori explained. Plus, it’s helpful to have one set of teeth serve as a reference point for how the two sets meet when the patient bites down or closes their mouth. 

Herbert Griffith holds up fish he caught, before his cancer operations. Credit: Courtesy of Beverly Cole
“If you’re operating on both, now you’re changing everything.”
A complicated procedure did not surprise Griffith after a difficult medical journey that included an initial misdiagnosis. When the tooth pain first started, Griffith’s dentist cycled him through antibiotics for three months before Cole booked him an appointment with a Hattiesburg-based oral surgeon. 
“Dr. York looked at it and he said, ‘That’s cancer,’” Cole recounted.
By the time surgery was an option, Griffith’s jaw had deteriorated so much his doctors needed to reconstruct his jaw from skin and bone from his leg before they could screw in the titanium scaffold. Then, in a rare occurrence, the temporary plastic scaffold broke during his recovery and Griffith had to go through the multi-hour surgery again.
“He’s really been through a lot,” Cole said of her brother. “He’s a trooper.”
Still, while in the waiting room for a follow-up appointment, accompanied by Cole and his girlfriend, Griffith was positive about his procedures. 
“They’re going well enough,” he said. “Let me tell you, I have my faith.”
Cole is now trying out different foods with her brother, who eats slowly and carefully, making sure each morsel is soft enough to swallow. Just the other day, she said, “Herbie” was able to chew and swallow one of his favorite desserts: a slice of apple tart.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Job cuts at News 12 trigger letter from top CT regulator
description: The widely-reported layoffs could require notice to PURA, even though the agency can't block the changes or order a rate reduction.
text:
Connecticut’s top utility regulator recently sent a letter warning cable provider Optimum that it may have violated state law by not notifying the agency about job cuts to its in-house cable news channel, News 12.
It’s unclear what penalties, if any, regulators might impose on the company in response to those changes.
Thomas Wiehl, chair of the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority, sent a letter to Optimum’s director of government affairs, Brian Smith, on Aug. 27, inquiring about reports of widespread layoffs at News 12, which operates newsrooms in Connecticut, New York and New Jersey.
Those cuts — if they are as severe as was reported — could constitute programming changes that require prior notice to regulators, Wiehl said.
Wiehl specifically cited one report from CT Insider that said the layoffs could affect the channel’s ability to provide “Connecticut-focused coverage” to viewers. No notice of such a change was received by PURA, he added.
“My sincere hope is that this lack of notice is indicative that the above-cited reporting is incorrect, and that there will in fact be no changes to the local news programming that benefits the people of Connecticut who, in turn, pay Optimum’s consistently increasing rates and charges,” Wiehl said. “However, if Optimum does plan to change News 12 programming, please promptly notify PURA in compliance with Connecticut law.”
A spokesperson for Optimum declined to answer specific questions about the scope of the News 12 layoffs. However, company leaders disputed some of the chairman’s assertions in a response letter last Wednesday, written by Smith.
Alexis Aziz, the Optimum spokesperson, said in a statement Thursday that the company is “taking proactive steps to ensure News 12 remains strong, relevant, and sustainable for the future.”
“Our mission remains unchanged,” Aziz added. “We remain committed to delivering trusted hyperlocal journalism, serving the communities that rely on us, and providing viewers with the news and information they want, where and how they want it.”
As part of a deregulation bill passed in 2007, Connecticut lawmakers effectively removed PURA’s authority to set cable TV rates or approve franchise agreements. However, the agency retains some vestiges of its prior oversight of the cable industry, including a law requiring that video service providers give regulators at least 30 days notice of any “planned programming or rate changes.”
In his response letter to PURA, Smith said his understanding of the law was that it generally requires cable companies like Optimum to notify regulators only if they plan on adding, moving or discontinuing a TV channel.
“It is our view that the updates to News 12’s local news programming on an existing channel do not fall within the scope of the notice requirements” under the law, Smith wrote.
Smith nonetheless offered to meet with Wiehl and PURA staff to discuss those changes. “Optimum feels that it is important to keep the Authority apprised of developments that impact its Connecticut customers, beyond its strict regulatory requirements,” he wrote.
In interview with the Connecticut Mirror, Wiehl said he planned to take up Smith on his offer for a meeting.
Wiehl, who previously served as an attorney at the Office of Consumer Counsel, added that his view of “programming” extends beyond just the lineup of channels offered by a cable provider.
“If they could just run a black screen for 24 hours a day, as long as they called it ‘News 12’ …. Presumably, the Legislature would want them to have to let us know that that’s happening,” Wiehl said.
Despite his concerns, Wiehl said the law is clear that his agency lacks the authority to review or block any of the proposed changes in News 12’s programming, or to order a rate reduction on behalf of customers. He said he was unsure whether the law even allowed PURA to issue a notice of violation — or impose fines — if it determines Optimum failed to properly report those changes to regulators.
Part of the reason for his letter, Wiehl said, is that there was little publicly available information about what Optimum’s actual plans are for the station. In statements to other news outlets, including CT Insider and the New York Post, company representatives have not divulged the extent of layoffs or efforts to consolidate operations across its newsrooms.
The Post reported that the layoffs impacted “at least three dozens employees,” including Connecticut-based anchors Becky Suran and Mark Sudol. 
“I don’t know that anyone knows what the plan is based on the public reporting I’ve seen, other than there have been layoffs,” Wiehl said. “There seems to have been some confirmations from sources — I can’t even tell whether they’re speaking for Optimum or not — that there’s going to be changes to the content, at least, that’s being broadcast.”
Wiehl’s former boss at OCC, Claire Coleman, also released a statement last week regarding the reported layoffs at News 12. She encouraged cable customers to reach out to PURA if they have ongoing concerns about the availability of certain channels.
“While the details of how Optimum’s plans for Channel 12’s future operations will affect subscriber programming and channel lineups are unclear, it is important that Connecticut customers continue to have access to in state news,” Coleman said in a statement. “Local programming serves as a lifeline to residents, connecting neighbors, highlighting available services as well as local news, events and relevant information that may not be available elsewhere.”
Wiehl also said he believes it is important for regulators to exercise the powers given to them by state lawmakers, even if those powers are limited. 
“I think if there’s a statute saying this is something supposed to be happening and isn’t happening, I think we need to take it as importantly for a cable company as we would for an electric company,” Wiehl said.

name: VTDigger
title: St. Johnsbury community works to combat surge in ‘bad behavior’ downtown
description:
Caledonia County State’s Attorney Claire Burns said the courts struggle to impose meaningful bail. The area is also a “human services desert,” she added.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  St. Johnsbury community works to combat surge in ‘bad behavior’ downtown.
text:
The Welcome Center in St. Johnsbury on August 9, 2022. File photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger

The St. Johnsbury community has been working overtime to quell a months-long surge in “bad behavior” by a limited number of people in its downtown area. The situation’s epicenter is a park adjacent to the town’s Welcome Center, a three-story former train station that also houses the town offices.
“We’re struggling,” said Town Clerk Stacy Jewell during the town’s July 27 selectboard meeting. “It’s very, very difficult to come to work every day and deal with that. I’m at the point where I’m just going to put paper up over our windows. … What we’re seeing is very inappropriate.”
Behaviors in the park include open alcohol consumption, violence, overdoses and a can being thrown through a window of the Welcome Center building, Town Manager Chad Whitehead wrote in a plea for help sent to state officials, human services agencies and local leaders in early August.
At that time, just 18 people were the cause of 131 of the calls to the police department in the two weeks prior, according to Whitehead. Many of those were arrested, charged with a misdemeanor, potentially held overnight and then released back into the community where they went on to be arrested again, the town manager said.
“I am equally frustrated when repeat offenders are not held accountable,” Whitehead wrote in a post on the town’s Facebook page. “I believe we need to work closely with our State’s Attorneys’ offices and the Judicial Bureau to understand why this is happening and what changes they need from the Legislature to correct it.”
Indeed, the challenges are not unique to St. Johnsbury: Whitehead said numerous other Vermont communities’ police logs look just like his town’s. In Burlington, city councilors approved a resolution in late August asking Gov. Phil Scott to direct state resources to help combat persistent struggles with homelessness and drug use downtown.
In St. Johnsbury, others who work in criminal justice and mental health echoed the town manager’s frustrations with what they feel are limited tools for changing unwanted behavior. 
‘Be compassionate, but there also needs to be accountability’
Whitehead, who has been the town manager for over a decade, said the spike in “bad behavior” and lack of accountability is the worst he’s ever seen. The surge corresponds with cutbacks to the state’s motel voucher program, which has served as an overflow system for the typically full traditional homeless shelters, as well as the cleanup of several local homeless encampments on nearby private property.
The town manager is quick to note that not all unhoused people in town are acting poorly. “There are homeless folks in town that are absolutely pleasant,” he said in mid-August, adding that a now-homeless man he went to high school with raked the entire park of his own accord that very morning. Some, though, have committed more than a handful of misdemeanors and continue to violate conditions of release — such as staying away from the Welcome Center park.

The park outside the St. Johnsbury Welcome Center, seen here on August 20, 2026, is one of the epicenters of “bad behavior” occurring in town. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger

Whitehead does say that some of the “bad actors” have had a “rough go of things.” However, he said, “there’s a fine line between — you can be compassionate, but there also needs to be accountability.”
As a result of Whitehead’s plea for help, the Vermont State Police has increased patrols downtown, the town manager said, and he has been working with the public safety commissioner and other state agencies to explore solutions.
In addition, the selectboard authorized $25,000 to fund foot patrols in the community, which town police officers are voluntarily working outside of their regular shifts. The town typically has just two police officers on duty, Whitehead said, and they are often tied up with calls and not able to patrol proactively.
Whitehead said he has spent much of his time over the past two months working on public safety issues, especially responding to the multitudes of unhappy residents who want the town to do more and explaining how officials’ hands are tied.
‘A huge strain on judicial resources’
According to Caledonia County State’s Attorney Claire Burns, the courts have little to work with in terms of holding people on bail or imposing restrictions on repeat offenders.
“Low-level misdemeanors are the ones that we see the most frequently with this population that is really wreaking havoc on businesses and citizens,” she said Thursday. “We can ask for $200 cash bail, and only in terms of risk of flight.”
For suspects who are already on conditions of release, such as not going near the Welcome Center park, Burns said the court can ask for higher bail — but there is often pushback on doing so considering this population’s limited financial resources.
It’s hard to put a meaningful bail situation in place to deter repeat offenses, Burns said. “They just keep doing it, and we’ve seen it time and time again,” she said. “It’s a huge strain on judicial resources, my office and law enforcement in particular.”
Chris Dennehy, crisis outreach coordinator with Northeast Kingdom Human Services, has worked for a year as an embedded mental health clinician within the St. Johnsbury Police Department. He accompanies officers on calls where mental health is a component, providing support and working to connect people with the resources they need.
“A disproportionate number of people down there (at the Welcome Center park) are disabled or elderly,” he said Tuesday. “They’re working on fixed incomes, folks who have brain injuries or cognitive disorders. They have some extraordinary barriers to maneuvering the system, preventing them from connecting with resources on their own.”
As for the location, Dennehy said that staying near the Welcome Center, where the area is lit and visible, can provide a sense of safety, especially for single women. The building also has Wi-Fi and access to bathrooms and water.
Dennehy said that many of the people in question don’t have phones or an address, which makes it even more difficult to connect them with the resources that are “going to help them get unstuck.”
A ‘human services desert’
Burns said, however, that available resources can also be lacking.
“We are a human services desert in the Northeast Kingdom,” she said. “The wait lists are a year long, and we don’t have any true rehabilitative addiction treatment facilities.”
When the governor was asked about the situation in St. Johnsbury on Thursday during his weekly press conference, he pointed to the “accountability court” model, piloted this year in Chittenden and Windham counties, as a potential solution. The court fast-tracks defendants with numerous legal cases, hires social workers to connect them with services, and has made significant progress with Chittenden County’s backlog.
However, Burns said that Caledonia County doesn’t have the same backlog of cases as in the rest of the state. In addition, she said places like Burlington have more resources with which to connect defendants.

Downtown St. Johnsbury adjacent to the Welcome Center on August 20, 2026. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger.

“We don’t have mental health resources. We don’t have beds. We have nothing to do with these people,” Burns said. “We say, ‘We want to give you treatment,’ and I mean, that’s my No. 1 priority: I want people to be rehabilitated and treated. But that’s just unrealistic. We can’t. We don’t have the resources.”
Burns also said available resources are worth little unless a person really wants them and is motivated to engage — which can be a tall order.
“That is the core tenet of any therapeutic program, any addiction recovery program, is that it has to come from the individual,” she said. “Sometimes we can force a structure on them — i.e., jail — and that might be enough to kickstart the process, because when you’re in the throes of addiction you want to hit your substance, your whatever it is.”
“It’s incredibly hard to overcome,” Burns added.
‘Quite a bit of improvement’
On Thursday, Whitehead said there had been “quite a bit of improvement” over the past two weeks.
Twice a month, he sits down with the police department and local service agencies for a public safety task force meeting where they review the list of people having frequent interactions with police and brainstorm solutions. There were only 20 individuals reviewed during the most recent meeting, he said, in contrast to 44 at the previous meeting.
The town manager attributes the positive changes to Dennehy’s work as well as other community agencies proactively making contact with people and offering them services, in addition to foot patrols keeping a closer eye on things.
Whitehead, the fire chief and police chief also held a stakeholder meeting with interested town and business leaders Aug. 26, where eight goals were identified, from cleaning up trash and weeds downtown to updating the town’s vague and outdated loitering ordinance. They plan to meet again Sept. 9.
In pursuit of those goals, Whitehead said, a local business owner coordinated a group of homeless people who spent the better part of a Monday cleaning up a public parking lot downtown.
“I take heart in the response that I saw with people cleaning up yesterday,” Dennehy said of the event. “I think the people involved were really happy to be involved and it seems like there was a very positive response from the community.”
