name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Press freedom shouldn’t be a casualty in Arkansas’ data center wars
description: There’s no such thing as a slam dunk court case, but the constitutional argument against prior restraint comes close. For nearly a century, the U.S. Supreme Court has ruled against efforts to prevent news outlets from publishing material. That includes the landmark Pentagon Papers decision that showed the heavy burden the government must meet. An […]
text:
A marble plaque inscribed with the First Amendment sits on Independence Mall in Philadelphia, Pa.
(Photo by Raymond Boyd/Getty Images)There’s no such thing as a slam dunk court case, but the constitutional argument against prior restraint comes close.
For nearly a century, the U.S. Supreme Court has ruled against efforts to prevent news outlets from publishing material. That includes the landmark Pentagon Papers decision that showed the heavy burden the government must meet.
An agreement about an Arkansas data center that doesn’t include any details about national security wouldn’t meet that burden. 
So it would have been easy to shrug off Entergy Arkansas’ unsuccessful attempt to block the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette and Arkansas Times from disclosing more details about that agreement. 
But the fact that the utility even took such an extraordinary step, and the legal threat news organizations may still face, highlights the threat to a bedrock principle of a free press.
It’s also another sign of how transparency is being sacrificed during an increasingly unpopular nationwide data center boom to meet the growing demand for computing power.
Entergy argued that trade secrets were at risk if the Democrat-Gazette published further details about its agreement with a Google subsidiary for a solar facility needed for a multibillion dollar data center. 
The newspaper published a story based on confidential, non-public documents that were released to a central Arkansas woman, Jessica Kivell, through a Freedom of Information Act request. Entergy said those documents were released in error.
Entergy’s lawsuit also targeted Kivell and the Arkansas Times, even though the Times said it has never received the documents. In addition to seeking to block publication, the lawsuit also asked for an order requiring the details be removed from their online stories.



Let us know what you think...


 


There’s a reason why these kinds of prior restraint efforts are rare. A long line of cases in state and federal courts, including ones from Arkansas, spell out the high bar that must be met.
“In the First Amendment, the Founding Fathers gave the free press the protection it must have to fulfill its essential role in our democracy. The press was to serve the governed, not the governors,” Justice Hugo Black wrote in his concurring opinion in the Pentagon Papers ruling in 1971.
That reasoning is partly why U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky denied Entergy’s request for a temporary restraining order. But the risks of further action and legal threats still remain.
A day after his ruling, Rudofsky said in a court docket entry that Entergy would not be pursuing a preliminary injunction. But it’s not clear whether that closes the door on the utility seeking civil damages over the publication.
Even if Entergy doesn’t pursue any further action, the case risks creating a chilling effect on everyday citizens, journalists and news organizations trying to seek more information about data center projects around the state.
The secrecy surrounding these projects has fueled the bipartisan pushback just as much as concerns about the facilities’ energy usage.
Arkansans are being asked to trust policymakers’ decisions about data centers and companies’ assurances about them. But it’s hard to justify that trust when vital information is being kept from them. 
It’s even harder to trust those promises when data center supporters ask a court to ignore a core tenet of the First Amendment and when threats loom against citizens seeking more information about the projects.
The battle over press freedom comes at a perilous time for journalism, with reporters facing political attacks, threats of violence and legal intimidation. 
But it also comes at a politically fraught moment for data center supporters, who have seen the concerns about the facilities and artificial intelligence become a defining issue in midterm races around the country.
There should be vigorous debate about data centers and how to balance the need for them with the growing concerns that communities have. The First Amendment, however, shouldn’t fall by the wayside during that debate.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Volunteer fire departments are shrinking. For some, it’s a call to action
description: Career firefighters who also volunteer in local departments have become increasingly vital to the fire service in CT as membership shrinks.
text:
An occasional look at Connecticut’s remarkable people, places and things

David Elliott stood on his front porch in sweatpants in the pre-dawn darkness in rural Northeastern Connecticut, waiting for his golden retriever to come inside for breakfast.
His alarm went off at 4:40 a.m., the start of his second 24-hour shift of the week. This is the hard one, he said.
Elliott waited for the Keurig to fill his carrot-colored mug with coffee. His duffel bag was packed.
He turned the TV to the morning news and changed into his red Fairfield Fire Department T-shirt. It takes nearly two hours to drive there, where he works as a career firefighter.

Before the sun rises, David Elliott prepares for a 24-hour shift as a Fairfield firefighter. He leaves his house in Woodstock with dogs Sweetie and Finley on Aug. 19, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Finley (Elliott’s pup) and Sweetie (Elliott’s girlfriend’s dog) piled into the back seat of his car. He drove just down the street, to the house where his parents still live, on Lake Bungee in Woodstock. They would look after the dogs while he was at work on the other side of the state.
Elliott’s next stop was the Bungay Fire Brigade, the volunteer fire station where he is chief, to drop off reports he wrote the day before. Then he started his commute southwest, through the mist and the sunrise. 
Elliott is not the only firefighter in Connecticut to work in a paid department and volunteer elsewhere. But Elliott also works as a fire marshal, he serves on committees in the Fairfield department and is a state firefighting instructor, among other things. 
He and others like him have become increasingly vital to the fire service in Connecticut as the number of certified firefighters shrinks.
David Elliott drives an emergency response vehicle along Pole Bridge Road in Woodstock on July 29, 2026. His volunteer fire department covers 31 square miles with some homes along narrow dirt roads, making access difficult or impossible for larger emergency response trucks.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Data released by Comptroller Sean Scanlon’s office in May 2025 revealed “sobering insights into the severity of Connecticut’s dwindling firefighting forces,” according to the report. Since 2017, the state has seen a 62.7% decrease in volunteer firefighters.
In 2020, the National Fire Protection Association recorded the lowest overall number of volunteer and career firefighters since 1991 and saw a drop off in the number of volunteer firefighters about 10 years ago. Almost 25% of volunteer firefighters have left since 2008, according to the NFPA.
But the shortage of volunteers indirectly points to an increase in the number of paid firefighters across the country as more departments realize the only way to keep their forces intact is to pay them.
Keith Wucik, the chief of the Preston Fire Department, said the town transitioned from an entirely volunteer to partially paid department when a 2005 consultant recommended hiring administrative and chief roles. A couple of years later, the department started hiring paid firefighters as well. 
“The town of Preston had to hire full-time firefighters and part-time firefighters to make sure we could get out the door to do our job,” Wucik said.
The fire department now has six full-time, 12 part-time and nine volunteer firefighters, and the department spends $1.2 million on firefighter salaries and benefits, excluding gear and training costs. 
“It’s a lot of money,” Wucik said. 
Fire departments across Connecticut, like Preston’s, rely on grants along with taxpayer money to fund fire departments, but budgets in small communities are generally tighter.
Woodstock’s town government budget for fire protection is $631,760 for the 2026-2027 fiscal year, which includes funding for the town’s three volunteer departments, administrative work and contracts, notably without any firefighter labor costs.
According to a 2022 report, about 64% of all Connecticut fire departments are fully volunteer.
“The volunteer service is dying. There’s no question about that,” Elliott said. Especially when called to larger emergencies, like structure fires, the three volunteer departments in Woodstock have shifted toward relying on automated and mutual aid programs that dispatch multiple stations at once just to send enough personnel. 

Places for firefighters to leave their gear at the Woodstock Volunteer Fire Association remain empty on July 29, 2026. The station is one of three in Woodstock and provides emergency medical services for the town as well.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

The problem with the volunteer service is the unavailability of people to drive to the station and suit up, according to Elliott. 
“It could be a Tuesday at 2 o’clock in the afternoon, and I could get 12 people ready to go right out the door and volunteer, or it could be a Friday at 6 p.m. and I got nobody,” he said.  
Jeffrey Morrissette, the state fire administrator, said he saw similar concerns about recruitment and retention through a statewide fire service survey, which concluded in late 2024. A bill passed this year was partially inspired by those survey results, he said, and aims to make public fire protection in Connecticut “more transparent.”
“There’s a lot of fear out there about the legislation that just passed this past session that the state is trying to take over,” Morrissette said. “I don’t think that was anybody’s motivation.”
The law requires fire departments to register with municipal authorities for review with the The National Emergency Response Information System, to develop local fire protection plans identifying emergency response procedures, and to create programs “to incentivize the regionalization of fire protection services and sharing fire protection resources,” among other things.
Morrissette also recognizes that departments in smaller communities have limited capacity to respond to emergencies, especially during the work week, and that people with multiple roles, like Elliott, are crucial.
“Sometimes I wonder what we would do without those people, but sometimes it’s almost to the detriment of their personal lives,” he said. 

Commitment
Elliott’s personal life seems to blend with his work, especially when he’s called on weekends and holidays. 
“We may have sat down for a meal and had a house full of people, but if there was a call, he would leave,” his mother, Barbara Elliott said, adding that it didn’t matter if it was Thanksgiving dinner or a birthday party. 
Her town “would really be hurting” without firefighters like her son to answer those calls. “These people commit a lot of time and effort to helping the community by helping people not only with fires,” she said. 




The Bungay Fire Brigade motto, “neighbors helping neighbors,” appears on engines and other vehicles that respond to calls in Woodstock on July 23, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
David Elliott displays memorabilia from his decades of volunteer and career firefighting jobs across Connecticut on his porch in Woodstock on Aug, 20, 2026. Items are arranged for the picture.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
David Elliott holds extrication equipment in Woodstock on July 23, 2026. Firefighters use the Jaws of Life to cut apart vehicles and access victims during car accidents.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror




As the volunteer fire service has atrophied, the diversity of calls fire departments respond to have expanded. 
“We are the fix-all of emergency services,” Elliott said, referring to firefighters as “professional problem solvers.” Calls often include car accidents, search and rescue, downed power lines from storms, hazmat issues, medical incidents, animals caught in trees and beeping smoke detectors. Beyond that, Elliott’s job also includes aspects of fire prevention. 
He joined the fire service in 2000 when he was just 16 at the same station in Woodstock where he volunteers today. 
“I was just hooked,” he said, remembering when he watched his older brother respond to a brush fire call. 
Firefighters from left to right, David Elliott, Josh Bottone, Adam Bottone, and Glenn Elliott in a picture on Elliott’s Facebook page, Aug. 20, 2026. Josh Bottone was the assistant chief of the Bungay Fire Brigade when the picture was taken and before he became the deputy chief for the Woodstock Volunteer Fire Association, where he volunteers now. Glenn is David’s brother. Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
Culture
Familial ties like these are central to the fire service community and culture, along with recruitment and retention. 
Josh Bottone, the deputy chief of Woodstock Volunteer Fire Association down the road from Bungay and one of Elliott’s mentors, joined the fire service after his neighbor’s house burned down. One of the people who responded to that fire was Elliott’s aunt, a family friend and an EMT. Bottone then joined the fire service along with his two brothers and eventually became a chief in Woodstock.

Josh Bottone stands by a ladder truck in the Woodstock Volunteer Fire Association station on July 29, 2026. Bottone is the station’s deputy chief.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Both Elliott and Bottone attribute their long careers volunteering to their community connections. But Elliott sees that dedication as a rarity, since young people often leave the town for college or work after high school. If teens or young adults join, they often volunteer as a “stepping stone” to career firefighting and other emergency response jobs, he said. 
“You invest in the people as much as you can and you hope they stay,” Elliott said. After the volunteer fire department pays for basic certification classes, priced at $1,200, and one set of gear, worth $6,000, it’s costly if firefighters leave.
Richard Baron, a captain at Muddy Brook Fire Department — another volunteer department in Woodstock — sees the benefit of supporting new recruits who apply to career firefighting jobs. In that case, they also return to the volunteer departments with more experience. 
“The problem is the daytime,” he said, when they’re not available for calls.

Richard Baron stands by a tanker in the Muddy Brook Fire Department in Woodstock on July 29, 2026. Baron is a captain at the volunteer fire department and a veteran firefighter.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Like those career firefighters, Elliott brings valuable expertise to Bungay Fire Brigade. The job “helped me bring more knowledge and skills and training back to this [volunteer] department,” he said.
Establishing a presence in the community is important, but “age is legit the key,” Bottone said. Bottone, 54, says he relies on younger volunteers to go into burning buildings — a physically taxing job. In short, the fire service needs new young recruits, which is reflected in the comptroller’s 2025 report. Firefighters in Connecticut are on average older, compared to firefighters in the rest of the country.
As firefighters age out and leave the fire service, the remaining responders manage contracting departments, but a consistent call volume leads to a higher burnout rate, Elliott said.
“At some point, a system will fail,” he said.  
David Elliott boards an engine after responding to a call for his career job in Fairfield on Aug. 17, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
The next morning, after his 24-hour shift in Fairfield, during which he responded to medical calls and a fire at Sacred Heart University, Elliott began the drive home. Nearly two hours later, a quick stop at the farm stand in Woodstock transformed into a catch-up with Mrs. B. — Josh Bottone’s mother and Elliott’s neighbor — among the peaches and nectarines. He stopped for a bagel and cream cheese, washing it down with an iced coffee on the porch next to Finley. 
Elliott changed into a Bungay Fire Brigade polo and climbed into his pickup, riding to a meeting for water rescue access at a nearby lake in town.
The day had just begun.
David Elliott fills his gas tank along his route to work from Woodstock to Fairfield on Aug. 19, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

name: Kansas Reflector
title: After 9/11, this Kansas town forged an unlikely bond with the FDNY. It is honored in tumbling steel.
description: ANTHONY — Why? That’s the word that hovers over Memorial Park here, just before dusk on an evening in early September when the wind swells from the southwest and the swaying branches of the trees break the rays of the setting sun into dancing shafts of gold. There is peace here, the kind of tranquility […]
text:
An American flag framed by twisted blocks of steel from the World Trade Center was seen Tuesday, Sep. 2, 2026, at Memorial Park at Anthony. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)ANTHONY — Why?
That’s the word that hovers over Memorial Park here, just before dusk on an evening in early September when the wind swells from the southwest and the swaying branches of the trees break the rays of the setting sun into dancing shafts of gold.
There is peace here, the kind of tranquility that settles over a small town at the drowsy end of the working day. This community of 2,108 in south central Kansas is like others across America, a one-stoplight town with a clock above the county courthouse that might as well have stopped decades ago.
But Anthony is different than other towns.
At Memorial Park, there are three chunks of twisted steel set above a brick and concrete base. The pieces are from the ruins of the World Trade Center and form a sculpture that seems to tumble from the blue prairie sky.
Anthony — founded in 1878 and named after the governor at the time — is the unlikely site of the state’s official 9/11 memorial. Another governor, Kathleen Sebelius, signed a bill in 2006 proclaiming the city as such, and not just because the city set a few pieces from a fallen tower of the World Trade Center on a pedestal.
In the days and weeks following the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, the residents of Anthony came together to support a ladder company in the Bronx that had lost colleagues in the twin towers. The town raised money, first for the Red Cross, then directly for the widow and children of a young fireman who died, and finally to create a memorial to the victims of 9/11 and to celebrate the friendship between the Kansas city and Engine 88, Ladder 38 of the New York department.
Donna Crowe was at work as a secretary at the Anthony Police Department that Tuesday morning, 25 years ago, when her husband called to say a plane had crashed into one of the World Trade Center towers in New York. She turned on the TV at the police department and, with the chief of police, watched on live television as a hijacked jet slammed into the other tower.
“We couldn’t believe it,” she told me. “And then it just started like a tumbling effect (with Washington and Shanksville). I can remember going outside and looking up in the sky, and it was this eerie feeling, the quietness of it. There were no planes in the sky, because they had grounded all the planes.”
Wichita is 60 miles by road to the northeast, and normally there would be commercial jets approaching or departing the national airport there.
Crowe struggled to explain what had happened to her children, an 11-year-old boy and a 10-year-old girl. They had watched the news at school and were frightened.
“For several days, we made pallets on the floor and slept together,” she said. “How do you explain it to them? I said there are some people in the world that are bad people and want to hurt others. It was hard to explain to them why, because I didn’t know. Why did it happen?”
Twenty-five years on, a library of books have been written trying to answer why. The facts give us the what but barely touch the why: Three hijacked commercial aircraft, part of a coordinated terrorist attack by al-Qaida, a Muslim militant group founded by Osama bin Laden, were flown into the World Trade Center towers in New York and the Pentagon at Washington, D.C. A fourth hijacked aircraft, United Airlines Flight 93, believed to be headed for either the White House or the U.S. Capitol, crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers who had been alerted to the previous attacks rushed the cockpit.
All told, it was the deadliest single day of terror attacks on American soil, with 2,977 dead, including the 19 hijackers who committed murder-suicide. Most of the victims died in New York, included 343 firefighters. But the numbers don’t reflect the first responders and others who died of illness related to toxin exposure at the trade center site.
Donna Crowe, a lifelong resident of Anthony, points to soil from the Flight 93 crash site, as incorporated into the town’s 9/11 memorial. Below the soil is a brick from the Pentagon. Crowe was chair of the committee that established the memorial. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)
The attacks kicked off the Global War on Terrorism and the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, in which some 7,000 American troops and 8,000 contractors were killed. Indirect deaths from post-9/11 wars were estimated by a Brown University report at 4.5 million.
The day after Crowe watched the second tower fall on television at the Anthony police station, Mayor John Schott came to her at the city offices and had a task for her — they were going to adopt one of the first responders who had died.
She began researching but was soon overwhelmed by the names and photographs of the firemen who had died. She made calls to New York, but didn’t find anybody who was receptive.
“That last thing they wanted,” she said, “was to answer a call from Anthony, Kansas.”
But Schott kept trying.
Schott owned the local True Value hardware store and was serving his first year as mayor. He had relocated from Southern California, where he was a mid-level manager for Pacific Bell. Although his parents had been from Anthony, they were Baptist missionaries, and he was born and raised in the Philippines. Every few years the family would come back to the area and Schott would be re-introduced to small-town life. He had fond memories of riding his bike in Anthony, going to the local swimming pool, and visiting his grandparents in nearby Manchester, Oklahoma.
Schott wanted the same experience for his kids.
In the days after 9/11, Schott called the mayor’s office in New York and was eventually referred to Ladder Company 38, in the Belmont neighborhood of the Bronx.
“So I called them,” Schott said. “And the guy who answered the phone said ‘Hang on, let me get my lieutenant.’ And Joe Huber gets on the phone and says, ‘Yeah, what do you want?’ He was very, very skeptical, and he wouldn’t give me any information until he checked some stuff out.”
Huber called back and said one of the young men at their house, Joe Spor, had recently transferred to Rescue 3 and had been killed in the collapse of the south tower. Spor left a widow and four children, ages 6 years to 9 months.
Spor, 35, had joined the FDNY in 1994. He was a handyman who did carpentry work on the side, according to Schott, and his dream was to serve in the same rescue company his fireman father had, according to his obituary. The special operations rescue companies, of which there are only five, are the elite of the New York fire department.
Six others from Rescue 3 also died in the collapse.
Now that 25 years separates us from that Tuesday morning in September, the events have taken on the patina of history. At my elbow I have five books about the attacks, including a paperback copy of the official report of the 9/11 Commission, and all of them seem remote now, as do the histories we have here at home on the Vietnam War.
But there is one image that still conveys the terror and disorientation of the day, and that is the photo of the “Falling Man” by Associated Press photographer Richard Drew. Captured head-down in his tumble from the north tower, the unidentified man is seconds away from death. The image, at first denounced for its insensitivity, has become recognized as one of the most human images to come from the tragedy.
It not only conveys the plight of the doomed, but the sickening feeling of witnesses unable to help.
The Engine Company 88, Ladder Company 38 firehouse was built in 1908 and reamins in use today in the Belmont neighborhood of the Bronx. It has been designated a historic landmark by the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission. (Photo from NYC Landmark Preservation Commission)
Both Schott and Crowe said they were driven by a motivation to do something — to do anything — . The only thing they could do was to raise money, so they organized bake sales and other community events. But Schott said it really wasn’t about the money, or the Christmas gifts that went to the Spor children. The money represented support, an effort from one tiny community in Kansas to connect in a meaningful way with the greatest of American cities that had suffered an unimaginable tragedy.
Huber, and other firefighters from Ladder 38, would eventually come to Anthony, to talk with the grade school children and attend ceremonies and make new friends. The school kids would make the firefighters Valentine’s Day cards and send them cookies.
“We just really became close to this day,” Crowe said. “I talk to (Huber) and other fireman every year on Sept. 11.”
For the memorial at the city park, Schott showed the same determination he had in finding Spor. Through Huber, he located some of the World Trade Center steel, and with the help of the national True Value cooperative managed to have it shipped to Anthony. A local artist, Sam Beam, made the design for how the pieces would be displayed, and welder Howard Hatfield put it together.
From a friend who worked at the Pentagon, Schott obtained a 250-pound limestone block from the Pentagon, and from another source received dirt and ashes from the Shanksville crash site. The block and the Shanksville material are displayed in the base of the monument.
Schott, who was mayor from 2001 to 2005 and now lives in Wichita, doesn’t remember how much money was collected for the Red Cross or Spor’s family, but he said the cost for the memorial was $80,000. All of it was raised through donations, he said, including the sale of bricks at the monument. Crowe became chair of the memorial committee, and Schott was its motor. The work, Schott said, made demands on him that at times felt uncomfortable.
“Actually, I’m an introvert,” Schott said. “It goes against everything in my body to do something public like that. But I grew up in a family that believed very strongly that you were put on this earth for a purpose. You do what you can, and what you can do is help other people.”
At an event at the Anthony memorial to commemorate the anniversary, Schott is expected to give a speech. He said he didn’t yet know what he was going to say, but that he would probably include a recitation of a Jewish prayer of remembrance. But what he really wanted to talk about was how, on 9/11, America was united.
“That’s not the case anymore,” he said. “What needs to happen is that we need to get back to understanding the golden rule, to respect and honor others, to reach out and help people when we are able.”
While the community came together to make the memorial a reality, Schott said, it wasn’t without internal soul-searching.
“In a small town this remote from New York or Pennsylvania or Washington, the question that came up a lot was, ‘Why?’ Why should we do a memorial? The simple answer is so that our children are able to feel, touch, and see actual pieces of what happened that day, so they won’t forget. There is evil in the world, but good people stand up and do something.”
Schott said the families of those who died on Sept. 11 need to know that their loved ones have not been forgotten, even 25 years later.
Crowe agreed.
“The connection, it’s terrible, it’s such a horrific ordeal that brought New York and Anthony together,” she said. “I just don’t want people to forget.”
There will be speeches at Memorial Park here, not just this month but in the years to come. There will be talk of patriotism and heroes, and candidates for public office will use the memorial as a backdrop for their own ambition. But with luck, the park will remain a place where, as the September sun dips low in the sky, one can contemplate the nature of sacrifice, compassion and the challenge of living in difficult times.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The longest commute
description: It seems only fitting on this, the 25th anniversary of the attacks that we remember those Connecticut commuters who perished.
text:
No single event in my lifetime had a greater impact than 9/11.  And for veteran commuters it is still fresh in their minds.  So I asked them to share some of those memories, excerpted below (longer remembrances can be found here).



Wrote one commuter: 
“I was just entering my office at 48th and Madison Avenue when building security told me that a plane had struck the World Trade Center. At first, I thought he must have been referring to a Cessna or some other small plane hitting a tower by accident.  It was only when I got upstairs to my office that I could see down Madison Avenue to the smoke rising from one of the towers.”  
After the attack, subway and train service was suspended, leaving commuters to get home via Grand Central Terminal on their own.
Another commuter’s recollection:
 “When we were finally able to leave the building I headed directly to Grand Central. It was still locked down and a crowd of people were waiting to get in to take a train out of the city. When they did let the crowd in I went to the front car. I remember the car had police in the front of the car and when we started to move through the tunnel to exit the terminal the police and engineer were looking at the tracks.  I didn’t understand why until later when it was explained to me that there were concerns that bombs had been placed in the tunnel. The train was so quiet and my last memory was a man in the car in a suit covered in grayish/ white dust.”  
And from another rider… 
“As the trains filled up, they left Grand Central Terminal.  I remember sitting across the aisle on the train back home from a guy who was wearing suit pants and an undershirt covered in soot, dirt, and smoke. He must have started the day with a jacket and tie, but lost them along the way. He talked a little about his experience trying to get out of the Wall Street area and said how many people were in distress and how he had stopped to help some as he made his way uptown. There were so many unsung heroes from that day who simply stopped to help others in need. I think that’s how he lost his jacket, shirt, and tie.”
And from a Stamford commuter…
“The commute back from Manhattan to Stamford that day was quite eerie. Although business had immediately shut down, it took a while for Grand Central Terminal to be secured and reopened. Once it did, the walk to the terminal was eerily quiet. When we pulled in to Stamford Station, the taxi staging area was filled with ambulances.”
Retired Captain Thom Lombard from the Stamford Police Department remembers:
“On September 11 I was the Emergency Management Director for Stamford. We were notified that remains of victims would be brought to Stamford.  I made arrangements for the use of refrigerated trucks and enlisted the assistance of local funeral directors to store remains in their facilities.  All but one agreed to assist.  No bodies were recovered (that day).”
But the pain of 9-11 didn’t end that day, as David Parent of Wallingford recounts: 
“What I remember most was what I never saw: the family and friends who had to go to the train station parking lots to retrieve the cars of loved ones who were never coming home.”
“Connecticut Explored” magazine’s Fall 2026 issue contains photos of some of the memorials to 9-11 in our state, including a discreet plaque at the Glenbrook Station honoring Sean Rooney who died in the south tower after climbing stairs to try to reach the roof hoping for rescue, which never came.  
And in Westport at Sherwood Island State Park is a more impressive, black granite memorial with 161 names, many of them commuters.
In Sherwood Island State Park is the Living Memorial for the 161 people with ties to Connecticut who los their lives in the 9/11 attacks.  Credit: Luke G. Boyd, Connecticut Explored Magazine / Connecticut Explored Magazine
It seems only fitting on this, the 25th anniversary of the attacks that we remember those Connecticut commuters who perished.  Let’s keep them and all of their loved ones in our thoughts this week.
Special thanks to Connecticut Explored magazine and photographer Luke G. Boyd.
